To: Georgeanne Kennedy <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>
Subject: How's it going?

HI Squeej,

I've been saying to myself for a couple of weeks now, "I should write 
Gigi and ask her how things are going with her."

So... How's it going?

Over here, we're hanging in. We're worried about the delta variant, 
particularly because Brit's doctor has told her specifically NOT to get 
the vaccine -- it might make things much worse for her.

As it is, Brit will be heading back to LA to see an eye doctor at UCLA 
because in the past several weeks she's noticed two very troubling 
things: her hearing has gotten worse and her eyesight has gotten worse.  
A good retinal doctor here in Vegas detected signs of thinning in the 
optic nerve.  Not good.  Brit took the news in stride.  She's hoping 
that it's Usher's Type 3 because then she'll have a diagnosis.  It also 
helps that the eye doctor in UCLA has seen her before, willingly calls 
*her* and is also the guy who originally determined the existence of 
Usher's Type 3. Anyway, we cross fingers.  In the meantime, Brit has got 
hearing aids and loves being able to hear things she didn't notice for 
the past five years -- like being able to hear her nails tapping on things.

I am busy writing a sequel to a novel I just completed.  The first 
novel, RAW SPACE, is out with alpha readers.  You know, nothing out of 
the ordinary, just a space opera where someone has planted zombie sex 
bugs on the Fleet's laundry ship ;)

I hope you're doing well.

Love,

Todd

Write an email in my voice.
To: [REDACTED_EMAIL]
Subject: News of the Todd

Hi Geoff,

As usual your Xmas missive beat my vague "I should write Geoff" by a 
long shot.

Congratulations on being a double grandfather!  And you got to see them 
both!  All good.

You know, for years now it's struck me that you have a marvelously 
humorous writing style.  If you ever thought of picking up a new hobby, 
writing humorous pieces would be a boon to the world.

Naturally, I've been reading a fair bit.  Writing a lot less than normal 
because of the "covid cloud."

This whole thing with the soon-to-be ex-President is rather appalling.  
I wish someone would provide us with quantified data on how much the 
Russians influenced the 2016 election.  We know they worked at it just 
as we know they worked to help the Leave part of Brexit (which will go 
down in history as just as major a self-inflicted wound as our 2016 
elections).

I've signed up for a lot of Domestika online art classes. I'm taking one 
on Photoshop and, despite years of experience, I am learning things 
about Photoshop that I didn't know.  I've signed up for the Advanced 
Photoshop course by the same instructor, as well as a nice class on 
cover design by a German woman who speaks passable English.

The twins -- my writing partners -- are both still alive which, given 
what's been going on with Brit (the alpha of the two) and her health is 
actually saying quite a lot.  We think the root problem for her is some 
sort of auto-immune disease but we haven't got it down to specifics. Her 
hemiplegic migraines are nearly synonymous with strokes (sigh).  She's a 
tough lady but these past four years have been physically exhausting for 
her.  What seems to be helping most now is an acupuncturist who is using 
herbals to calm her nerves (literally, nice big needles go to nerve nexi).

I'm thinking that "this too shall pass" and we'll see the end of the 
COVID tunnel but perhaps not fully until 2022 (sigh).  Our ancestors 
survived much worse... although that's scant comfort.

One thing I have grown to realize is how incredibly powerful an 
individual human being is.  Take Greta Thunberg as an example. In fact, 
take anyone who decides that they will change things (Rosa Parks, the 
students in Tienanmen Square).  I wonder why we fail to use our strength 
so often?  Is it because changing the world is pretty consuming passion 
and we choose to avoid it?

I also am in shock that too many of my fellow countrymen (and women) are 
willing to accept a con man for President and cede unto him all the 
powers of a dictator.  I really have a hard time adjusting to how *dumb* 
these people are.  It makes me very sad.

I recall reading an article not too long ago praising some young black 
kids for their genius IQs. It wasn't the color of their skin that 
intrigued me -- it was that one of the kids scored a 142 on the 
Stanford-Binet IQ test.  I scored a 156 at the same age.  That made it 
really strike home that I am genius (gush, shucks, folks!).  I have 
always held the belief that everyone on this planet is as empowered as I 
am; that given the right set of circumstances, they could accomplish 
whatever they set their minds to, that we were universal in our 
potential.  Now, with the whole mess of the last four years, I have to 
question that and that has been causing me a great deal of angst.

Television-wise, I am now particularly spoiled.  I acquired a marvelous 
ASUS 34" ProArt curved monitor which now graces my desk in my bedroom.  
Over the holidays I acquired a Amazon Roku Firestick and discovered that 
I can pipe TV signals through my HDMI2 port.  So I've been getting 4k TV 
from 18 inches. Whew!

I've been watching the new Star Trek Discovery.  The first season nearly 
killed it for me because every episode pretty much stopped dead when the 
Klingons came on.  Season Two was better and now Season Three is quite 
enjoyable (forgiving such complete inanity as "parasitic ice").

I watched the Mandolorian with a skeptical eye particularly as so much 
of it was just pure re-cast western. And there was one episode that 
stopped me for weeks but I was assured that things got better.

I've also been re-watching Dr. Who, starting with Eccleston who was such 
a marvelous Doctor.  I'm sorry he couldn't stick around longer (but 
maybe he would have gone stale).

Anyway, that's a taste of life at Dell Ridge.

Always glad to hear from you, my oldest friend!

Love,

Todd

Subject: Crime Assign #2

**

*Actually, holiday crime stories aren’t something I think much about.  I 
had to do a search online just to get ideas.*

*

The was one d’ohthat came back:

How the Grinch Stole Christmasby Dr. Seuss (aka, Theodor Seuss 
Geissel).  The basic story is a heist reneged: the Grinch decides to 
steal all of Christmas from the town of Who-ville, figuring that the 
Whos will all be sad.  When the deed is complete and yet stillthey 
celebrate, he learns the true meaning of Christmas, repents, and returns 
the gifts.  This is a feel-good story.

As I thought about it more, I realized that Harry Potter and the 
Philosopher’s (Sorcerer’s, US) Stoneby J.K. Rowling is alsoa Christmas 
crime story.  In fact, multiple crimes are attempted, several 
committed.  At Christmas, Harry receives mysteriously an invisibility 
cloak which enables him to perform many capers and ultimately to track 
down the criminal who wants to steal the philosopher’s stone.  At which 
point, Lord Voldemort, co-inhabiting the body of Professor Quirrell, 
attempts murder.  Harry survives.  This is another example of a 
feel-good story.

The next book, Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secretsis also holiday 
related (Halloween), as is the fourth (Harry Potter and the Goblet of 
Fire) which reprises the Yule holiday.  And, of course, all the books 
involve unsuccessful attempts to murder Harry Potter.

And, just now, I realized that an old favorite, Donna Andrews’ Murder 
with Peacocks,centers upon three weddings and a murder.  This is another 
example of murder and attempted murder. Also an example of a feel-good 
story.*

To: [REDACTED_EMAIL]
Subject: Op-Ed: How I didn't become a racist

**

*How I didn’t become a racist*

*

By Todd McCaffrey, BSME, MFA, SFWA, New York Times Bestselling author

I think it’s important to understand America’s underlying inclination 
toward racism. It doesn’t just come from our parents. It comes from our 
community, our society, from the people we grow up with.

I am an alien, so I think my point of view may be helpful. When I say 
I’m an alien, I’m an alien in Ireland: where I lived for my high school 
and college years. I describe myself as “mid-Atlantic and sinking.”

My journey toward racism started in late elementary and early middle 
school, before I moved to Ireland.

I moved to Long Island, New York, in time to enter third grade. The 
school was small and the community tight-knit. There were only two black 
kids in the whole school — they were brothers, a year apart. Nice guys. 
The younger one had a small bit of iris detached in the white of his eye 
which amazed everyone who saw it.  I remember constantly asking to look 
at it — it was just so cool!

My parents were determined to raise broad-minded children and when the 
chance came, introduced us to people from all  over the world, including 
a Nigerian who stayed the weekend with us, arriving in the marvelously 
bright Nigerian native clothing.

Still, in school hallways, there were the whispers. That blacks would 
beat kids up, that you couldn’t trust them.

This whispering became more apparent in middle school and I think, had 
it not been for my relocation to Ireland, that background whispering 
would have lodged firmly in my mind.

But, barring that lingering underlayer of fear, I like to think that the 
full implant of racism didn’t take with me.  And I think that’s because 
of my time in Ireland… and two people in particular.

In Ireland my classmates said: “I hate all Yanks!” to which was hastily 
added, “But not you, I know you.”  Such statements are examples of 
prejudice and bigotry. It was my first experience of prejudice directed 
at me.

The two people who broke the back of racism for me were strangers.  One 
was a classmate, the other an actor.

We’ll take the second first.  He is Lenny Henry — now SirLenny Henry.  
He is a black comedian. Hearing a very English accent on a black man 
broke the mold that society had tried to impose on me about black people 
— that they all spoke the same.  That was a revelation to me, a “Wait, 
what?” moment. Not all blacks are the same.  My fourteen year-old 
thinking went like this: “So… this notion that blacks are a threat or 
menace… that’s a lie!”

My second revelation came with my classmate, Obudan Obesan. Obudan, for 
me, will always be the primal proof that skin color means 
absolutelynothing!  Also, he proved that James Joyce was a second-rate 
author. I can’t remember when we read Joyce’s The Dubliners.  I’m pretty 
sure it was after I’d first been exposed to Mr. Obesan’s writing.  The 
thing is, Obudan gotthe feel of the Irish, the Dublin Irish, down pat.  
He had it better than Joyce. Waayyybetter than Joyce. Nearly fifty years 
later, my opinion has not changed.

Between Obudan and Sir Lenny Henry, I threw out that notion that black 
people were inferior.

With the benefit of hindsight, I can see how American society has a 
built-in underlying prejudice against people of color.  It starts as the 
whispers in middle grade and high school corridors: “You can’t trust 
them.” “They’ll beat you up.” It’s something that we should be aware of, 
should recognize... and banish.

Because black culture has imbued our society with somuch. Even while we 
derided it, it gave us rock’n’roll, starting with Chuck Berry. The black 
culture is more vibrant and alive than the old, tired white culture. We 
can and should learn a lot from it.  The first step is to recognize 
that. The next step is to embrace this difference, to grasp it and learn 
from it. Our society will grow stronger when we do.

*

But I gotta say... if you're rebuilding a country, don't start
 with outdated systems.  Dams, locks, bridges... why?

Dams I can see for flood prevention and energy generation but I
 don't see why the ideal should be re-inventing what existed before
 -- the trick is to step BEYOND that.  Again, the lack of
 population is going to demand labor-saving at all levels,
 particularly in agriculture (farming).  You aren't going back to
 the old ways, they won't work (they require a much larger
 population).  You've got to think smart, and different.

Solar and wind power are available (and the Dutch have been using
 windmills for centuries).

Why rebuild a road infrastructure?  Why not revitalize rails? 
 Why not automate rail transport, using roll-on-roll-off containers
 and automated movement systems?  And, for that matter, how much
 cargo is there to move?

The biggest issue is population sustenance and growth.  The US
 build up so well because there was a flood of immigration.  This
 time would be very different.

Is there conversation group for this?  One of my pet peeves is
 the desire to build a self-managed medical system.  You've a
 dearth of doctors, instead of following the old Johns Hopkins
 hyper-perfectionist model why not develop home-use systems that
 allow people to mostly tend to themselves?

 localized systems are possibly best (I can it "a farm in a box"),

 Guyana?  Did SpaceX do a "soft landing"? (I'd think so, Musk is a

 anticipate the level of destruction leveled by the virus.  The
 younger, more nimble corporations were better suited to handling

How much do you want me to lead and how much do you want me to

To: Amelia Johnson <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>
Subject: Memories of your Dad and stuff

*

Hi Amelia,

Here's a quick partial brain dump to give you some more info about who 
your Dad is. Feel free to share with Eliza. I'll write more as I get the 
time. (I'm still REALLY sad about Chadwick Boseman - his is a great loss.)

We grew up in several locations in the US, all in the northeast:

 1.

 Montclair, NJ.  I left when I was two and have no memories.

 2.

 100 Danforth Place, Windybush, Wilmington, Delaware

 1.

 With one interruption, we lived there from the time I was 2
 (1958) until we moved to 369 Carpenter Ave., Sea Cliff, Long
 Island, NY in 1965

 3.

 369 Carpenter Avenue, Sea Cliff, Long Island, New York

 1.

 We lived there from 1965 until we (Gigi, Mum, and I) moved to
 Ireland in 1970

 4.

 In Ireland (just to continue the record), we first lived in:

 1.

  14 North Avenue, Mount Merrion (1970-71)

 2.

 Meadowbrook House, Dundrum (1971-72)

 1.

 Alec joined us there and became a trawler fisherman.

 3.

 Site 11 Rochestown Avenue (1972-73)

 1.

 Alec wasn’t here

 4.

 79 Shanganagh Vale, Cabinteely (1[REDACTED_PHONE]?)

 1.

 Nor was Alec here.

 5.

 Dragonhold, Kilquade, Co. Wicklow (1[REDACTED_PHONE])

 1.

 He visited here occasionally

 6.

 From there, Mum moved into Dragonhold-Underhill and lived there
 until she died in 2011.

I have many memories of Alec, some of which are great and some of which 
are not.

When we were in 100 Danforth, we all got kittens: Tasso (Alec), Tallabar 
(me), and Silkie Blackington (for Gigi with much adult supervision in 
the naming else the cat would have been simply “Blackie”).

Tasso was a tortoise shell.  He lost an argument with a car not long 
after we got him. Alec was devastated.

Tallabar was a multi-color, a mix of grays and oranges.  Quite the 
pretty cat.

Silkie was your average black cat.  She was sweet and her fur was very 
soft, hence the name.

Silkie and Tallabar went on to have many, many litters.  Tallabar was 
good at producing orange marmalade cats.

We also had dogs, starting with Wizard (a German Shepherd) followed by 
his son, Merlin.  Wiz decided that I was his human charge. We had a 
sloping hill outside our front door and it went down to join the street 
which formed part of the branches of a tee-junction (the other street 
tee’d into Danforth Place).  Wiz decided that I was not allowed to go 
down that hill when I was an infant and took to blocking me.

Our next door neighbors (to our left as you’re standing in the front 
door looking out) were the Estes.  Larry Estes was Alec’s age.  I think 
their daughter was close to Gigi’s age.  Alec and Larry hung out and I 
did my best to tag along, often successfully.

There was another housing estate being built across the railroad tracks 
beyond a small woods at the edge of Windybush and we used to trek there 
many a  time. The woods had some pretty decent undergrowth. One day 
Larry got a hold of his father’s machete (from WWII) and he and Alec 
took turns “clearing” the underbrush (think Indiana Jones in South 
America at the beginning of Raiders of the Lost Ark).  I must have been 
around six.  At one point Alec told me to stand back.  I did but, 
apparently, not far enough and the machete tore into my shin.  I think 
it was Alec who carried me back to the house. I went to the ER and got 
four stitches.

Another  time, when I was eight or so, we had a particularly hard but 
dry winter.  It was decided to go exploring (“mountain climbing”?) in 
the culverts at the upper side of the estate.  Alec had brought a hammer 
along to poke holes in the ice as handholds.  He told me (seems to be a 
pattern here) to get back and swung immediately after I said, “Okay” but 
before I could comply (well, that’s my story) and I got the claws of the 
hammer hitting my head -- just on the eye socket.  A bit lower and I 
would have lost the eye.  As it was, I got two stitches without novocaine.

Ah, the good years!

Alec and I fought often enough that I have many recollections of 
variously being forced to eat grass or dirt to escape being buried under 
him.

In 1962 we moved to Dusseldorf, Germany for six months because Dad had a 
job doing PR work for DuPont that required him to work there.  Overall, 
it was a marvelous experience.  Alec, Gigi, and I were all very 
nordic-looking and, when we didn’t speak, had no trouble passing for 
German (Dad’s family had roots in Schleswig-Holstein on the 
German-Danish border).  Mum place Alec and I in the local German 
school.  I can’t say how well Alec did but I flourished, having a 
teacher who could speak English (she was raised in England during the 
war) and I learned excellent “gekauft Deutsch” -- as Mum called it 
(“shopping German”).

We all adored the chocolate over there.  We took the tram everywhere, 
un-parented.  I recall once having some old Frau look at us and scoff, 
“Ach, Englander!” to which I replied, “Nein, Amerikaner!” -- that seemed 
to both affront and appease her, somewhat (the English had ruled the 
area after the war and weren’t particularly good at it).

They had these marvelous parades where they’d throw candy.  We all loved 
that.

We got a VW station wagon while we were over there and, when our time 
was up, drove around Europe (France, Germany, Holland, at least).  We 
took the ferry to England.  We were broke, so we camped one night all in 
the VW and discovered later the next day that we’d stopped outside an 
insane asylum.  We dropped the car off for transport to the States and 
headed to Gatwick airport (Heathrow was not then built), only to 
discover that there was some tax that we still had to pay before we 
could board the flight back.  This caused the parents immense distress 
until a nice American couple, hearing the panic, loaned us the money 
(there were Texans).

*

what's the docker command to exec a bash on web?

To open a bash shell in your running web service container via Docker Compose, use:

```bash
docker compose exec web bash
```

- `exec` = execute a command in a running container
- `web` = the name of the service in your `docker-compose.yaml` (adjust if yours is different)
- `bash` = the shell you want to start (use `sh` if your image doesn’t have bash)

If you get an error like `No such container`, make sure your containers are running (`docker compose up -d`), and the service is actually named `web`.

Example full workflow:
```bash
docker compose up -d Start containers in the background
docker compose exec web bash
```

The time difference between Las Vegas, Nevada (Pacific Time Zone) and London, England (Greenwich Mean Time or GMT) depends on the time of year due to daylight saving changes:

. Standard Time (November–March): London is hours ahead of Las Vegas.
 - Example: If it's : PM in Las Vegas, it's : PM in London.

. Daylight Saving Time (March–November): London observes British Summer Time (BST), which is GMT+. This makes London hours ahead of Las Vegas.

Las Vegas also observes daylight saving time, so the shift between the two locations changes in sync during the year.

She turned her head up, saying, “You’re getting married and I will give your bride away.” Captain Owami Branford met her friend’s eyes and nodded. “It’ll be good for morale.” “Fuck morale,” Chelly told her fiercely. “I want to see you two married. Clone sisters. I want them all with me.” “But just for a bit,” Owami cautioned. “Long enough to hug and love,” Rochelle agreed. She sighed. “But then we’ll have to separate again.” Her eyes took a distant look but Owami knew where she was: She was in orbit, above Nouveau Franconia, looking down as it fractured, as three billion people died horribly, without warning. “We have to disperse. For safety.” “No one could have known --” Owami began again to assure Chelly that there was nothing she could have done. “But we should have,” Rochelle declared. She was still Princess Rochelle, because she hadn’t yet been crowned queen. That should have been in the Royal Cathedral, just outside the Royal Palace, with all due pomp and ceremony but... there was no Cathedral. No Palace. No planet. She shook herself and took a breath. “Go on, Owami, stretch out the paw of friendship.” Owami smiled at her, closed her eyes and stretched out her hand. A moment later, she pulled Ophelia Branford into the boat bay. Ophelia had one arm wrapped around a small bundle and the other arm pulled Millisor Rau behind her.

They still persisted in dressing how they pleased, working their own hours, and torching any red tape that stood between them and the requirements of the job. Commander Emily Steele's original disdain for the 'undisciplined', 'sloppy' her own words engineer had changed to grudging acceptance as she noticed, working closely, Mac's meticulous attention to detail and extreme dedication to the job. "Yeah, I'm careful, Captain. I live right next door to the storage tanks," Mac had retorted when Steele had first mentioned it. Steele's opinion had improved steadily through the tense periods leading up to Voyager's first flight as Mac had stomped on any brass attempting to shorten the ground test phase. "Admiral, you can order these tests skipped," Mac had said in tones just short of violent, "but it'll be an order I won't obey." As the Admiral had prepared an indignant response, Mac had added: "Nor will any other of my engineers. We'll shut you down." "She's the oldest cruiser in the Navy and her captain's almost older," Nick grumbled by way of bragging. Captain Adrian Wardlaw was nearly two hundred years old, had seen combat with the old Pevencee pirates, and was famous for his refusal to accept higher rank or retirement. As he'd been personal friends with the first King and known the current King when he was only in diapers, there was no one who would tell him otherwise. His ship was also the command ship for the Home Fleet which put him at the beck and call of Admiral Omicron Katzelos – though it was rumored that it was mostly the other way around. Ophelia recalled only that her mother never said anything about the Home Fleet's admiral, and that all she'd heard in the Academy was that the admiral was "a great administrator." And now, Queen Rochelle held up the first crown for all to see -- both in the crowd and on vids. “This royal crown was commissioned from the master jeweler of Mantanzas, Philippe de Cuesta,” Queen Rochelle said loudly. She lowered the crown back onto its velvet casque and moved to the second crown and raised it with the same flourish. She beckoned to Princess Lux who moved forward, curtsied, and took the proffered crown. Rochelle moved back to the first crown and lifted it. Together the two moved to stand behind Clio and Alara. Four young girls moved in pairs beside them. With a smile, Rochelle surrendered her crown to one pair while Lux surrendered her crown to the other pair -- the four Smileys. “People of Penzance,” Rochelle said loudly, “I give you Queen Clio.” And June and July crowned Clio. “And I am equally proud to crown you, Queen Alara,” Crown Princess Lux added, as May and August lowered the second crown on Alara’s head. Trumpets blared loudly, marking the accession of the two to the Thrones of Penzance. When the flourish ended, Queen Clio and Queen Alara rose and nodded their royal heads to the cheering crowd. The royal procession, led by the two new queens, moved regally down the aisle and out to the royal carriages where they were paraded about the capital of Tortuga, their progress cheered by crowds and relayed by eager reporters. # Two hours later, they repaired to their royal quarters -- the palace being still very much under construction -- shedding guards as they moved further and further into their apartments.

Karl shook his head. Elodie hissed her displeasure. A beep from the main Comm console distracted them. Elodie glanced over at the telltale light, deftly called up a window on their main display and pointed to the stream of numbers: "See? Code groups." Karl glanced at them and grunted. Her eyes traveled over me critically. She was unsatisfied. She hobbled over to me and slid the leather strap of my necklace under my shirt. Ashamed, I lowered my eyes. She hobbled back to her place. Master's rules on the strap that held the small leather bag around my neck were strict: in company I was to keep it hidden; in private I was to display it at all times on penalty of whipping -- or worse. A bell rang inside the study and my Master's voice boomed out, "Send her in." I shot a glance to my mother. I could see that she wanted to accompany me. Instead, she limped back a step or two. I raised my head and nodded, as I was taught, to my Master, and walked into the study. My mother, emboldened, followed on my tail. "Can I bring anything?" Master frowned at her impertinence but waved her away. "I'll ring if I need." "Sir," Mother said, lowering her head and retreating, carefully closing the doors with an audible click. Inside, I stood waiting. The Captain was seated with his back to me but he craned his neck around for a moment before languidly returning his gaze to the big table to which my Master returned. "Step closer," Master ordered, as he sat down, "so the Captain can see you." I did as told, calming my breath as taught even though inside I was trembling. Was I to be sold? Would I never see my mother again? Why else would I be here? Master Evans loudly proclaimed to any who would listen that he raised "good horses and passable slaves, preferring mares in both." It was only recently that he'd decided to branch out. "I had not thought she'd be so tall," the captain said after a moment, his eyes still traveling over me. I had suffered such looks before; they made my stomach queasy. "She's well-fed," my Master replied, adding with a chuckle, "comes from good stock." "Was that her mother?"

That being the case, Ophelia had discounted the veracity of his previous pronouncement: undoubtedly it contained a certain amount of prevarication. The sort of thing that non-psychiatrists might call "lies." In childhood, Owami and Milly had hung out quite a bit. Ophelia had found herself and Sebastian occasionally joining in on their adventures or being cast in the position of opposing forces – there were always opposing forces in their games – until Millisor hit adolescence. And then he changed. Oh, Owami had already changed somewhat; Ophelia had looked at the whole coming of maturity with a mixture of concern and curiosity but, for Millisor Rau, the dark day probably came shortly after Ophelia had consumed the books from which her friend acquired his name. It was around then, too, that 'Milli' transformed into 'Milly' – with all the masculine-challenging overtones thoroughly explored, expounded, and exploited. That at least, hadn't been the fault of the girls but rather of the school at large, particularly the boys who suddenly found themselves in competition with a dark-haired, blue-eyed gorgeous adolescent. Chapter One The sun was rising on our east as I spotted the barns of the manufacturies, smoke rising from their chimneys. Beyond them was our barn and, to the left, was the landing ‘T’. Only the torches were dim in the morning light and I could make out the smudge that was our carrier. Dart -- bless her! -- had valiantly risen to a full two thousand feet in our five hours’ flight in return. She had done it slowly, sometimes reluctantly, and occasionally dipping back downwards, as if reconsidering her disposition. But here we were. “Charles, if you look to your right you may spot some of the buildings that may become precious to you,” I called. I hadn’t heard from him in a while although once or twice I thought I heard snores. He would be the very first person to sleep on an airship, to my best knowledge. “Be careful, the sun’s rising on that side!” “Oh, indeed it is!” he called back a moment later. “Quite the glory it has, too! And, yes, I see some buildings below. Would you care to enlighten me as to their purpose?” “I believe that the owner would do a better job of that, if you’d permit,” I replied. “The famous Lieutenant Clarke of whom I have heard so much, perhaps?” he replied. “Also, no disrespect to your fine vessel, Captain, but I do wish it had a head.” “If you’re desperate,” I said, thinking quickly. “As you’re a man, you could probably just go over the side.” He was silent for a moment. “And I won’t rock the deck too much?” “Move slowly, keeping the stay line tied around you and stop at a safe distance from the edge,” I cautioned. “I would not, under normal circumstances, engage in any such activity -- will I be the first?” “That I can guarantee,” I told him, my own bladder now questioning the prudence of my gender. “Well,” he said, untying himself with a tone of relish in his voice, “you know, I always fancied the notion of peeing on England.” As he rose and the deck ducked, he added, “Scotland, on the other hand…” He moved closer to the edge and undid himself.

“We’ll be under way soon,” Captain Morton allowed. “Put your things where you can, stay out of my way, and try not to get sick.” “Yes suh.” # But it was not me who got sick. Even though the good captain had crossed the Atlantic once already, he was not a good seaman. Not at all. For the first four days I spent my time cleaning up his spew and doing what I could to ensure that he would reach England alive. I did not like the man. That did not mean that I didn’t have sympathy for him. In turn -- to my surprise -- the good captain was grateful for everything I did to succor him. I refused to shave him, however. Not because I couldn’t but because I feared the seas were too high and it might cause me to cut him more than his beard. When I explained, he relented. I had less luck in finding food for the both of us. The captain could keep nothing substantial down. I knew enough of illness and sickness to know that bread and water were his best sustenance, the thick porridge that was standard fair would be too rich for his tender stomach. The cook refused to serve me at all, at first. “You’re to eat with your master, girl!” he had declared. “Don’t need more shade here than we’ve got!” To my surprise and gratitude, Thompson interceded, telling the cook, “Her master is with the Admiralty, fool! If he doesn’t get back home alive, who do you think they’ll blame?” “Not me!” Cookie had cried. “No,” Thompson agreed, “not you. The captain.” The cook’s eyes widened as the notion sank into what must have been a very small brain. “And then what? Or do you like the press gang so much? Want to get back on a real man-o-war, do ye?” Thompson scowled at him. “Looking forward to a taste of the cat, are ye?” “No, damn ye!” Cookie said. He glared at me and pulled up a couple of biscuits, throwing them at me. I caught them awkwardly and nodded to him. “Thank you sir! My master thanks you, too!” “Bah!” Cookie swore. But I think he looked pleased anyway.

Chapter One "Sir, there's a mistake with my orders," Midshipwoman Ophelia Branford said, holding out her hard-copy orders to the Academy's Personnel Officer, Lieutenant Commander Madsen. With a grunt, Madsen flicked out a hand for her orders, put them on the desk in front of him and scanned them quickly before handing them back to her. "No, those are the right orders," Madsen said. "But these orders assign me to Sparkle." Lieutenant Commander Madsen raised his head for a moment, as if to confirm the identity of the whining newly-minted officer, sighed, and tapped a quick inquiry into his tablet. "You requested an engineering assignment," Madsen said, as he perused the tablet. "Sparkle has put in a request for an engineer. The computers made the match. You have your orders." He glanced up at her again. "I fail to see where there is a problem." He bit his lips before adding, with a twinkle in his eye, "Unless you are complaining about the ship." His Majesty's Auxiliary Ship Sparkle, in all honesty, was a glorified freighter. Her crew was a strange conglomeration of the traditional "dregs of the Navy" and assorted misfits, odd-balls, and those unfortunate enough to have earned the displeasure of their Lordships in some way. Her armaments were a few targeting lasers, a pair of missile tubes to deal with any asteroids or comets that might stray unavoidably in her path, and a pair of outdated mine-launchers that were added as a convenient way of hiding an accidental over-supply of the same by some unfortunate Ordnance Acquisition Officer who was later discovered to have financial relations with the selling company. On the other hand, for all her lack of speed, grandeur, and general sexiness, Sparkle was a busy ship, on a busy schedule and deemed a vital naval asset. Unlike her sister ship, Gleam, which provided the far-spread Fleet with ordnance and general supplies, Sparkle was tasked with more mundane but no less essential duties. To whit, she was the laundry ship for the Navy, or, as her commissioning orders read, "To provide fresh accouterments and auxiliary materials for naval personnel."

Ophelia caught herself quickly, "I imagine the captain wants us to be prepared for anything." "It's customary that the officer in charge of midshipmen be the assistant tactical officer," Ensign Rau reminded her. "Or perhaps you weren't aware?" "Sorry, sir," Ophelia said, telling herself to control her temper and mind her words, "I had assumed that as a fleet auxiliary ship our tactical control would be under fleet command." Under certain circumstances, Ophelia's mind would go racing off to conclusions that seemed quite logical to her but quite impossible for others. This, apparently, was one of those circumstances. In rapid order she determined that Ensign Millisor Rau had doubtless been appointed midshipman to Sparkle upon his delayed graduation from the Academy – he was, after all, only a year younger than her sister – probably under the aegis of the same mysterious strings that had assigned Ophelia to the same ship her sister commanded. Someone had been very devious in that assignment – for there would certainly be questions asked if Midshipman Rau failed his middy cruise aboard a ship commanded by a long-time enemy family. Not that the Branfords had started the feud, nor had the Rau's – the name of Rau hadn't even existed until Milly – er, Ensign Rau – had been hatched; the name was the result of his parent's strange decision to combine the names of two fictional villains. Valeria Lawson, his mother, had been within her rights to do so and, as a naval veteran – albeit one forced out of the service under a cloud – she was supported by her generous pension. Of course, whatever it was that got ex-Captain Lawson beached had been under the same hush-hush secrecy that covered everyone else involved with the events leading up to the Battle of Canaris. The best that the children had ever managed to wheedle out of their father – he being more easily wheedled, particularly when his daughters ganged up on him – was that Captain Valeria Lawson "had been under a great deal of stress and might have made a poor call." This information had been acquired long before the two girls were old enough to recognize their Admiral father's phenomenal ability to dissemble.

Chapter One The sun was rising on our east as I spotted the barns of the manufacturies, smoke rising from their chimneys. Beyond them was our barn and, to the left, was the landing ‘T’. Only the torches were dim in the morning light and I could make out the smudge that was our carrier. Dart -- bless her! -- had valiantly risen to a full two thousand feet in our five hours’ flight in return. But here we were. “Charles, if you look to your right you may spot some of the buildings that may become precious to you,” I called. I hadn’t heard from him in a while although once or twice I thought I heard snores. He would be the very first person to sleep on an airship, to my best knowledge. “Be careful, the sun’s rising on that side!” “Oh, indeed it is!” he called back a moment later. “Quite the glory it has, too! And, yes, I see some buildings below. Would you care to enlighten me as to their purpose?” “I believe that the owner would do a better job of that, if you’d permit,” I replied. “The famous Lieutenant Clarke of whom I have heard so much, perhaps?” he replied. “Also, no disrespect to your fine vessel, Captain, but I do wish it had a head.” “If you’re desperate,” I said, thinking quickly. “As you’re a man, you could probably just go over the side.” He was silent for a moment. “And I won’t rock the deck too much?” “Move slowly, keeping the stay line tied around you and stop at a safe distance from the edge,” I cautioned. “I would not, under normal circumstances, engage in any such activity -- will I be the first?” “That I can guarantee,” I told him, my own bladder now questioning the prudence of my gender. “Well,” he said, untying himself with a tone of relish in his voice, “you know, I always fancied the notion of peeing on England.” As he rose and the deck ducked, he added, “Scotland, on the other hand…” He moved closer to the edge and undid himself.

Chapter One The sun was rising on our east as I spotted the barns of the manufacturies, smoke rising from their chimneys. Beyond them was our barn and, to the left, was the landing ‘T’. Only the torches were dim in the morning light and I could make out the smudge that was our carrier. Dart -- bless her! -- had valiantly risen to a full two thousand feet in our five hours’ flight in return. She had done it slowly, sometimes reluctantly, and occasionally dipping back downwards, as if reconsidering her disposition. But here we were. “Charles, if you look to your right you may spot some of the buildings that may become precious to you,” I called. I hadn’t heard from him in a while although once or twice I thought I heard snores. He would be the very first person to sleep on an airship, to my best knowledge. “Be careful, the sun’s rising on that side!” “Oh, indeed it is!” he called back a moment later. “Quite the glory it has, too! And, yes, I see some buildings below. Would you care to enlighten me as to their purpose?” “I believe that the owner would do a better job of that, if you’d permit,” I replied. “The famous Lieutenant Clarke of whom I have heard so much, perhaps?” he replied. “Also, no disrespect to your fine vessel, Captain, but I do wish it had a head.” “If you’re desperate,” I said, thinking quickly. “As you’re a man, you could probably just go over the side.” He was silent for a moment. “And I won’t rock the deck too much?” “Move slowly, keeping the stay line tied around you and stop at a safe distance from the edge,” I cautioned. “I would not, under normal circumstances, engage in any such activity -- will I be the first?” “That I can guarantee,” I told him, my own bladder now questioning the prudence of my gender. “Well,” he said, untying himself with a tone of relish in his voice, “you know, I always fancied the notion of peeing on England.” As he rose and the deck ducked, he added, “Scotland, on the other hand…” He moved closer to the edge and undid himself.

"He'll have me sleep with him tonight." He would. My last night here and Master would be certain to spend it with my mother, to remind us both of our place, of the power he held over us. “Jacob, I want you to command the rescue mission,” Cody said as he started handing out major assignments. “You’ll lead Alice and Morgan Summers.”

“Okay,” Jacob said. He turned to the two older women. “We good?”

“Sure thing, Commodore,” Alice Summers told him. “You lead, we’ll follow.” Morgan Summers nodded in agreement.

“Okay, so I need you three to get out to the sims for a final rundown with your full crews,” Cody said, gesturing them out of the briefing room. Cody turned to Nora and raised an eyebrow. She nodded. “Viola, we want you to stay here on watch.”

“Yes sir,” Viola Summers said, nodding toward her crew and urging them out of the briefing room. She turned back to add, “While you all are hunting glory, we’ll be here keeping the home fires burning.”

“It’s not a slacker job,” Cody warned her. “You and your crew will be responsible for training. We expect to find thirty great ships ready to go when we get back.”

Viola nodded and followed after her crew. She was good, a better trainer than a leader. Ellaz had said of her, She always argues! Which was true, Viola liked a good argument. But Don Hartman had told Cody the secret — “Those are my orders” were magic words to Viola Summers. After that, she shut up and got down to business.

“That’s going to leave us with twenty-six ships for the attack fleet,” Dorit Williams said, rising from her chair to stand by Cody. “Admiral Ford here has split you into three groups — two groups of nine and the command group with eight.”

“We expect that to go down to twenty-five when we get to Quark,” Cody added, nodding to Captain Governor Don Hartman, “as we’ll be dispatching Captain Hartman and his crew to the planet.”

“So we’ll have one group of nine and two groups of eight,” Nora said, moving to stand beside Cody. He grinned at her. She’d won the race to lead the largest group. Everyone had agreed that she’d edged Cody out in the last test that Ellaz had thrown at them.

Recon ships were manned by the maddest of people, people hoping to find new planets or rare resources so that they could strike it rich. At least a few were cultists looking for another “promised land” but most were malcontents who preferred the vastness of space to the crowding of humankind. Cody had a certain respect for them.

This one! Cody said, pointing to the largest dot. The Maru.

A family, Ellaz told him. Five. Father, mother, three children.

That’s a light crew, Cody thought in surprise.

So is six, Other Cody reminded him.

But… warp watch! I mean, who could keep watch and —

The children were older than me, Gail replied. And they all had implants. The captain, Horace Mayhew, made a lot of money back at Quark but he also made a lot of enemies.

What else do we know about him? Cody wondered.

That’s it, Ellaz replied. There’s just not enough room in the computers for a lot of useless data. Anyway, what about the other two?

The Reliant disappeared earlier, Cody thought. But she was a solo crew. And the Doorman was later. He frowned. I don’t know. But, Ellaz, imagine if aliens stopped your ship and threatened your family unless you did what they wanted?

Why not just kill them all? Ellaz asked. Or kill some… and. Nasty.

Very nasty, Other Cody agreed.

Only if the aliens consider us worth living, Gail’s ghost thought. Sentient or whatever they would call it.

Any ship that bumped into them they’d either have to capture or destroy, Nora’s ghost added.

Which means, if that’s true, they know how to catch a ship in warp, Cody thought with a sinking feeling. I wish we’d known that earlier.

We made the best plan we could at the time, Other Cody consoled him.

And, if they don’t see us, they won’t know we’re there until we attack, Nora added.

From the rear, Gail reminded them with a wolfish grin.

So they sent out scouts and they caught these ships — or one of them — nearly two years ago, Cody thought.

Which means they’ve got a scouting shell two years ahead of them, Nora agreed.

So how many systems have they already scouted? Other Cody wondered.

“My hair’s not even dry and you want to — what?”

“I’ve just found a signal from Carlow Ships,” Cody told her with a grin. “I’m going to volunteer to check it out.”

Ellaz considered that. “Okay…” she turned back to her computers and started typing. A moment later, she turned to him with a raised eyebrow. “And…?”

“Control, this is Wasp,” Cody called over the radio. “We’ve been checking telemetry and we think we found some more survivors…”

#

Five minutes before they were due to depart, someone rapped hard on the outside airlock. Cody checked the vids. It was Bamber. There were three people behind him, including the grizzled spacer they’d rescued and one of the young girls. Cody didn’t recognize the woman standing next to Bamber.

Fuming, he gestured at Ellaz to check it out.

“They want to come with us,” Ellaz reported. “They’ve got suits.”

“And the kid?”

“She’s got a suit, too,” Ellaz replied, opening the hatch and letting them aboard.

“You’re going to need crew for the survey, Captain,” Clive Bamber said as he came into the main cabin and peered around into the cockpit. “I’ve got us four trained hands, including myself.”

Cody nodded and smiled. What else could he do? “Welcome aboard Wasp.”

“I’ve got a skinsuit and tanks,” the grizzled spacer reported.

“This is my wife, Moira Collins,” Clive said, introducing the woman behind him. “And you know the other two.”

“My daughter, Jasmine,” the willowy old spacer said. “She’s had a few EVAs and she listens.”

“Glad to have you aboard,” Ellaz said. “Secure the hatch and let’s get cleared for departure.” She scrambled back to the cockpit to join Cody, giving him a shrug. He answered with an accepting nod and went back to his preflight checklist.

They took off at a steady one gravity, they didn’t need more. Besides, it gave Cody — and Ellaz — a chance to check out their new crew. Clive Bamber was an administrator with years of experience in ground control and logistics. His wife, Moira was a trained engineer, currently assigned to keep one of the deep space dishes online but she had ship experience, being an apprentice ship’s engineer and working on construction.

“So you want to trust the fate of mankind on one ship?” Ellaz snapped.

“Okay… so what if we use the monitor?” Cody said.

“That’s tuned to the two of you,” Edie replied, taking another sip of her restorative drink. She frowned. “I suppose we could rework it for me. Or Jazzy. But…”

“Ellaz and Jasmine,” Cody said. “How do they pair?”

Edie considered that. “We can test, I suppose.” She didn’t sound enthusiastic.

They took a break for lunch and when they came back they tried all four combinations — Ellaz and Jasmine, Ellaz and Edie, Cody and Jasmine, Cody and Edie.

“The results are in,” Edie said. “Top match — Cody and Ellaz. Next, Cody and Edie, Cody and Jasmine, Edie and Ellaz, Edie and Cody.” Cody was surprised by that, thinking that he and Edie had made a better team. She made a face as she added, “I’m afraid it’s a plasticity thing — brain plasticity. I’m a bit too set in my ways to work well with anyone.”

Jasmine patted her arm consolingly. “When I get older, and we train together…?”

Edie smiled at her. “Then maybe we could work together.” She smiled at her daughter. “But I have to admit, it was great playing with you.”

“You just can’t fly a starship that way,” Ellaz murmured in a voice meant only for Cody’s ears. Then, louder, she said, “Could we make a monitor to pull you out if you fell into the Playground?”

Edie considered it. “Maybe,” she said. “But would it be fast enough? Quick enough to stop us from blowing out of warp?” She shook her head.

“Could we get more implants?” Cody asked. He waved around the room. “Isn’t this one of the places where they install them?”

“Yes,” Edie said. “But usually it’s done at a major hospital. This is just for repairs and tuning.” A moment later, she added, “And, you need trained specialists to perform the implants.”

“And it takes months for them to settle,” Ellaz added. “I had nightmares for months.”

“I still get nightmares,” Jasmine admitted.

“You do?” Edie said. “Oh, baby, you should have said! No one should ever go into a simulator with nightmares!”

“That would explain the incompatibility,” Ellaz said. “How long ago —?”

No one knew how fast the aliens could travel in warp. As it was, they’d been gone for twelve days now, and it’d be twenty-one before Hope would arrive at Deneb. At the earliest.

And there was no way that Cody could pilot the ship by himself. He glanced up as someone dropped a tray beside him. Ellaz. She gave him a nod and slumped into her chair.

“Sorry,” Ellaz said grumpily. “I’m worried. I didn’t sleep well.”

Cody nodded.

Tom Walker strode in, looked for Brenda Hogg and marched over to her, standing above her with his tray in his hand while he rattled off a quick bunch of comments.

Cody frowned. Brenda seemed to sag under Walker’s tirade. She spotted Cody, grit her teeth and shook her head — begging him not to get involved.

He didn’t have to; Clive Bamber and Moira Collins came over and started talking with Walker. A moment later, Clive and Tom left the cafeteria and Moira sat next to Brenda, patting her soothingly on the shoulder.

#

They ran through the usual list of space disasters — micro-meteor punctures, failed systems, problems with sanitation and hydroponics — the lot.

Nora and the four engineers handled them with growing confidence even as the three nursery attendants managed the twelve babies with aplomb. Of course, the nursery was on-going, the only difference was that they added the chatter from the emergencies to the mix, to see how the kids would handle it.

“We are going to mute that klaxon!” Mandy Barquess said when they came up to their first debrief. “It set all the babies off.”

“But what if it was a real emergency?’ Scott Ellis replied. “What then?”

“Um,” Nora began slowly, “in the case of a catastrophic emergency in warp…”

“We die,” Ellaz said. She shrugged. “I mean, we’ve got all the shuttles as lifeboats but… well, we’d best not have that sort of emergency.”

“Because we’d be drifting somewhere in interstellar space,” Nora agreed with a slow sigh. Then she brightened, “Which is why we practice.”

Ellaz! The alien! You saw it, right? Cody said, surprised that that would be her first thought.

Yeah, Ellaz replied. But it doesn’t have to be an alien.

Really? And how many upright caterpillars do you know?

A warp — how could anyone make a warp bubble that small? Cody demanded. Can you? Could your mom?

Ellaz shook her head.

And the spacer? He was turned to dust!

Actually, that could be — someone turned the warp into a weapon, Ellaz thought very quietly. That looks like what happens when a warp collapses. All the atoms are — well, it burnt out the lighter materials and left — just dust. Carbon dust.

And the blue flash? From the alien? Cody pressed. Then, Wait a minute! Your shield! When you were hit there was a blue flash.

The energy converter, Ellaz agreed. It’s still experimental. It shouldn’t flash at all, just convert energy, absorb it.

The alien, Cody said. Why was it on the ship? I mean, they blew the whole ship up, why did it have to be — Ellaz?

I… I think it came for us, Ellaz thought back in a very small voice. Mom and me.

Because of the energy converter, right? Cody guessed. But how would an alien know?

Passage:
“That’s only because we’re the last two alive in this system!” Ellaz said. She shot him a hot look. “And don’t think that we’re going to do any repopulating. I’m a clone from a long line of clones.”

“Me, too,” Cody said.

“Well, not to be mean, but you can’t be,” Ellaz said. “Your name is Cody, so you’re only the third in line, right?”

It was traditional to name clones alphabetically. The first would have an ‘A’ name, the second a ‘B’ name and so on. Only the Fords didn’t do it that way. It was a closely guarded secret that the first Ford was Zacharias.

“You said your mother was Elle,” Cody remarked.

“Well… yes,” Ellaz allowed. “We decided to stick with the same first letter until we —” she broke off abruptly and shook her head “— sorry, that’s classified.”

“I won’t tell anyone,” Cody said, waving to the debris surrounding them, pointing out that there was no one to tell. Then he had a thought. “So, is E for Engineering or Electronics?”

Ellaz hissed in surprise before admitting, “Energy.”

“Right, like your power converter,” Cody guessed.

Ellaz gave him a reluctant nod. Her panel beeped and she sat up excitedly. “Can you make the emergency signal?”

“Do you mean the Mayday squawk?” Cody asked her, moving to bring up another control panel on his displays.

“Squawk?”

“That’s what we call it,” Cody said, programming the emergency code and hitting the switch that broadcast it. “It’ll take about forty-five seconds at light speed.”

“Ninety round-trip,” Ellaz observed. Cody nodded and got busy, turning the shuttle toward the least time course for the farthest moon and checking his fuel levels.

Ninety seconds later there was a beep. Someone had replied.

“This is cargo shuttle Wasp from the freighter Hornet,” Cody said quickly in a calm, professional voice. “Two souls aboard. Air for two hours. Request vectors for approach.”

Ninety seconds later, on the same frequency, a voice replied, “Say intentions.”

“We need to refuel, resupply — we had an air leak — and then we’re going to search for any survivors,” Cody replied.

“Wasp, you are cleared to approach the Deep Space One, orbits and speed in data,” came the reply.

“And yet you did it in eight,” Admiral Cartwright observed.

“We didn’t have a choice, Adam,” Don Hartman replied. “Speaking of which, why don’t you come with me to Hermes and I’ll show you around?” He nodded to include Emma Forster. “Both of you!”

“I’d like to get Commodore Russell and Captain Sheers, too,” Admiral Cartwright said.

“Excellent! Say, ten minutes?” Don Hartman said, rising from his chair. Everyone else rose and the meeting broke up. As he moved to the doors, he put an arm on Nora’s shoulder and leaned down to her, “Excellent work!”

Nora beamed back up at him.

#

The moment they were in Nora’s shuttle, Phoenix, she grabbed Cody tight, dropped her head on his shoulder and just held him. After an awkward moment, Cody returned her hug and patted her gently on the back. She pushed him away, grabbed his hand, and pulled him to the cockpit. “Come on, I’ve got a spare helmet,” she told him.

In the cockpit they pulled their helmets down. “Ellaz!” Nora called. Ellaz! I’ve got him!

You do? Ellaz appeared out of the mist. Cody frowned. She looked different, younger than the Ellaz he’d just spoken to on his own Wasp. Hey, Codes, how ya doing?

Codes? Cody thought to himself. Nora had been eyeing him carefully and nodded to herself as if his reaction had confirmed her feelings.

Did you guys have a good trip? Cody asked her.

Certainly, a deep strong voice replied from the distance, why do you ask?

It was Nora’s version of Other Cody.

The blastocysts have attached and created viable embryos, Nora’s Other Cody added, sounding very adult.

Good, good! Cody replied, wondering why this version of himself was so aggressive and forward. We developed a design for a tachyonic communicator —

Is that possible? Cody, how? Nora’s — or Phoenix’s — Other Nora said, coming into view and grabbing Other Cody’s hand possessively. Well that, at least, was the same on his ship.

Chapter Nine

Chapter Nine

“Nine… eight… seven… six… five… four… three… two… cut warp!” Nora called. In front of them space shimmered back into reality.

“I have the hab,” Cody called. “Rotating.” He turned Hope around so that it was facing backwards.

“I can spot the ship,” Ellaz reported. “We’ve got a good look. Prepare the mirror, Cody.”

“Roger,” Cody replied. “We’re going to bring up the forward bubble and put all power into it.”

“Then you’ll execute pattern Alpha,” Ellaz agreed. “In three… two… one!”

Hope engaged the forward part of her ring, projecting a circular disk two thousand kilometers in front of her.

“Got it!” Ellaz cried. “We’ve deflected their lance but… Cody!”

“I see it!” Cody replied, twisting the ship in space so that its shielding warp mirror twisted the alien’s warp lance around — and back on the alien ship itself.

“Impact!” Nora called. “Impact and — Jeez!”

The alien spaceship blew up. The virtual view screen went black as it dimmed to protect their eyes and only slowly brightened.

“We’ve got debris everywhere!” Nora called.

Cody! Ellaz thought to him. The spare shuttles!

On it! Cody replied, firing off all the empty shuttles and sending them out to intercept any debris coming toward the spacehab.

“I’ve got eyes on the alien ships!” Nora warned. “They’re… wait a minute! Wait.” Then she whooped with joy. “They’re leaving!”

“How many?” Cody said aloud.

“All of them!” Nora crowed with glee.

Cody! Ellaz warned him.

Cody looked where she was pointing in virtual space. Oh, shit!

“Eject, eject, eject!” Cody shouted, pushing the buttons that fired the remaining shuttles away from Hope. Those weren’t the right words, he realized. “Abandon ship!”

Wasp flew away from Hope just as a large chunk of debris bounced off her warp ring, shattering it.

Cody! Ellaz’s voice came to him. And then, it was gone. Just like Hope.

#

“Everyone got off, Cody, they’re safe,” Nora told him when he’d recovered. He looked at her and shook his head. “Who?”

“Ellaz,” he told her.

“Sorry,” she said. “What do we do now?”

“Unknown ship, unknown ship, this is spacehab Elantra on 121.5, state your intentions,” a voice came over the speaker.

“And hurry, we can’t stay here long,” the voice said. “Jazzy is having so much fun playing and I… Cody? Are you really here?”

There was something in the voice — Ellaz’s voice — something lost, hurt, worried.

“Yes, I’m here,” Cody said, because Ellaz needed him to say that. Needed him to pull her — them — all three of them back to — “I’ve got you, don’t worry.”

“Oh, thank you!” Ellaz’s voice came back. “Did you hear that, Jazzy? Cody’s got us!”

“Cody?” Jasmine’s voice came back, confused, uncertain. “I can’t — I see —”

“C’mon Jazzy, we’ve got you,” a new voice — Edie’s called out — “We’ve got what we need, sweetie. You were brilliant.”

#

Cody gasped as his vision went black. It took him a moment to recover then he snapped at his interface controls. He was back in the Wasp. Profile: Nominal.

“Edie?”

“They’re back,” Edie said. “And the extruders are running. According to this, we’ve got twenty hollow arcs with a flexible power cable to run through them and electronic couplings. We can slide them up or down — and the shape on the ring itself is —”

“Pretty cool,” Cody agreed. “It’ll throw a field forward and back. About one thousand kilometers forward, five hundred kilometers back.”

“So it sits near the stern,” Edie said. “And… Cody what’s this other thing? There’s a new file.”

“Oh! That!” Cody said. “Well, that’s the ship.”

#

“I’m going to leave Baker up in orbit with her cargo,” Cody declared as he approached the moon hours later. “I’ll send Able down first and then bring Wasp in.”

He still wasn’t sure how it all fit together but already he’d gotten Bamber to agree to let them fire up the bots and begin the initial assembly.

“We found food, and… well, you might want to come see what we’ve got,” Bamber said. Cody frowned, remembering Ellaz’s worries.

“I’m in the middle of something,” Cody said. “Can you just tell me? Or send an image?”

Bamber sighed. “We found the shuttle bay,” he said. “Rather we found the shuttle warehouse. There are about —”

Cody perked up, tapped a command into the computer systems. There were ten ships on the building slips which meant, with a crew of roughly one hundred, there had to be four shuttles for each ship. Maybe they weren’t all here but…

“Forty shuttles?” Cody guessed.

“Only about twenty in this warehouse, at a guess,” Bamber replied. “And they’re in mothballs.”

“Mothballs?” Ellaz piped up.

“I mean they’re not prepped, they’re wrapped up for storage,” Bamber replied.

“Then why didn’t you say so?” Ellaz murmured acerbically.

“Spacers know mothballs,” Cody said.

“Not this spacer,” Ellaz corrected him.

“So…” Cody typed in a series of queries, tied it in with Bamber’s location and said, “If you go from there across the field, you’ll find Warehouse Two. There should be another twenty shuttles there.” Of course they’d need fuel, charging, oxygen and… well, it was something.

“I’ll check it out, right after I pull up the systems in this other warehouse,” Bamber replied. “And Captain?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t fall asleep!”

Cody shook his head and looked back at the screens in front of him.

Plans. Tried-and-true. Because building a starship wasn’t just science, it was art, too.

They needed a power plant, no matter what. Preferably a “tried-and-true” plant and, more importantly, they needed one that was here, at the shipyards, ready to be installed. Only… there were only so many power plants lying around.

The power plant sized the ship. A big ship, a big power plant.

And all that depended on the size of the ship. There was no way they’d be able to build a two megatonne starship in less than four months. And they didn’t have four months. So, what was the biggest ship they could build in three weeks?
The computers didn’t have an answer to that. What was the fastest ship they could build?

Back in the flight deck, Ellaz shot him a look. He waved it away, pulling up the trajectory list and frowning. He shot her a copy silently and she started looking, hissing as she read the numbers.

“Largest first,” Cody said as he heard a group of people stomp aboard, pushing a supply trolley. He turned to wave at them and grinned, “Hey guys! Glad to have your help! Just top us off with anything you think we need but please hurry!”

“Yes, sir, we’ll be quick!” One of them answered. A couple of minutes later, they clambered off and Cody heard them securing the airlock.

“Detaching,” Bamber called. “You’re good to go, we’re raising you now.”

“Roger, ready to go,” Cody called back.

“And Captain… best of luck, sir.”

“Captain?” Ellaz murmured softly as the shuttle was bathed once more in the light of the distant sun and they were raised back up to the surface.

Cody grinned. “They… um… might think that they’re dealing with Daniel Ford, my father.”

“I thought he was dead.”

“Well, there was some confusion,” Cody said. “He might have been just undergoing regen.”

“‘Regen?’” Ellaz repeated, an eyebrow raised in disbelief.

“Well, they had no trouble dealing with Captain Ford,” Cody said. “I’m not so —”

“Wasp, you are cleared for departure,” the controller told them.

“Roger, initiating automated departure sequence one, shaping course for —” He shot a look toward the girl.

“Target Three,” Ellaz murmured to him.

“Target Three,” Cody finished.

“Godspeed,” Clive Bammber told them.

Cody turned to Ellaz. “How many gees are you good for?”

“Gees?” Ellaz said. She shrugged. “Three?”

“Life or death,” Cody reminded her.

“Maybe five,” Ellaz said. “But not for long.”

“Wuss,” Cody said, firing up the main engines and putting them to full power. Seven gees for twenty minutes. He eased back only when his relays from Ellaz’s co-pilot seat showed her approaching extreme distress. He pulled them back to two gees and turned to her. “You okay?”

She glared at him. He could see blood in the whites of her eyes where capillaries had broken under the strain.

“Boom!” Edie cried. “You didn’t dodge fast enough! And your warp core shredded.”

Shredded? Cody thought.

“You died,” Jasmine explained.

So what do we do? Ellaz thought.

“Whenever you find yourself in a warp stream like that, the smart course is to offset your course and stick to it. It means you’ll have to recompute your astrogation, of course.”

I thought the routes were safe, Cody replied.

“They’re safe at Warp Five,” Edie explained. “Everything comes faster — and thicker — at Warp Nine.”

Why aren’t there routes for Warp Nine? Ellaz wondered.

“If there are, only the military has them,” Edie said. “Regular freighters don’t need them and mapping such routes… it’s expensive.”

In time or in ships? Cody wondered.

“Both,” Edie told them. “Okay. Again. Warp Nine.”

They did two more runs before Edie pulled them out. She and Jasmine passed them drinks.

“You are getting it,” Edie assured them.

Cody and Ellaz exchanged looks. “Excuse me,” Ellaz said, “but as near as I can tell, all we’re getting is dead.” Cody nodded in agreement.

“But you’re getting really good at that!” Jasmine teased.

#

Outside, Jacob and Gail waited with lists of disasters. Although, Cody noted, some of the disasters were crossed off his list. He glanced to Ellaz’s list and smiled.

“What?” Ellaz demanded, still grumpy from their exertions.

“Our aides are doing their work,” Cody said, pointing to the eliminated items.

“We talked it over,” Jacob admitted, “and asked ourselves what you would do.”

“Good work,” Ellaz told him with a grin. She gestured for his touchpad and peered down at it. “Now… we’ve got the supplies, the diapers, the formula. What about water?”

“Handled,” Cody said, pointing to his list. “What about soil?”

“We won’t be needing that until the ECLSS units are complete,” Gail said. “And that’s not for another three days. And then they have to power them up —”

“And where are we on power?” Cody asked, looking at his list.

“How many times have you flown a starship?” Ellaz countered.

“Who says I’m going to be the pilot?”

“Who says you aren’t?” Ellaz replied. She blew out a sigh. “Are you with me or what?”

“Let’s get the computer on line and see what we can learn,” Cody said. “This may not be a problem.”

“Very well,” Ellaz said. She was not happy but she was willing to follow his logic. “So, what type of computer is it?”

“It’s big,” Cody said, eyeing the whole floor of computers.

“Very helpful,” Ellaz said.

“Hang on,” Cody replied, bringing up a couple of screens and trying out a few commands. “Okay, it’s not just one computer. It’s about — huh, ten. Apparently two for each slip.”

“Makes sense.”

“And… okay, these are Compudyne Twenty systems with the latest software,” Cody said.

“How do you know it’s the latest software?”

“Well… it says so,” Cody replied. “Last update, two days ago.”

“Hmmph,” Ellaz sounded impressed. “Okay, so find the inventory system, find the schematics, the production schedule, the —”

“Slow down, slow down!” Cody called back. “I’m in a suit and I can only do one thing at a time.” He fumed. “Besides, I wanted you to see if you could use the shuttle’s computers —”

“Them!” Ellaz cried. “You’ve got a state-of-the-art construction system and you want to slave it to a dinky shuttle?”

Cody frowned. It was not a dinky shuttle. He glanced out to the ruins beyond him and spotted the skeleton of a two megatonne freighter. Well, okay, it was a dinky shuttle. But it was his dinky shuttle.

#

How To Build A Starship

Get a lot of money.

Get a lot of materials.

Get a lot of trained people.

Get a tried-and-true set of plans.

Spend about two years building it from ribs to rigging.

Get a warp ring tuner, tune the rings.

Get a cargo/destination/crew.

Pray everything works.

#

Money? Check. Well, unnecessary.

Materials? Maybe

Trained people? Zero.

Tried-And-True plans? Huh?

#

“Captain!” Clive Bamber called on the guard frequency, the one that everyone had tuned in. “Captain!”

“Sorry,” Cody replied, switching frequencies. “I’m up in the Quadrant Two construction center.”

“I’ll take anything!” Nora said, dropping into a chair and looking around wildly. “What could they do?”

“Really, what?” Ellaz called back from halfway down the corridor.

“I need you to program baby bots,” Cody shouted back, smiling down at the little boy who’d winced at his bellow.

“Roger, initiating automated departure sequence one, shaping course for —” He shot a look toward the girl.

“Target Three,” Ellaz murmured to him.

“Godspeed,” Clive Bammber told them.

With that error? We might just go scooting by, Cody said. Then, What if we let them hit us?
What?

We know they want to hit the hab, what if we put us between them and it?

Calculating, Ellaz said. Cody frowned. That sounded more like a computer than the girl he’d known. For just under three weeks. Maybe she said that and he’d never heard her before. Or maybe… Cody gave himself a mental shake.

It could work, Ellaz said minutes later, it could also mean that parts of this ship would crash into the hab and destroy it anyway.

How likely?

Sixty-five percent, Ellaz replied.

“What are you two doing?” Nora Wright’ voice came to Cody’s ears.

“You’re supposed to be resting,” Cody snapped to her.

“Well, I’m not,” Nora said. “I managed to get him to sleep but she was just all ants.”

Ants? Ellaz thought. Then, “Ants?”

“Like ants in your pants, antsy,” Nora explained. “So what are you doing?”

“Playing 3D chess,” Cody said.

“And what else?” Nora demanded. She slipped into the co-pilot’s chair and tapped his shoulder. “I’m going VR.” She pulled on her headset and a ghostly version of her joined them in the simulation. She glanced at the clock which now read fifty-nine minutes. Then she pulled up a virtual console and ran through the ship’s logs. Cody hadn’t thought of that, she’d doubtless see — “Two kilometers?” Nora groaned. “And you’re thinking — what? Interpose Hope between them and the hab?”

“We could abandon,” Cody said. “Anyway, five hundred million souls.”

“Against twenty-four,” Nora finished. “But then what?” Cody shot her a look. “So we die gloriously? What then? If the aliens scarper, what then? Just Elantra, right? No docks, no shipyards, nothing.” She blew out a sigh. “Ellaz, I want a better solution.”

“Yeah,” Ellaz said. “And if you’ll give me a chance to think, maybe I’ll come up with one.”

That sounded more like Ellaz, Cody thought to himself.

“What about the mirror?” Cody asked. “I mean, if we used that, and mirrored —”

“Reflected!” Ellaz objected. “How many times do I have to tell you?”

Cody smiled to himself. “Reflector, then.”

“What?”

Cody agreed. He thumbed the freighter’s emergency airlock controls and the cargo hold door blew out. “Holy shit!” Ellaz cried, pointing behind them. “They got everything!”

Cody followed her finger with his head and his jaw dropped.

The freighter Hornet was docked at Parminter Station Number One, the largest of four orbiting cargo stations for the planet Meath. Meath was a planet of over a billion people, with orbital satellites providing homes for another half billion. Was.

Parminter Station One and the dozen freighters that had been docked were only shards of metal and smaller objects floating haphazardly in the light of the planet’s star.

“They got the orbitals, too,” Cody said, pointing to a smaller object in the distance. The orbitals were — had been — giant circular space stations — habitats for the half billion people who preferred to live in their own artificial atmosphere. He made a face. “I can’t tell about the planet —”

“Infrared,” Ellaz said.

“We can’t use power,” Cody said.

“Passives,” Ellaz replied, tapping a command into the shuttle’s computer only to have her hand smacked away by Cody.

“No power!” Cody hissed at her.

Ellaz put her fingers in her mouth and glared at him. “You don’t know —”

“I don’t!” Cody agreed. “And until we do, we’re going to be a piece of debris.”

“If they can track IR, they can see our heat,” Ellaz said.

“Which is why we’re staying close to the freighter,” Cody said. “We’ll be in the thermal shadow.”

Cody nodded. “Not only that but we have figured out how to detect ships in warp. That’s why we know that they have twenty-six.”

“So… twenty-six plus or minus zero,” Thomas said with a chuckle.

“And if this grav lance fails?” Eric asked.

“That’s why we’re here,” Cody said. “Because if it fails, there are twenty-four of us and over five hundred million on the spacehab Elantra, which we think will be the last target.”

“Okay,” Scott Ellis said, “And?”

“You want to ram them, right?” Eric Doohan guessed. He shook his head.

“We’ve got the shuttles,” Gail pointed out. “We can abandon ship and pilot her remotely.”

Or let Ellaz pilot it, Cody thought grimly to himself. He didn’t have his helmet on so no one could hear him.

“And then we’ll be in shuttles, in the middle of a war,” Scott said. He frowned. Then nodded. “I’m okay with that.”

“I’d like for us to vote,” Cody said.

“All in favor?” Nora called out, raising her voice and then pouting apologetically at the baby in her arms.

“All right,” Cody said. “So, I’ll be taking Gail, Jacob, and Nora with me on Wasp.”

“No you won’t!” Nora said. “You’ll be taking Gail. I’m not leaving my Phoenix.”

“I can’t say,” Cody admitted. “And what are you doing with that camera?”

“She’s my sister,” Cody said, remembering their cover story. “She’s okay with shuttles but —” he shrugged “— I think she wants to do more.”

“Well, I mean flying a shuttle, how hard is that?” Jasmine asked. Cody felt his face go red. Jasmine noticed and added quickly, “I mean I’m sure that it’s terribly important and all but… don’t they have autopilots?”

“No, they don’t,” Jasmine answered immediately. “A robot might be able to produce a first order approximation but… you wouldn’t want to fly a ship that way.”

“Mr. Bamber?” Cody called back. He shot a look to Jasmine who shrugged and turned back to her camera display.

“I’m going in,” Ellaz called. A moment later, she called back, “Cody, Jasmine, you need to get here. And Miz Collins.”

“Why?”

“It’s a nursery,” Bamber called back. “One teenaged minder and twenty babies from months to years.”

“Let’s go,” Cody said, unbuckling himself.

“I’m staying here,” Jasmine said. “There’s…” she turned to her displays and waved him off.

“Miz Collins?” Cody called.

“Twenty-one more mouths to feed,” Moira Collins said, shaking her head. “What are we going to do?”

Cody didn’t have an answer.

“You’re saying that anything too small they didn’t notice?” Clive asked. Ellaz nodded. “That explains all the kids you found.”

“Kids aren’t a threat,” Jasmine added. “At least, I’ll bet that’s what they thought.”

Go on! Ellaz thought with a mental wave to him. And Pawn to Queen Four.

When Cody came back, he reported, “Downstream, T+3, all systems nominal.”

“Roger,” Nora’s voice came back immediately. “We’re good here.”

Cody turned back to their view of space at Warp Nine.

Two hours later, after winning two games of chess, Ellaz said, Are we there yet?

Cody laughed.

#

Cody jerked when someone touched him. He pulled up his helmet. “You need to eat,” Gail said to him, passing him a hot tray.

Cody nodded in thanks and started gulping down his food.

“And I’m bored,” Gail added five minutes later when he’d finished and passed her back his tray. “Also, when are you going to sleep?”

Cody fumbled for an answer but Gail waved him off. “I’ll tell you,” she said, turning to back out of the hatch. “Ellaz needs to eat, too.”

Cody smiled at her and pulled back on his helmet. Chow time!

Ellaz took a moment to respond. What?

Chow time, Cody replied. He frowned. What were you doing?

Updating the system, Ellaz replied. Is — oh, someone’s poking my arm. I guess I should go.

Go!

#

Okay, now you need to sleep, Cody thought to Ellaz, thirty minutes after he woke up from his four hour “nap.” I’ll call if I need help.

I’m not sleepy!

Get your helmet off, crawl back to bunk and lie down, Cody ordered. Close your eyes, get some sleep.

Can’t I sleep here? Ellaz half-begged.

No, Cody replied, you need to lie down, get some shut eye.

Okay, Ellaz replied glumly.

Cody waited a moment then reached over to tap her hand. I said go.

He felt Ellaz rise and the cabin shake as she moved back to the main cabin. She patted his arm as she left.

And Cody was alone with the command of a starship moving at Warp Nine. He checked on their monitor program and came to the conclusion that it was bored.

#

Are we there yet? Cody thought to Ellaz when he plugged back into the mind-link two days later. I never thought that space could be this boring.

Don’t jinx it, Ellaz warned. You good? I want to take a break.

Passage:
Cody found Ellaz already asleep when he came to the dorms for sleep. Jacob was sleeping in the bunk next to her. Cody sent Gail off to change, checked his latest updates, and then swapped with her, sending the little girl to the bed next to his. As he changed, he smiled at how fierce the two kids were with their “officers.” Gail was conscientious and tended to work herself too hard. Jacob was about the same. Ellaz could be difficult — what was that at dinner? — but she cared for the two kids, cared for everyone in her own, taciturn, grouchy way.

Cody got into his bunk, called the lights out and went to sleep.

He woke up sometime in the middle of the night. Jacob was giving Ellaz a glass of water. She saw Cody’s eyes and frowned at him, waving any questions away. Nightmares, Cody guessed. Well, Edie had thrown everything she could at them and… they were flying an experimental ship, aliens had wiped out over fifteen hundred million people in this system, and they needed to get going.

Tomorrow they would be three days from launch.

#

“You’re burning up!” Cody exclaimed when he felt Ellaz’s forehead the next morning. “And you look green!”

“Shut up!” Ellaz said. “I’m fine. I’ll meet you at breakfast.” She turned to Jacob. “Okay, Jake, what have we got?”

“In the last five minutes?” Jacob said, shaking his head. “Nothing new.” He shot Cody a look but Gail was tugging on his sleeve, dragging him down to the cafeteria for breakfast.

“We’re going to be late!” Gail warned.

In the cafeteria, Nora found Cody alone and raised an eyebrow to him.

“Ellaz will be coming down shortly,” Cody lied. “She had nightmares last night and didn’t sleep well.”

“She’s not getting sick, is she?” Nora asked. “I mean, the babies were fine and that’s where bugs usually start but…”

“I think she’s just worried,” Cody said. He remembered the way she looked — green, pale, with bags under her eyes. She couldn’t be sick. They needed her. Everyone needed her.
