Passage:
“This Captain Ford is too tired not to take all the help he can get,” Cody said with a breezy wave of his hand. “Ellaz, can you fire up the sensors, see what we’ve got?”

She shot him a look — they knew what they’d get — but she nodded and played along.

“Nothing from the target,” Ellaz reported back a few minutes later. “We should go in for a closer look.”

“Yes,” Moira Collins agreed. “In fact, let’s see if we can find a pad, then we’ll get out and take stock.”

Cody brought the shuttle around in a long slow sweep over the nearest landing pad. They spotted the remains of several shuttles. Some looked intact.

“Did they target only the living?” Clive Bamber asked. He was following their displays on the remotes in the main cabin.

“It sure looks like it,” Edie Crump agreed. Then, “You know, if we wanted more lift, that might be a good thing for us.”

“Yeah,” Moira Collins said numbly. “At least…” she broke off.

Cody and Ellaz exchanged looks. Ellaz turned her head back to the main cabin. “You did the math.”

“Before you, I’ll bet,” Moira Collins replied.

“Twenty-five more mouths —” Edie Crump added.

“Plus we were never designed to be self-sustaining,” Clive Bamber added. He unbuckled himself and moved forward to the entrance to the cockpit, standing in the doorway. “So… what’s the plan?”

Cody considered his options and went with the truth. “We could take one of the fuel farms, steal the tanks —”

“That gets you the fuel,” Bamber said. He waved a hand around. “But I don’t see a ship, do you?”

“We haven’t looked yet,” Edie Crump said. “Let’s get down and scout.”

“We’ve got to warn the others,” Cody said, pressing on with his answer.

“What others?” Moira Collins demanded.

“The other worlds,” Ellaz said.

“We’ve got to fight the aliens,” Cody added.

“What aliens?” Edie asked.

“I saw one,” Cody said. He heard Clive Bamber hiss in surprise. “It was fuzzy, like a caterpillar but much bigger — man-sized — and it stood on its butt.”

“Did you get any imagery?” Moira asked.

“No,” Cody said. “But I’ll bet we can search for some.”

“Ellaz?” Cody said, suddenly shaking with a brilliant idea. “Could we use your —”

Cody wondered what they’d do when they got there. First up was Deneb Approach — if there was a Deneb Approach. They’d have to drop into sunlight to identify themselves. He pulled up the contact procedures.

“Captain?” Nora’s voice came to him through the simulator.

“Yes?” Cody said.

“Um, do you know where Ellaz is?”

“I sent her to rest,” Cody replied, feeling weird speaking out loud.

“Jacob can’t find her,” Nora said with a sigh. “I’ll send out a search party.”

“Sure,” Cody replied, eager to get back to his run-through on approach procedures. Then, feeling guilty, he added, “How’s everything going?”

“You mean aside from everyone being bored out of their minds?” Nora replied. “Fantastic.” A pause. “And I like being bored out of my mind.” A moment later, she said, “Pawn to Queen Four.”

“I’ve got to —” Cody protested just as a new interface popped up in the simulation. A chessboard. Marked Cody and Nora. Huh. Pawn to Queen Four.

Two games later, Ellaz hooked back into her helmet.

You okay? Cody thought to her, reaching a hand for hers.

She squeezed it back. Lost track of time, talking with Jacob.

I thought Jacob was looking for you.

He was, then we talked, Ellaz replied quickly. She pointed a virtual hand toward the chessboard, Is that Nora?

Was, Cody agreed. She’s resting. Want a game?

Cody and Ellaz exchanged looks, then looked to their “shadows” — Gail and Jacob — but the two looked just as confused.

“We’re cleared on the schedule,” Edie continued, leading them up to the command center and then veering sharply left to a door marked SIM LAB. She opened the door, pulled the two inside, waved a hand at their shadows and closed the door.

“Good, you’re here,” Jasmine said, turning at the sound of the door. “I think I’ve got it right, could you check?” The question was delivered to her mother.

There were seats inside the SIM LAB. And a lot of computers stacked up on the walls. There was a table in the middle where the seats were arranged. And helmets.

“Okay,” Edie said, waving to her daughter. “You two, get seated but don’t put on the helmets until I say so.”

“What are we doing?” Ellaz demanded.

“Practicing,” Jasmine said excitedly. “This is going to be fun!”

Cody and Ellaz glanced to each other. Fun?

Edie turned back to them, having inspected the computers. “Good job, Jazzy! You got it just right!” Under her breath she added, “I hope.” Then she looked to Ellaz and Cody. “First out we’ll just use you two.”

“So we can pull you out if you get lost,” Jasmine explained. Her mother gave her a pained look.

“What are we doing?” Cody asked.

“Ring watch,” Edie said.

“Because…?” Ellaz asked.

“Because this is all new and someone needs to keep on top of the ring,” Jasmine explained. “Some people, I should say.”

“Helmets on,” Edie said. “We’ll go easy at first.”

With a sigh, Cody pulled the helmet over his head, covering his eyes and aligning it with his implant. The last he saw, Ellaz was doing the same.

The world dissolved.

Cody? Ellaz’s voice came through his senses. It wasn’t just hearing, it was feeling, smelling, touching. Implants used all the senses.

Here, Cody assured her. Now where was here?

“Okay, guys, a single ring’s never been tried before,” Edie’s voice came to them.

“Successfully,” Jasmine added.

Cody could feel Edie’s reaction. Ellaz laughed. “It’s a good thing this is a simulator!”

“One hundred and sixty-eight hours and it will be real,” Jasmine corrected.

In anticipation of their crew placements, they split the station duties so that the Hope crew managed their babies and the Revenge crew managed theirs. The baby-bots were a big help.

“We’re going to have to rush the boarding of Hope when she’s ready,” Nora reported as she met with Cody, Ellaz, and their two shadows (Gail and Jacob).

“Should we practice?” Jacob asked.

Nora considered it, ate a bit of her dinner, made a face at the taste and shook her head. “You two set up a scheduled boarding order, that should be enough.”

Brenda Hogg came over and sat at their table. “How’s it going?”

“Pretty good,” Nora said. “We’re in sims, of course, and the few problems these two —” she glared good-naturedly at Cody and Ellaz “— have sprung on us have been nothing hard.”

“So far,” Gail said, smiling at Cody.

“So far,” Nora agreed with a sour look at her Captain. Then her expression brightened. “But I’d rather make mistakes here where we can fix them —”

“And start over,” Ellaz interjected.

“— and start over,” Nora agreed. She eyed Ellaz. “Are you all right?”

“Sure, never better!” Ellaz said. Then she frowned. “Why do you ask?”

“You’re just picking at your food,” Nora said.

Ellaz grumbled and shoved her tray over to Nora. “You try it! Tell me what you think!” She got up and rushed out of the cafeteria. Nora shot Cody a look, Cody glanced to Jacob.

“She says she’s not been hungry these last few days,” Jacob said.

“Nerves,” Brenda guessed.

“Yeah,” Cody said. “Nerves.” He took a bite of Ellaz’s dinner, looked at it in surprise and took another bite before guiltily returning to his own meal.

“Was it bad, then?” Nora asked.

“No, ‘s good,” Cody said around a mouthful of his dinner.

Nora smiled and shoved Ellaz’s discarded tray over to him. “Finish it off, then. No point in having it go to waste.”

Cody, who was famished, decided not to argue.

Chapter Eight

“I wish there was some way we could warn them,” Cody said as he woke up and smiled at Gail who held a cup of coffee in front of him. He took it with a grateful nod and sipped it. “How long was I out?”

“Hours,” Gail said airily. “We’re two hours out.”

“They’ve started their attack,” Cody guessed.

“Yes, and we think we’ve got readings on them,” Gail replied. She made a face. “It looks like they’re using your plan.”

“Not my plan,” Cody objected, appalled at the notion.

“Get dressed, get moving,” Gail said, reaching a hand out to help him up. She was way smaller than Cody. He shook his head at her and stood on his own. She made a face. “Look, you smell. You need to wash off, change clothes, and eat before you put on that smelly helmet of yours again.”

“Smelly?”

Gail wrinkled her nose. “Well, it was! I cleaned it,” she admitted. “Again.”

“Thanks,” Cody said, moving past her to the restroom. Five minutes later he was out, dressed, presentable, and hungry.

Gail intercepted him with a tray. “This is cold,” she apologized. It was a set of protein bars. Cody smiled at her, pocketed one and opened the other.

Cody didn’t need to be told twice. He pointed to Ellaz’s helmet. “We need to go in,” he said, pulling his helmet over his head.

They entered a dark world.

Edie? Cody thought. He felt Ellaz’s “hand” touch his in the simulation and he gave hers a quick comforting squeeze in response.

In the distance, they heard giggles. Cody “tugged” Ellaz behind him as he raced toward the sound.

We can’t get caught! Ellaz warned him just as he was about to jump down a hole that appeared suddenly before them.

Edie! Cody called out. “Edie!” he said out loud. “Can you hear us?”

Play, play, play! Laugh, laugh, laugh! It sounded like two voices, singing in chorus. Cody turned toward Ellaz and imagined her in front of him.

What do we do? Ellaz said.

Rope, Cody said, pulling a rope out of the air. Tie it around me, I’ll go in.

Ellaz considered his suggestion and started tying one end of the rope around her waist. This is a really stupid idea, you know.

What’s yours? Cody asked.

Build a bot to find them, Ellaz replied, snugging her knot tight.

Okay, Cody thought back, raising his hands out in front of him and sketching out a shape. Ellaz nodded, moved to join him, adding arms and a head. In a few moments they created a standard hand bot. Okay, boy, go find Edie! Bring them back to us!

Only the bot came back moments later holding one of its arms with the other. When Ellaz and Cody noticed it, the bots head fell off its shoulders and it collapsed into nothingness.

They got swords? Ellaz asked.

I’m going, Cody declared, imagining a shield on his right arm.

I’m following, Ellaz said, pushing him forward.

They went down the hole. They fell for a long time, following the sing-song voices.

When they landed, they found themselves on a pile of old diapers.

Ew! They thought in unison. The voices weren’t too far away.

They found two little girls in a meadow throwing leaves at each other and singing, Ring Around the Rosie, Pocket Full of Posies! Ashes, Ashes, We All Fall Down!

What’s that song? Ellaz said. I feel like I know it.

“Nursery,” little Franny Harper piped up, “we’re ready. Babies are ready. Is it okay if we seal off from the ship?”

“Actually, I think you should wait,” Nora replied.

“No,” Ellaz said, “seal off. Be ready to deploy. Set your controls to automatic.”

“Is Jacob…?”

“On my way!” Jacob Falcon piped up. “Captain —?”

“Go!” Cody told him. He wasn’t happy with just the three of them but, if Jacob survived, he might be able to tell their story. And that might help the survivors. “Take a complete copy of our log with you.”

“Okay,” Jacob replied, his voice distinct from his VR voice.

“We’re going to have to do some snappy maneuvering for this to work,” Ellaz said aloud.

Cody grinned. “Aren’t you glad I’m a shuttle pilot?”

“What?” Ellaz said, surprised. “I was talking about the computers.”

Beside him, Nora snorted in amusement.

“We’re going to need to fire up the RCS on the shuttles,” Cody said.

“Yes, yes, I know!” Ellaz snapped back. Then, in a slightly more subdued voice, she added, “And I don’t suppose it’d hurt to have you ready, if we need you.”

“Thanks,” Cody said. “Nora, let’s get the preflights up and running.”

#

“Eight minutes,” Cody said unnecessarily. Ellaz had refined their readings, they’d seen the destruction of the space docks, the moons, and now… the spacehabs. Four had been destroyed.

“I want us to start a track on the shipyards,” Cody said. “I want to know what we can find out about what’s intact, what we can use to —”

“Build more starships,” Ellaz said approvingly. “Working.”

“You sound like a computer,” Nora complained. Then she hushed, embarrassed.

“I’ve been told that a lot of times,” Ellaz replied, sounding unperturbed. “Cody? Didn’t you say mate in four?”

Cody’s eyes went wide. They’d finished that game. He’d beaten her just as predicted.

“I can play you,” Nora offered.

“But —” Ellaz broke off. “Oh! We finished that game! I didn’t — I mean, I was distracted.”

“We’ve got under eight minutes,” Cody said, “can you play a timed game?”

“No,” Ellaz replied. “I think I’d best… I’d best keep an eye on things.”

Carlow Shipping was the name of the spaceport, the city, and the industry. It had been set up by the magnate William Buckley over thirty years before, Cody saw from the data entry on it. Carlow Shipping had produced over forty starships, mostly in the two megatonne range. It had the reputation of making good, moderately priced ships.

When Cody looked at the displays of the ground beneath them, all he saw were wrecks. The main dome was shattered, as were all the corridors connecting to other habitats, workshops, power plants, hydroponics gardens — anything where humans might live.

“They nuked the Nautilus,” Edie murmured from behind him. “That ship was nearly flight ready.” She examined her displays more. “Huh, they didn’t spend any effort on the new builds, though.”

“Why?” Cody asked.

“My guess?” Clive Bamber said. “They were raiders. They came in quick and left quick.” He made a face. “Which is why we’re here.”

“But not for long,” Ellaz said, starting up a new tracking routine. “Even without the extra mouths —”

“We know,” Clive said, jerking a hand toward young Jasmine.

Ellaz scowled. “She’s just two years younger than me and I’m pretty sure she can do the math.”

“Less than a year,” Jasmine piped up. “Even with the original five hundred, that’s all they’ve got. They’re not rigged to be self-sustaining.”

“What would it take to do that?” Cody wondered. “I mean —” he waved a hand toward the shattered hydroponics dome “— we’ve got soil here.”

“You need bacteria,” Moira Collins pointed out.

“The compost tanks,” Ellaz said. “We could pull from that —”

“You need transport, fuel and —” Clive added grumpily.

“Wait one!” Cody said, turning the shuttle sharply around and descending. He pointed to one side and had the displays updated with a red circle where he pointed with his hand. “What’s that?”

They spotted a light, blinking.

“That’s Morse,” Ellaz said. “It’s SOS.”

Chapter Six

Chapter Six

“H minus 6, Captain,” Gail Eber called cheerfully the next morning. “All systems are green. We are go.”

Cody felt his heart pound as he lifted his head from the cot. He looked over to Ellaz and saw that she was still sleeping. So was little Jacob.

Well, they’d had a fright — two frights. Both caused by traitors. Of the two, Tom Walker was the lesser. Cody couldn’t imagine him being willing to kill fifteen hundred million people just to — kill an inventor. Cody drew in a quick breath — that’s what the alien had done — he had killed Elle Whirly, the inventor of the energy converter. Did he know about Ellaz? Or did he think she didn’t know enough, or was too young to understand her mother’s secret? Did he know that Ellaz had an implant? Cody made a note to himself to ask later.

Things were moving fast. He got up, got dressed, grabbed breakfast and then suited up to go out and check on Hope.

“She’s looking good,” Moria Collins said as she spotted him in the airlock. “You can go and have a look, if you want, but don’t get too close — we’re lifting her for the rings. Uh, ring.”

Two hours to get the ring installed then a mad four-hour dash to get all the crew and consumables in place. After that, a pair of tugs would haul her up into orbit and then — they’d see whether the whole thing worked.

Cody watched the assembly for twenty minutes, then Gail called to him and he spent the next several hours dealing with all the last-minute details that no one had thought of.

The eighteen shuttles were all attached, their connecting tubing pressurized and tested. Two failed the first test but it was only because some of the tubing needed to be freed of lint and dust — Cody remembered polishing his fuel intake valve so many days ago. Then all systems were green.

“Ellaz,” Cody called over his comm, “we’re ready to board.”

“Coming out through Tube Three,” Ellaz reported. “Where are — what are you doing down there? Get up here, now!”

Cody blushed, turned and headed back into the airlock.

“People who work in debris fields,” Cody said. He put the two seats back, secured them and looked around. “I’ve got two balloons still in the air. I’m going to keep us in microgravity until we’re certain.”

“Pressure is stabilized,” Ellaz reported, glancing to the ECLSS panels. ECLSS — Environment Control and Life Support Systems, usually pronounced “ee-class.” Cody grunted, turned and kicked himself back to the cabin.

He buckled himself in, pulled up the navigation system and checked their fuel levels. “If we go there, we won’t be much good after.”

“Unless we get refueled,” Ellaz agreed.

Cody nodded and ran a sweep of the debris near them. “Nothing here to refuel with,” he said, his hopes of finding a spare tank or something similar dashed. If the aliens — or really dumb space pirates — had been in a rush, they’d also been thorough.

“Okay, they’re alive,” Ellaz said, bouncing in her chair with glee. “See? I can see when they shut down their systems —”

“When?”

“It looks like — it looks like just about long enough for light speed from Xerxes,” Ellaz said.

Xerxes was one of the largest asteroids in the solar system’s asteroid belt. It was — or had been — inhabited and was a major mining and research center for the whole system.

“So either someone was looking or talking with them,” Cody guessed. He frowned. “Both observatories?”

“Everything went dark within five minutes,” Ellaz replied. “It was like someone threw a switch, it was so fast.”

“That doesn’t mean anyone’s alive,” Cody said with a grimace. “It could be that these aliens have fitl and they destroyed the bases first.”

“Fitl?”

“Faster-Than-Light,” Cody translated.

“‘Fitl?’” Ellaz repeated, crinkling her nose in disgust. “You call it ‘fitl?’”

“It’s easier than saying FTL or Faster-Than-Light,” Cody replied. “And everyone says it.”

“Well, how come I haven’t heard it before?” Ellaz challenged.

“I dunno, maybe you don’t have any friends,” Cody shot back with an evil grin. Ellaz’s face fell and she looked like she was frozen. “Hey! It was a joke!”

“I don’t have any friends,” Ellaz said in a small voice.

“Well, you’ve got me,” Cody offered.

“Well…” Gail began slowly. “They used all of them for the planet.”

“They had to,” Jacob said. “And, if I had to guess, they used either Warp Two or Warp Three to… kill the planet.”

“Why?” Cody challenged.

“The time, the power, the destruction,” Nora said. She looked ill, even in the simulator. “They twisted the planet into little bits.”

“And everyone with it,” Gail added. “And the atmosphere.”

“Right, so there’s no hope of going back,” Cody said. “They didn’t just want to kill us, they wanted to kill the planet, too.”

“The spacehabs, how were they hit? What direction?” Cody asked.

“We have imagery,” Gail said. “Analyzing.” A moment later she hissed in surprise. “A straight line, sweeping through the middle. Either the ship was above and in front of the hab — about thirty degrees leading — or it was under and below the hab with the opposite angle, three hundred and thirty degrees.”

“Above or below?” In their simulator, Cody glanced to each of them in turn and finally, to Ellaz’s ghost. Ellaz.

“Above,” Jacob said. “Below and there’d be a danger of debris hitting them as it fell to the planet.”

Right. And how much more did that contribute to the destruction of the planet? Not much, really. The planet was already dead.

“How far away?” Cody said. “From the ship to the spacehab?”

“If they have the same lance we do…” Ellaz began. “Not more than a thousand kilometers.”

“Okay, so we come out a thousand kilometers from the spacehab, three hundred and twenty degrees off the planet’s rotation, rotate our nose ten degrees to port and fire the lance,” Cody said.

“Bots?” Tom said. “You have bots building the ships?”

“Well, we don’t have ten thousand trained techs,” Ellaz said. “So we work with bots.”

“We double-check their work but they do all the heavy-lifting,” Edie explained.

“Bots,” Tom muttered to himself, shaking his head.

#

Fortunately, Tom Walker was not typical of the other survivors. The babies — the under threes — were added to the nursery. That left sixteen people, from age four up to age thirteen. Brenda Hogg was the next eldest and nothing at all like Tom Walker.

“What’s its name?” Brenda had asked.

“That’s for you to decide,” Clive Bamber told her with a grin. The question of Bamber becoming captain was settled when he flat out turned it down. “I’m better with machines,” he’d said, holding up his hands defensively. “Make me the engineer. And my wife, of course.” Because Moira Collins had actual experience on starships whereas Clive Bamber had rapidly moved into management.

“Revenge,” Brenda said immediately, her expression fierce. She looked to Cody. “What are you calling yours?”

Chapter Five

Cody slept in late and was woken by a splash of water on his face. Ellaz called grumpily to him, “Come on! Get up!”

Cody scowled at her and went to the restroom to clean himself up. He ate quickly, sitting in his cot beside Ellaz and then they rushed off to the Simulations Lab.

“Today, we’re going to start with Warp Nine,” Edie said.

“Okay, and then?” Ellaz asked.

Edie grinned. “And then things will go wrong.”

“We don’t even know if the ships will work and you want to practice disasters?” Ellaz growled.

Edie smiled at her and nodded. “Helmets!”

Warp Nine was a strain, even with the monitor program to help. When they were done — and they’d only been “gone” for two hours — both Cody and Ellaz were exhausted.

“Five minutes,” Edie told them, as she passed a drink to Ellaz. Jasmine had one for Cody. “Now, while you’re getting ready, what’s the first thing to do in an emergency?”

“Fly the ship,” Cody said.

“Wrong, check life support,” Ellaz replied. “If you can’t breathe, you die.”

“That’s part of fly the ship,” Cody said.

“It’s the first part,” Ellaz said.

“Hull integrity, power, nav, propulsion, comms,” Cody said, reciting the standard list for a shuttle.

“Warp ring?” Ellaz said. “Where does that fit in?”

“Propulsion,” Cody said.

“Time,” Edie said sternly.

“We’ve got fifty seconds —” Ellaz griped.

“Helmets on!” Edie said.

And they were in the simulation again.

Sorry, Cody thought as he felt a virtual hand touch his.

Fine, Ellaz thought back, giving his hand a squeeze.

“Prepare for Warp Nine,” Edie’s voice came to them. “And… enter!”

They entered. They flew. And then…

What’s that? Cody thought as their monitor beeped in warning. He and Ellaz examined the artificial world around them, spotted the problem — a chunk of something darker, thicker in front of them coming fast and —

“Good job!” Edie called as they dodged around the chunk of thick space-time. “Now, get back on course!”

That took more finesse than they’d used before but they got back on course. And then another chunk of thickness came at them.. They dodged it. And another. And another. Two more were just ahead and —

“Okay, so pay attention,” Edie said. “Because we don’t know how these rings —”

“Rings?” Ellaz asked.

“One on each ship,” Cody told her.

“Right. Rings.”

“We don’t know how they’re going to react and we’re going at Warp Nine,” Edie continued. “On warships it’s customary to have ring tuners jacked in or prepped in case the rings needed twitching.”

“‘Twitching?’” Ellaz asked.

“You’ll see,” Edie said. “And normally, we fly one watcher at a time but you’re new, the rings are new, and… Warp Nine.”

“You want us to watch the ring?” Cody said.

“You’re the only other two with implants,” Jasmine said. “You can’t watch a ring unless you have them.”

“Okay,” Ellaz said. “And…?”

“First thing, the ring interface,” Edie said.

Cody gasped. He felt Ellaz gasp, too. Then he felt her hand on his, like she needed comfort. He squeezed back — I’m here.

Duh! Ellaz thought in her normal fashion. But — look!

They were surrounded by space. And more. They could see the glow of a warp ring surrounding them. Normally, with two rings, the warp bubble was the shape of a bulging cylinder — smooth along the ship’s axis, curving outwards at either end of the ship. The warp bubble engulfed the ship into another dimension.

But this one ring warp was different. It was shaped more like a spinning top — two cones back to back. At the front the cone was much longer, the cone at the rear cut off more quickly.

“Okay, so this is the shape we expect,” Edie said. “When you’re ready, apply thought to make it real.”

Cody squeezed Ellaz’s “hand” twice. Then he imagined the bubble surrounding them thickening, going more and more opaque until it was almost impossible to see the stars outside.

“Too much, Cody!” Edie said. “That’s about Warp Nine point five. You want to see some stars or you’ll go too fast.”

And run out of fuel, Ellaz added through the mind-link. It was really a computer link but with two or more people using the same system, they could speak mind to mind. Like Ellaz was doing now.

We were at a Symposium, the same one Edie was at, Ellaz said. Rather, mother was. I was watching in our room. Mom presented “An Investigation Into The Possibilities Of Complete Energy Conversion.”

So the aliens heard about that?

Not… aliens, Ellaz replied after a moment. Cody, what if someone wanted to steal the energy converter?

But they didn’t, Cody thought. You still have it. Right?

I… do, Ellaz admitted. But it was damaged, so I hid it. It’s safe. The materials fused. They’re inert now.

Okay, so either someone wanted to steal it and brought an attack that killed fifteen hundred million people or —

There are aliens, Ellaz replied. Maybe there are.

But why would they want the energy converter?

They didn’t, Ellaz thought with a chilling certainty. Someone else did.

Someone —!? Cody was silent. Finally, Ellaz, are you saying that there’s a traitor? That someone sold us out to aliens so that they could get the energy converter?

Or keep others from getting it, Ellaz thought back.

There’s a traitor, Cody thought. A traitor with tech no one else has —

Maybe the aliens, Ellaz replied. Maybe he swapped them for it.

But how did they know?

The Symposium was announced months — nearly a full year — before, Ellaz replied. Everyone was there. Mom was looking for funding. We were at our limit, almost broke.

I thought you Whirly’s were rich!

Were, Ellaz agreed. The energy converter — it was very expensive. And the research before, even worse.

A warp bubble, Cody thought. If it were possible, the alien could just pop on the ship, and pop back off — the ship could explode around it and it would be protected by the bubble.

Yes, Ellaz agreed wearily. Cody… I don’t feel well.

“I need to sleep,” Ellaz said when she’d recovered enough to talk.

“Actually, because Hope is going faster, we can get them help sooner than with Revenge,” Cody pointed out hopefully.

“We’re taking your aids, right?” Nora asked. Cody blinked. “Jacob and Gail? Because they’d pitch a fit if you didn’t take them.” She smiled. “And, they’re pretty good at what they do.”

“Which is?” Edie asked.

Nora pointed her finger at Cody and Ellaz. “Keep those two from collapsing.” She made a face. “We’ll need to take the bots, of course.”

“And maintenance bots,” Cody added. He turned to Edie. “Could a bot work the ring?”

“Once,” Edie said. She made a little explosion image with her hands and smiled.

“Right,” Cody said, catching on.

“Give us three, just in case,” Ellaz said. “Same for Revenge.”

“And how am I supposed to do that?” Nora demanded.

“I was talking to him,” Ellaz said, pointing to Cody.

“Gee, thanks!”

“Okay,” Jacob said. “So, we find an AMC, hook it up and then what, sir?”

“We’ve got consumables —” that meant food, uniforms and all the other things that a starship used up on a daily basis — “for thirty-five days. So…”

“Well, at Warp Nine we can get to Quark in eight point eight days,” Jacob said. “So we’d have a bit over twenty-six days’ worth of food even if we don’t top off.”

“Right,” Cody said. “And if we get to Deneb before the aliens?”

“Well, we warn everyone,” Jacob said immediately. “And then… I don’t know. What do we do?”

“Which is why we’re asking these questions,” Cody told him.

“I think we have to fight the aliens,” Jacob declared. “And we have to figure out how.”

“Exactly,” Cody agreed, “Ellaz and I sketched out a couple of possibilities. One is to extend the front of our warp bubble to create a lance.”

“A lance?”

“It’s like a sword only a lot longer,” Cody said.

“And how do we find the aliens? Won’t they be in warp?” Jacob said.

“Yes,” Cody agreed. “But if they’ve already attacked, we might be able to guess where they are.”

“So, close our eyes and hope?” Jacob asked incredulously.

“Well, I think we can be a bit more scientific than that,” Cody said. “And I want you to learn the lance.”

“Me?”

“The lance and we were also working on a warp mirror,” Cody said.

More like a reflector, the ghost of Ellaz corrected. It takes a warp and reflects it back on itself. But you’re right, Jacob, we need to figure out how to find a warp bubble.

“But —” Jacob spluttered. “I mean, how can you? A warp is a bubble into another dimension.”

If we can go there we should be able to see it, Ellaz’s ghost replied. Or… if we’re in warp.

Wouldn’t we have to be in the same level of warp? Cody thought. Then, remembering Jacob, he repeated himself out loud.

“What sort of research has there been on this?” Jacob wondered.

President Hanlan laughed so hard he couldn’t talk and pointed a finger at her while pounding the table with glee. When he recovered, he looked around and nodded. “Admiral Ford, Commodore Wright, may I introduce you to Admiral Cartwright, head of our navy here?”

“You destroyed twenty-six ships?” Admiral Cartwright said.

“We destroyed one,” Nora replied quickly. “The rest fled.”

“I don’t think they were prepared for any resistance,” Cody added. He turned to Nora. “And I don’t think they fled so much as they were leaving for their next target and it was too late to halt when we destroyed their ship.”

“And you’re offering your services to us?” the admiral guessed. He shot a probing look to the President who nodded in agreement. “And just what do you propose to do?”

“We’re going to detach Hermes and Captain Hartman here as guard and liaison,” Nora replied. “And the rest of the fleet —”

“Fleet?” Admiral Cartwright interrupted. “Are you referring to those brokedown ragtag ships you arrived in?”

“Yes, we are,” Cody said. “The ships we built in ten days —”

“Less —” Nora cut in.

“— to come to help you!” Cody finished hotly.

“We don’t —” Admiral Cartwright began just as heatedly.

“Adam,” President Hanlan said in a quelling tone. “You can either listen to what they have to say —”

“Or?”

“Or you can get the heck out of my conference and leave your resignation on my desk,” President Hanlan finished pointedly.

Nora turned back to Cody. “What did you do?”

“We,” Cody said, nodding toward Don Hartman, “brought the President up to date.”

“But you didn’t sign anything, did you?” Nora persisted.

“We were just getting to that,” Ed Hanlan said, shooting an amused look to Hartman.

“I might mention that Miz Wright is the daughter of the late Chloe Wright of Carlow Shipping,” Don explained.

“Chloey?” Ed exclaimed, rising from his seat and rushing over to Nora. “Your momma was Chloey?”

Nora nodded, looking surprised. She squeaked when President Hanlan grabbed her, lifted her off her feed and engulfed her in a bear hug. Cody shot a look to Hartman, wondering if he should rescue Nora but Don Hartman shook his head, eyes watering. Finally President Hanlan set Nora back on her feet, leaning forward to kiss the top of her head.

“Your pardon, young lady but your mother —” his voice broke and it was a moment before he could speak again “— she was something.” He shook a look to Cody. “Where did you find her?”

“She was baby-sitting a nursery,” Cody explained.

“I was only supposed to do it while my —” Nora forced herself to choke back a sob “— mother was in a meeting.”

“And then the aliens came,” Don Hartman said.

Nora nodded. “We had three hours’ worth of air left when Cody arrived.”

Hanlan glanced between her and Cody. “I see.” He waved her toward a seat and reclaimed his. “So, I understand that you’re here to rescue us.”

“That’s the plan,” Nora agreed. She glanced to Cody. “Did you eat?”

Cody shook his head.

“And where are my manners?” President Hanlan said, slapping himself on the forehead for show. “Well —” he broke off as someone knocked on the double doors and they opened, revealing a squad of servers, wheeling in two food carts. He broke into a grin, “Here they are!”

He had the servers set up and got them to provide Nora with the first pick, Cody second, Hartman third before gesturing to a server and saying, “The usual, if you please.” A tray arrived in front of him with a salad and a roast beef sandwich. “Imported from Meath, you know,” he said. “Best beef on the hoof.”

Cody shook his head. “I’m a clone.”

“Well, there’s nothing wrong with that,” Ellaz said. “I’m a clone, too.”

“I’d guessed,” Cody said. Most Whirly’s were clones. The family had perfected that two centuries ago. “So, Ell, what should we do?”

“Don’t call me that!” Ellax snapped at him.

“It’s shorter than Ellaz,” Cody said, drawling out the second syllable. “And when every second counts —”

“Call me Laz, then,” the girl said, glaring at him.

“You mean like lass, lassie, lassie go home?” Cody teased.

The girl hit him hard in the shoulder. “No, I mean like Laz,” Ellaz said.

“Or last?” Cody said, rubbing his sore arm.

“My mother was Elle,” the girl said, dropping her eyes down. Then she turned and glared at him. “And I’m not the last!”

Cody considered that. “We wait half an hour, then we change direction,” he said.

“Half an hour?” Ellaz said, consideringly. She nodded. “Right, because aliens use our clocks.”

“Half an hour because we’ve got four hours of air,” Cody said. “And that’s with just two of us.”

Ellaz was silent. Finally, “Right.”

Cody started counting. Slowly. In seconds. He got to eight when Ellaz said, “Pawn to Queen Four.”

“What?”

“Pawn to Queen Four, your move,” Ellaz said, sounding irritated.

“Pawn to Queen Four,” Cody said in reply. They were playing chess. Mental chess.

Ellaz beat him six times in a row. Then she said, “Time’s up.”

“Right,” Cody said, glad to be spared further humiliation. He fired up the shuttle, turned her and started up the scanners.

“Tracking debris,” Ellaz said, tapping in commands from the co-pilot’s seat.

“Just keep us clear,” Cody said, “then fire up IR. Look for hotspots.” He frowned. She noticed.

“What?”

“We’ve got an air leak,” Cody said. “Air’s down to two hours.” He pulled a pack of gum from his pocket, pulled a slice and passed the packet over to Ellaz.

She made a face. “That’s a disgusting habit.”

“Take one, start chewing,” Cody ordered. She took one, giving him a dubious look. “You know how to blow bubbles, right?”

“No,” Ellaz said, unwrapping her piece and sticking it in her mouth. She started chewing. “It tastes pleasant enough.”

“Spacer green,” Cody said, blowing a bubble experimentally. “IR?”

Chapter Nine

Chapter Nine

“Nine… eight… seven… six… five… four… three… two… cut warp!” Nora called. In front of them space shimmered back into reality.

“I have the hab,” Cody called. “Rotating.” He turned Hope around so that it was facing backwards.

“I can spot the ship,” Ellaz reported. “We’ve got a good look. Prepare the mirror, Cody.”

“Roger,” Cody replied. “We’re going to bring up the forward bubble and put all power into it.”

“Then you’ll execute pattern Alpha,” Ellaz agreed. “In three… two… one!”

Hope engaged the forward part of her ring, projecting a circular disk two thousand kilometers in front of her.

“Got it!” Ellaz cried. “We’ve deflected their lance but… Cody!”

“I see it!” Cody replied, twisting the ship in space so that its shielding warp mirror twisted the alien’s warp lance around — and back on the alien ship itself.

“Impact!” Nora called. “Impact and — Jeez!”

The alien spaceship blew up. The virtual view screen went black as it dimmed to protect their eyes and only slowly brightened.

“We’ve got debris everywhere!” Nora called.

Cody! Ellaz thought to him. The spare shuttles!

On it! Cody replied, firing off all the empty shuttles and sending them out to intercept any debris coming toward the spacehab.

“I’ve got eyes on the alien ships!” Nora warned. “They’re… wait a minute! Wait.” Then she whooped with joy. “They’re leaving!”

“How many?” Cody said aloud.

“All of them!” Nora crowed with glee.

Cody! Ellaz warned him.

Cody looked where she was pointing in virtual space. Oh, shit!

“Eject, eject, eject!” Cody shouted, pushing the buttons that fired the remaining shuttles away from Hope. Those weren’t the right words, he realized. “Abandon ship!”

Wasp flew away from Hope just as a large chunk of debris bounced off her warp ring, shattering it.

Cody! Ellaz’s voice came to him. And then, it was gone. Just like Hope.

#

“Everyone got off, Cody, they’re safe,” Nora told him when he’d recovered. He looked at her and shook his head. “Who?”

“Ellaz,” he told her.

“Sorry,” she said. “What do we do now?”

“Unknown ship, unknown ship, this is spacehab Elantra on 121.5, state your intentions,” a voice came over the speaker.

“We can’t swap it out,” Georgie said, anticipating his suggestion, “it’d take three days in a shipyard. At least.”

“And we don’t have three days,” Cody said. “Or… maybe we do.”

“What?” Georgie said.

“Well, when we get in system, let’s see what’s what, particularly with the rest of the fleet. Maybe we can get the nice people of Quark to let us use some of their slips,” Cody said. “After all, we’re going to save their planet.”

“But —” Georgie broke off. “We get there about two weeks before them. Point Midway is one day out which gives us thirteen days to prepare but we need three days to deploy the grav arrays, so that brings us down to ten days of slip. Maybe.”

“So if we can take three days for R&R,” Cody said, “and topping off, we’d still be sitting out there for a week, waiting for them.”

“And in three days… what?” Georgia asked.

“Well, not all ships have to leave at the same time,” Cody said. “We could send one group out ahead while the others —”

“You’re thinking we can build the tachcomms?” Georgie said. “How?”

“Well,” Cody sighed. “It’s a long shot but if we could get our virtual crew to work with a fab lab —”

“And what about the power?” Georgie protested. “How does that work?”

“Look, all I want is a simple Morse system,” Cody said. “Nothing too powerful but something we could put on each ship —”

“No time, that’d take weeks,” Georgie objected.

“The command ships?” Cody suggested. He shook his head. “No, that won’t work.”

“But your flare, that might work,” Georgie said.

“Huh?”

“A set of big flashes,” Georgie said. “We could probably tow another AMC and set it up to —”

“Blow with a tachyon trigger!” Cody said. “If we put our ships out of range and set the array to look for the aliens, we’d get a flash that would warn us and they’d head for the wrong target.”

I can’t guess, Ellaz replied. Are they more advanced than us? Do they think like us? How long have they had their tech? Can they build new things or are these ships the last of them? She shrugged. We just don’t know.

If they had it, wouldn’t they have spotted Hope when we defended Elantra? Other Cody asked.

Cody shrugged. Maybe. Or maybe they couldn’t react in time.

Or didn’t think that we’d be a threat, Nora added. Which may mean that the warp mirror was something they didn’t have.

Could they have it now? Cody wondered. And can we counter it?

They could, Ellaz agreed. And the best way to counter it is not to be seen.

Or make them look somewhere else, Cody thought.

How?

Make a big, splashy boom somewhere else, Other Cody thought. He smiled at Cody. I like it. Only… how?

#

“Forty-three hours, twelve minutes,” Georgie Cummings reported to Cody two days later. “It’ll be good to get out of this funky air.”

Cody nodded in agreement. The ECLSS had fouled the new filter and now they were on the last good filter but, because of the way that bacteria was clogging up so fast, Juan Suarez had suggested that they slow down the Environmental Control and Life Support System by eighty per cent.

“The system was designed for a crew of a hundred, and we’re just six,” Juan said, touting the latest excuse for why the system was misbehaving. They knew that one of the normal algaes used in recycling had overgrown, fouling the filters but they couldn’t say precisely why. Not even Ellaz and the other virtual people had a good idea. Worse, as Juan said, “This is why proper ships have at least two ECLSS. If one goes bonkers, we can purge it and restart it from the other.”

Fortunately for them all, if the ECLSS did totally pack it in, they could live in their shuttles on the canned air… for twenty-one days.

Which is why everyone was looking forward to planetfall at Quark. At the very least they could get a bunch of filters and work from there. Not ideal but… they’d live.

“That can work, right?” Ellaz said. “I mean, I looked at the specs and —”

“Sweetie, did you look at the field strength?” Edie said to her. Ellaz shook her head. “The strength is all wrong, we’d have a hell of a time tuning — well, I’m not sure we could tune rings so out-sized to —”

“It’s experimental,” Edie said. “And we — well, it’s experimental.”

“What?” Cody pressed her.

“One ring,” Edie said with a sigh. “A shaped field, a spindle, narrowing front and back.”

“That could work?” Cody asked.

“I’ve never heard of it,” Clive Bamber said. He narrowed his eyes at Edie. “Is this something —”

“Trade secret,” Jasmine said. She raised a hand to the side of her temples, adding, “Just like —”

“Jazzy, no!” Edie said, her eyes flashing angrily.

“You have a ring we could use?” Cody asked.

“We have a variable ring,” Jasmine said excitedly. “We needed a ship to test it on but —” she frowned “— we couldn’t get anyone to fund us.”

“I’ll fund you,” Cody said, waving a hand around at the wreck of the shipyard. “Take anything you want.”

“And that works,” Ellaz added darkly. “A single ring warp — that’s… I thought the math was impossible.”

“Was,” Jasmine agreed with a huge grin, her hands rising to her temples again.

Edie reached over and slapped her hands down. “Jazzy, no!”

Ellaz looked from mother to daughter. “You’ve got implants!”

“One kilogram anti-matter for every two thousand kilogram of mass,” Cody sang out. It was an old, old, old ratio, every kid knew it. Well, every spacer kid.

“At Warp One,” Ellaz corrected sourly. “And Warp Two?”

“The ratio drops by the root of the desired warp speed,” Cody rattled off. “So for Warp Two, you can only get forty-four kilograms per kg AM.”

“So, Warp 9?”

“Two point three two kg per kg AM,” Cody replied with a sigh.

“And the reverse?” Ellaz demanded. “So we know how much AM we need?”

“Roughly point four three kg AM per kg mass,” Cody said.

“Which is why freighters don’t go that fast,” Ellaz told him. “But, if you’re convinced that we need Warp Nine, then you’ve got to figure in the rings required and where are we going to find them?”

“We’re going about this wrong,” Cody said. “The farms use standardized cells, right?”

“Right,” Ellaz said. And then in a lower voice, “I think.”

“So with a Warp 5 core, a two megatonne freighter needs…” Cody did the math. “Four standard 100k containers.”

“Right,” Ellaz said. “And they do the swap-in swap-out but…”

“They need power for the change over equal to twice their load,’’ Cody said. Because anti-matter wasn’t comfortable around matter. It had to be kept in a special cryogenic magnetic containment field. Or… boom! “Why didn’t they just go after the power couplings?” Cody said, thinking about it.

“Who?”

“The aliens,” Cody said. “Get them on all the ships and — nothing left.”

“They didn’t do that,” Ellaz said. “In fact… I don’t think they got any of the anti-matter.”

“Did they steal the containers?” Cody wondered. “But if they did that, why didn’t they just steal the farms?”

“Aliens!” Ellaz snorted. “Do you really want to go down that rabbit hole now?”

“Okay, okay,” Cody said. “But if we used just a single container, we’d get a mass of… half a megatonne.” It was simple — divide two megatonnes by the four 100k containers.

“Go with that and you’ve got your mass, of course, minus that 100k container,” Ellaz said. “So four hundred kilotons.”

“And what if we miss?” Ellaz asked.

“We rotate another ten degrees and fire again,” Cody replied. “We keep firing until we can’t fire any more.”

“Why come out of warp?” Nora asked. “Why not just charge them at Warp Three with the lance? Turn around and charge again if we don’t hit something the first time?”

“How much fuel will we have?” Cody said, turning to Jacob.

“Not enough for more than Warp One,” Jacob replied. “And… well, we’d be moving awfully fast.”

“So we cut the aft part of the ring,” Cody said. He turned to Ellaz in the simulation. “We can do that, right?”

Cody, no one knows what happens with a partial warp!

“We could cut warp altogether and project a cone in front of us,” Nora said, her eyes gleaming. “We wouldn’t move, we’d just move the warp!”

“Can we do that?” Gail asked.

We couldn’t — Ellaz began and then spoke so that the others could hear, “We couldn’t with a different ring.”

“And with this one?” Cody asked.

“How much time do we have before we need an answer?” Ellaz said out loud.

“A bit under twelve hours,” Jacob replied.

“Cody, what if we can’t use the lance?” Nora asked.

Cody was silent for a moment. “There are how many people on that hab?”

“It’s the Elantra hab,” Ellaz said. “Among other things, they specialize in clones and cloning. The population is roughly five hundred and forty-three million.”

“And how many of us are on this ship?” Cody asked bleakly.

“Right,” Nora said. He didn’t need to spell it out. “So if we can’t use the lance?”

“We ram them,” Cody said.

“Yeah,” Jacob said. “That would work. But Cody, we’ve got shuttles. We can abandon ship, ram them and have all of us survive!”

All except Ellaz, who was tied to the Hope’s main computers. He might be able to get a copy but he doubted the shuttle — or any of the shuttles, separately or combined, had enough memory to copy her.

Ellaz, I need you to copy yourself, Cody told her.

Cody! I’m a ghost!

A large, wrenching metallic sound followed immediately by a sigh energized Cody as nothing else could. The ship was tearing apart. He raced around to the side of the shuttle, pounded on the airlock release and rushed inside.

“Wait!” A small voice cried out. He turned just in time to be slammed into by a small person. The girl. “Now, go, go, go!”

Cody didn’t need a kid to tell him, he raced to the pilot’s seat, plopped down… and looked at it in confusion.

“Don’t you know how to fly this thing?” the girl cried at him, dropping into the co-pilot’s seat. She hit a number of switches, the engines came to life, the airlock slammed shut and the shuttle twisted around, facing the bay doors.

“I know how to fly it!” Cody growled. “I’m just thinking —”

“Well, think faster!” the girl cried.

“We need to wait,” Cody said, taking grip of the joystick in front of him.

“Wait?” the girl cried. “The ship is coming apart all around us!”

“And we’re in a shuttle, we’re safe,” Cody told her, forcing himself to ignore his hammering heart which was busily questioning his sanity. “If we fly out — powered up —”

“They’ll see us and blast us,” the little girl concluded glumly.

Cody turned to her. Short-cropped strawberry blond hair, freckles, intense blue eyes. “You’re a Whirly!”

“Yes,” the girl said, “how astute of you!”

“But — but — you were shot!”

“Again, your perceptions amaze me,” the girl said. Well, Whirly’s were known throughout space to be some of the smartest people ever — and also some of the most sarcastic. Apparently, they started early.

“Cody Ford,” Cody said, glancing at the sensors, trying to get a feel for what was going on outside the steadily failing freighter. “As soon as we see enough debris, we blow the cargo bay door and fall through, powered down.”

The girl considered this. “Good plan,” she said finally. Then, “Ellaz.”

“Huh?”

“Ellaz Whirly,” the girl said, rolling her eyes at him.

“You’re not on the roster,” Cody said. He’d spent some time memorizing the crew and passenger rosters.

“‘Child, age eight,’” Ellaz replied. “Not listed on primary passenger cargo.”

A large, wrenching metallic sound followed immediately by a sigh energized Cody as nothing else could. The ship was tearing apart. He raced around to the side of the shuttle, pounded on the airlock release and rushed inside.

“Wait!” A small voice cried out. He turned just in time to be slammed into by a small person. The girl. “Now, go, go, go!”

Cody didn’t need a kid to tell him, he raced to the pilot’s seat, plopped down… and looked at it in confusion.

“Don’t you know how to fly this thing?” the girl cried at him, dropping into the co-pilot’s seat. She hit a number of switches, the engines came to life, the airlock slammed shut and the shuttle twisted around, facing the bay doors.

“I know how to fly it!” Cody growled. “I’m just thinking —”

“Well, think faster!” the girl cried.

“We need to wait,” Cody said, taking grip of the joystick in front of him.

“Wait?” the girl cried. “The ship is coming apart all around us!”

“And we’re in a shuttle, we’re safe,” Cody told her, forcing himself to ignore his hammering heart which was busily questioning his sanity. “If we fly out — powered up —”

“They’ll see us and blast us,” the little girl concluded glumly.

Cody turned to her. Short-cropped strawberry blond hair, freckles, intense blue eyes. “You’re a Whirly!”

“Yes,” the girl said, “how astute of you!”

“But — but — you were shot!”

“Again, your perceptions amaze me,” the girl said. Well, Whirly’s were known throughout space to be some of the smartest people ever — and also some of the most sarcastic. Apparently, they started early.

“Cody Ford,” Cody said, glancing at the sensors, trying to get a feel for what was going on outside the steadily failing freighter. “As soon as we see enough debris, we blow the cargo bay door and fall through, powered down.”

The girl considered this. “Good plan,” she said finally. Then, “Ellaz.”

“Huh?”

“Ellaz Whirly,” the girl said, rolling her eyes at him.

“You’re not on the roster,” Cody said. He’d spent some time memorizing the crew and passenger rosters.

“‘Child, age eight,’” Ellaz replied. “Not listed on primary passenger cargo.”

Chapter Six

Two days later, Cody checked in with his Engineering and ECLSS teams, bringing them up to date on the latest thoughts from the command deck.

Juan Suarez and ‘Chitty’ Brooks were on duty. Cody found them grumbling over a filter in the ECLSS unit.

“I say we just clean it out and keep going,” Juan said.

“And what if it goes down again?” Chitty demanded. “I say we pull one from stores and keep this in reserve.”

“What’s up?” Cody asked.

“It’s the danged air filter,” Juan said. “It fouled up two days ago and now it’s getting worse.”

“How many spares do we have?” Cody asked.

“Two,” Chitty said. “Normal complement for a ship this size. But… well, okay.” She shot a look to Juan. “Let’s pull it and we’ll keep an eye on the replacement.”

“And clean this one and put it back in stores,” Juan agreed. “Now, sir, what’s up?”

“We’ve been doing a lot of thinking,” Cody admitted. “Sorry I haven’t been around —”

“Georgie kept us up to speed,” Chitty told him. “Possible traitors, special energy converter, aliens in warp suits, tachyon communications — are we missing anything else, sir?”

Cody shook his head.

“Oh,” Chitty added, shooting a wink to Juan, “and your ghost self is flirting with your girlfriend’s ghost self. Plus ghost Gail is a hoot and Ellaz is the most annoying person imaginable.”

“In a good way,” Juan assured him. He shot a look to Chitty. “She warned you about this filter, right?”

Cody smiled. “Look, Ellaz was never really a people person,” Cody told them, raising a hand to urge compassion, “but she means well.”

“Beats my ass at chess, too,” Juan agreed. He pointed a finger to Chitty. “But she stonked the kid a couple of times.”

Cody frowned at them. “How do you —?”

“She appears on the displays,” Chitty said. “Wants to keep an eye on us.”

“I think she gets bored,” Juan added sympathetically. “And… well, she didn’t get a fair shake, did she, sir?”

Cody nodded.

“But you’re going to have bambinos —” Juan added enthusiastically.

“Six of them!” Chitty added. Then she shot him a look. “Have you lined up the babysitters?”

“Why, do you have any in mind?” Cody asked.

“It’s not just a question of people, it’s a question of duration,” Edie said. “Are we traveling for a month, a year, what?”

“How long is it to the nearest star?” Cody said. “Double that for safety and that’s our duration.”

“If you can build a warp drive,” Edie said.

“If we can build a warp drive, mother,” Jasmine said, grinning at her. “And aren’t we the best two warp tuners in all the system?”

“Jazzy, we’re the only two in the system,” Edie Crump reminded her.

“My point exactly!” Ellaz said, grinning at them. She turned to Bamber and Wilson. “So, what else do we need?”

“We can get the plans from the computers,” Cody said, jerking his head to the spaceport outside. “And they’ve got to have remotes, right? We can use them.”

“Son,” Clive Bamber said, “you want to build a starship here, in the middle of a ruined spaceport?”

“Do you think we’ll do better at Jurgens?” Cody asked. Jurgens was the other major shipyard on the moon.

“Let’s see what we’ve got here first,” Moira Collins suggested. She turned to their new crewmate, “Nora, can you watch the babies?”

Nora was practically asleep on her feet. “Uh, sure?”

“I’ll stay with her,” Ellaz volunteered, shooting a look toward Cody. “You get suited up.” Cody nodded but had the feeling that he was missing something, some signal the girl was trying to relay to him. “And while you guys are out there, I’ll start building a list.”

“Well, no matter what, we have to check for supplies,” Clive Bamber agreed, glancing to his wife who nodded in agreement.

Two hours later, Cody thought to Gail, You are now qualified as a ring master.

I am? Gail squealed with joy. Wait until I tell Jacob!

Don’t, Cody cautioned.

Oh, Gail sounded depressed. He can’t do it, can he?

Let’s not try just yet, Cody replied. But, if you want a break, can you get Nora here?

I don’t need a break! Gail declared stoutly. Do you? The monitor will help. Then, Why’d you name it Ghost?

It seemed like a good name, Cody lied. He had been surprised that the ghost of Ellaz had been shy around Gail — at least, at first. Later, when it was clear that Gail was just the natural that Ellaz had predicted, she’d been willing to come out more and more, revealing her true “self.” Cody dropped the issue, thinking, Okay, you watch the ship and I’ll get Nora.

Is she going to learn, too?

Yes, Cody replied. And, when there’s time, I think we should consider implants.

Implants? Gail squealed in surprise. I could get one? But aren’t they like mega-expensive?

I’m pretty sure we’ll be able to get them for you.

And Nora? Gail pressed. If she’s good, she should have them, too.

If she wants, Cody agreed. Your ship, Ensign.

My ship, Captain, Gail agreed, her “voice” only warbling a little in awe.

Cody took a deep breath and pulled his helmet off. He turned to the main cabin and saw, to his surprise that Nora was cuddled up with Jacob in her arms, asleep.

“Nora?” Cody called softly.

Nora’s eyes flew open and she gasped, looking from Cody to the cockpit.

“Gail’s been checked out,” Cody told her. “How about you?”

“Me?”

“Ellaz said you’d be a natural,” Cody told her, forcing himself to grin. What had Ellaz said about “people skills?” Then he added, “If I can get you checked out, I can get some rest.”

Nora considered that for a moment before rising from her seat. “Where is the VR headset?”

#

Ellaz was right — Nora was a natural. Two hours later, she shooed Cody to the main cabin and told him not to bother her.

Passage:
Five minutes later he was in his command chair on Wasp and Ellaz was seated beside him. Nora was seated in her Phoenix shuttle. The babies were in one shuttle along with their minders. ECLSS reported green. Engineering reported green.

“All systems are green, Captain,” Nora reported. “We are ready for tow.”

“Right,” Cody said. He switched frequencies. “Clive? Moira? We’re ready.”

“Confirm,” Moira Collins replied. “Engage on your command.

“Roger, commencing tug,” Cody said. He’d programmed the two heavy lift tugs himself and Mr. Bamber and Miz Collins had double-checked his calculations.

He watched his display as the two heavy-lift tugs rose above Hope and slowly descended, extending their cables down until they magnetically locked into place. He double-checked the readings then said, “XO?”

“Looks good,” Nora replied.

“Roger, lifting,” Cody said, commanding the two tugs to commence the lift.

Slowly at first, and then with greater speed, Hope rose into the vacuum above the ruins of the Carlow shipyards.

It took them twenty minutes to get on station, in low orbit above the moon,

“Final check,” Cody said.

“All stations, final check,” Nora repeated. They listened as the reports came in: ECLSS, Propulsion, Engineering, Comms, Nav, Astro — all green. Nav, Comms, and Astro were Cody and Ellaz with Nora tasked as backup, “Captain, all systems are green. Ready for detach.”

“Roger,” Cody said. He sent the commands to the two tugs and tensed for a moment until he felt the four lines unhook and retract. “Carlow, we are ready for departure,” he radioed five minutes later.

“Godspeed and good luck!” Edie Crump called back.

“Have fun!” Little Jasmine added. In the background, Cody could hear a chorus of others gathered around the microphone, shouting their encouragement.

Cody swallowed hard. If this didn’t work — a hand grabbed his and he turned to see Ellaz smiling at him. “Chicken?” she teased.

“Helmets,” Cody said, pulling his helmet down and sliding into the ship’s comp-link.

Here, Ellaz said, her ghost hand sliding into his. They looked around, found the stars they needed, double-checked their astrogation and then Cody thought, Fire up the ring.

A surge of power flooded through the makeshift ship. Cody fed it into the ring. And then…. Warp Nine.

“Are there others?” Cody asked while he took the data and fed it into his navigation computers.

“You’re the first,” the controller replied ninety seconds later.

Cody and Ellaz exchanged dismayed looks. Cody recovered first. “We’re on profile, systems on automatic, we’ve got sixty-three minutes until rendezvous.”

“Pawn to Queen Four,” Ellaz said a moment later.

#

An hour later, Deep Space One called out to them, “Wasp, you are on profile, cleared to land.”

“Roger,” Cody said. He’d actually won two games against Ellaz. She’d decided that she was tired afterwards but Cody was pretty sure that her ego had been bruised. He sent her back to get vac rats — rations designed for eating in microgravity. He also checked their inventory. That had been on his list, just after he’d finished clearing the fuel valve but… the world had ended.

Ellaz came back with four rats — two drinks and two smoothies. She glanced at the labels and passed two to Cody. A spinach smoothie and a vanilla drink. Cody didn’t bother to ask about the rations she’d chosen for herself, he was sure she was still miffed about losing her chess game.

“We’re bringing you inside, so don’t do anything until we’ve cleared you,” DS1 added.

“Wilco,” Cody said tersely, watching his displays as Wasp turned on her tail and slowly began the descent to a waiting platform. He would have to straighten her up to deploy her landing gear but that wouldn’t be until the last few seconds. “They didn’t really have to put us on our tail,” Cody said to Ellaz.

Ellaz nodded. “Um —”

“Let’s not say anything about your power converter,” Cody suggested. Ellaz shot him a surprised look but nodded. Cody kept a smile to himself — apparently he’d guessed what she was going to say. Well, clones tended to be more paranoid than others. “Do we need an alias for you?”

Ellaz considered that and shrugged. “What do you think?”

“I think… I think it’s best if you’re my little sister,” Cody told her. “I was getting you out of the bay where I’d had you stowaway because we needed to get you out-system.”

“Why?”

“To project the fields,” Cody guessed. Edie smiled and nodded at him. He frowned. “If you extended the field far enough forward, could you make a lance?”

“A lance?” Ellaz said. “You mean an energy lance?”

Cody nodded.

“Possibly,” Edie said. “But why would you — oh!” She gulped down her food and glanced to the other two. “Are you coming?”

They raced back to the command center, put on their helmets and linked in to the main computer systems.

Five minutes later, they each pulled off their helmets, their expressions ashen.

“Warp lance,” Cody said.

“They used a warp lance,” Ellaz agreed. “They tore everything apart.”

“What about the planet?” Edie asked.

“The lances warped the atmosphere,” Cody said. “No one below had a chance.”

“If the gravity didn’t twist them to pieces, the radiation was instantly fatal,” Edie said. “But — did you see the size of them?”

“I only caught glimpses, just the edge of the lances,” Ellaz confessed.

“Interpolating from the lances to the warp, the ships had to be massive,” Edie said.

“I counted twenty-six,” Cody added.

“That’s the double of a prime number,” Ellaz said. Cody shook his head at her. “Well, it is!”

“Doesn’t mean anything,” Cody told her. “But I got a timing… I think. From first shot to last was less than two hours.”

“That’s not counting what they did out at Xerxes,” Edie added.

“Right,” Cody said, thrusting them down to the moon’s surface. “Let’s see what’s what.”

#

The shuttle landed thirty meters away from the blinking light. Clive elected to go first, followed by Edie Crump. The rest stayed inside the shuttle.

The light came from a section of the spaceport, on the ground level. There was debris around it — metal girders, bits of smashed ships and building materials — which Clive navigated easily.

“We’ve got an airlock!” Clive cried triumphantly. “I’m banging on it.”

A moment later the flashing light went out.

“What’s going on?” Jasmine asked. “Why aren’t —”

“This is weird,” Clive said. “Captain, can you do a thermal scan?”

“You’re in the way,” Cody warned. “All I’d get is your suits.”

“Right, backing up,” Clive said.

A moment later, Cody fired up the sensors in infrared, looking for warm spots. “Okay,” Cody said. “I’ve got a number of small spots, nothing major but —” he broke off and turned to Ellaz “— I think they’re kids.”

“Kids?” Clive said. “Okay, we’re going in.”

“I need to go to them,” Ellaz said, unbuckling herself. “They’re going to need me.”

“Why?” Cody said.

“Those are kids,” Ellaz said. “I’m a kid. They’ll need me to talk with them.”

Cody frowned. “Have you ever talked to kids?”

“Sure, loads of times!” Ellaz swore. Cody gave her a look. “Well, no,” Ellaz said, “but they’re at the spaceport which means either they worked there —”

“Not likely,” Edie interjected.

“Or they were on a tour,” Ellaz finished. “Which means they are interested in construction —”

“What’s that got to do with you going there?”

“Skills assessment,” Ellaz said, putting on her helmet and walking into the airlock.

“And none of us can do that?” Clive Bamber demanded.

“Probably,” Ellaz said, “but I’ll be quicker.”

Cody shook his head. The girl was so conceited.

“We’re going in,” Clive said. “You can come when we’ve cleared the area.”

“Of course,” Ellaz agreed. “There’s no point in me risking my life.”

“Is she always like this?” Jasmine Crump asked, bustling up to the cockpit and dropping into the co-pilot’s seat. She glanced at the displays, tapped a window and redirected one of their outside cameras.

An hour later the monitor program beeped, Cody and Ellaz looked up and languidly steered Hope around the latest mass clump. A moment later they put her back on their new course. Then they went back to their “work.”

It’s not a perfect mirror, Ellaz thought as they admired their handiwork hours later.

It’s more like a reflector than a mirror, Cody thought in agreement. It’ll take a warp field and reverse it back on itself.

If there’s a ship inside —

It would be destroyed, Cody agreed. And… we don’t know if this will work.

Only one way to find out, Ellaz agreed. She blew out a sigh. I need a break.

Go! We can watch the ring!

“We?” Ellaz asked.

Me and the monitor, Cody replied.

Oh! Sure, Ellaz thought back, sounding relieved. He could feel it when she dropped out of the mind-link.

Cody peered forward to the warp space in front of them.

#

“Nora, where’s Ellaz?” Cody called out loud.

“I’m just sending her up now,” Nora said. Cody frowned. She sounded stressed.

“Is everything okay?” Cody asked.

“She’s on her way,” Nora said.

“Okay,” Cody replied, returning his attention to the simulation and the warp field in front of them.

A moment later, he felt Ellaz’s hand on his. Do you need a break?

No, I’m fine, Cody thought back. What about you?

Oh! Nothing, Ellaz… lied.

Why did you just lie? Cody asked her. You know I can tell, now, right?

I do now, Ellaz confessed, mentally sighing. We’ve got thirty-one hours, right?

Minus a few minutes, Cody thought back in agreement.

We’re almost there, Ellaz thought, distractedly.

What is it? Cody asked. He felt a sense of dread in the pit of his stomach. Something was wrong. Something was wrong with Ellaz. She’d been sick, had thrown up, had — That converter, Cody thought suddenly.

It was experimental, Ellaz thought back. It absorbed the energy.

There was a blue flash, Cody recalled. That means that it didn’t absorb all the energy. And you fell to the deck.

Yeah, it wasn’t perfect, Ellaz agreed. So?

What aren’t you telling me? Cody said. The belt. Where is it?

It’s safe, Ellaz said. Inert. It did its job and now it’s just melted components.

“Right,” Ellaz said. “Cody, we’ve got it. You were right. We set up a separate run without the filters, had the computers check for warp anomalies and we’ve got twenty-six targets, all of them ahead of us. Also, they’re traveling at… around Warp five point five, or five point six, I can’t be certain.”

“We’re going to be —”

“Just about two hours and twenty-four minutes too late,” Gail said.

“If we speed up?” Cody asked.

“We don’t have enough fuel to go more than Warp Nine point One,” Jacob told him. “And that buys us —”

“Only twenty-five minutes,” Nora said. “We’ll be nearly two hours too late.”

“We’ll do it,” Cody said, pushing up their speed, increasing the flow of their remaining anti-matter in the ring.

Cody! We don’t know how the ring will react! Ellaz warned him.

Every minute, every second, Cody replied. “What’s the population of Deneb?”

“The system or the planet?” Nora asked. “Four billion for the system, three billion on the planet.”

“Another billion plus in the spacehabs in orbit,” Jacob added.

“What are their priorities?” Cody asked. “What will they go after first?”

“The planet,” Ellaz said. “Although they took out Xerxes first back at Meath.”

“They might do the same for Virzen,” Jacob said. “That’s the largest asteroid in their inner belt.”

“We need to know where they’ll be in two hours when we come out of warp,” Cody said.

“They could be long gone,” Nora said in a forlorn voice.

“But what if they’re not?” Cody asked. “What was their order of assault?”

“Asteroids, planet, docks, moons — and Deneb has four — then the spacehabs,” Gail said. “But —”

“I know,” Cody said, raising a hand, “we can’t rely on that.” He frowned. “Which spacehabs? What order?”

And why didn’t they hit them when they hit the planet? Ellaz wondered privately to him.

“Deneb has five,” Nora said. “And they’ve got six docks. That’ll slow them down.”

“How much? How long?” Cody asked.

“Um…,” Nora did some rapid calculations on a spreadsheet. “Interpolating from Meath to Deneb, taking into account the extra targets…. Cody, they might take three hours.”

“Which gives us an hour,” Cody said. “And what’s going to be left?”

“One, maybe two spacehabs,” Nora said.

Cody shot her a look but he nodded. That had not been his first choice of names but it was a good one all the same. And, as Ellaz was going to be his first officer, he knew better than to argue. Edie would be chief engineer.

They were lucky to salvage five good extruders. The extruders could 3D print pretty much anything but… there was a penalty for size and volume. In fact, designing the connecting tubes and the hydroponic interiors were the most challenging parts of the overall designs for the two ships. That, and figuring out how to deal with the necessary sanitary facilities. Fortunately, as there were under fifty people, all told, and they were only going for five days, it was a simple matter of finding enough onesie coveralls for all.

#

The starships were still seven and eight days away from completion. The bots did great work, the kids — those old enough — helped as best they could and were quick to learn. Cody had a fondness for little Gail Eber — not so little at seven years — who had taken to following him around as an assistant. Gail was easier to work with than the prickly Ellaz. Like everyone else, she was an orphan and she attached herself to Cody with a certain amount of hero-worship. It was Ellaz who quipped that Gail was “in love.”

Fortunately, Gail wasn’t in love as much as she was lonely. Cody stifled Ellaz’s jibes when he found another youngster, Jacob Falcon, to attach to Ellaz. Ellaz didn’t notice at first, then she bristled, and finally worked Jacob to death. Cody was lucky 
when the world exploded. He wasn’t there.

Lucky, only he didn’t know it. Not yet. He was busy cleaning the fuel intake valve on the cargo shuttle 
Wasp
, inside the docking bay of the star freighter, 
Hornet
. 

He had a rag and worked to make sure that there was no dirt, lint, or “other hazard” that might stop the valve from accepting the fuel line. Such hazards led to a bad connection which could lead to all sorts of messes — most of which Cody was certain he’d have to clean up.

The 
Hornet
 lurched and Cody looked up. Freighters in dock occasionally had to fire thrusters to maintain station. Perhaps that was it. He went back to work. He was pretty sure that he was done, that the valve was clean enough but he didn’t want to ask the cargomaster to look too early.

There was a noise from outside in the cargo bay. Cody froze. He listened. A faint whine and a thud. Was that normal?

Cody put down his rag and slunk down under the shuttle, leaning to one side of the curving hull to look around.

A coverall-clad spacer raced into view — and disintegrated, leaving only black dust where he had been. Cody stifled a hiss and ducked back, hoping he hadn’t been spotted.

Who the hell had a blaster like that? And why kill on a 
freighter?
 Pirates? Was that what that lurch had been earlier? Had they been boarded?

Cody turned his head toward a sound that came behind him. He caught just a glimpse of something — green, furry, tall. It looked sort of like a caterpillar but standing on its butt, upright. The caterpillar bulged at its midsection and a blue flash shot out. There was a cry and Cody spotted a small figure slump down to the deck and lay still. A girl. Maybe seven, maybe eight.

“Implants?” Cody said.

Jasmine looked pleadingly at her mother.

“You might as well spill it,” Cody said, pointing to Ellaz. “She’s got implants, too.”

Ellaz shot him a horrified look, her mouth hanging open. “How did you — I mean, of course, brother, you would know.”

“Why did your father give her —” Edie Crump began but broke off. She glanced between Ellaz and Cody, comparing their faces. “You’re not a Ford,” she said to Ellaz.

“And he’s not a captain!” Ellaz said, pointing to Cody, desperate to deflect the attention away from her. Then she frowned at him. “Have you got implants?”

Cody smiled, pulled the hair back from his temples and displayed the lighter colored skin underneath it. “Dad figured we should step up our game.”

“And your Dad?” Clive Bamber said. “Daniel Ford?”

Cody shot Ellaz a glaring look and turned back to Mr. Bamber. “Yes. He died in that shuttle accident.”

“Four implants,” Edie breathed, looking from one to the other to the other. “We’ve got four implants!”

“So?”

“Don’t you know what we can do?” Edie cried triumphantly. She raced around the command center, pulling open cabinets, drawers and — with a cry of triumph — pulled out a glistening helmet. “Look around, there have to be more!”

There were, in fact, five implant helmets in the control center.

Cody grabbed the one that Edie threw to him, put it on and immediately went to the shuttle warehouse virtually.

Startup procedures for the shuttles popped into his mind. He examined them and snorted — three days. “I bet I can get it down to one,” he said to himself — this time with more conviction. He checked his remotes, found a number of bots and started them into action.

“Captain — er, Cody, what are you doing?” Mr. Bamber’s voice penetrated through Cody’s helmet.

Go on! Ellaz thought with a mental wave to him. And Pawn to Queen Four.

When Cody came back, he reported, “Downstream, T+3, all systems nominal.”

“Roger,” Nora’s voice came back immediately. “We’re good here.”

Cody turned back to their view of space at Warp Nine.

Two hours later, after winning two games of chess, Ellaz said, Are we there yet?

Cody laughed.

#

Cody jerked when someone touched him. He pulled up his helmet. “You need to eat,” Gail said to him, passing him a hot tray.

Cody nodded in thanks and started gulping down his food.

“And I’m bored,” Gail added five minutes later when he’d finished and passed her back his tray. “Also, when are you going to sleep?”

Cody fumbled for an answer but Gail waved him off. “I’ll tell you,” she said, turning to back out of the hatch. “Ellaz needs to eat, too.”

Cody smiled at her and pulled back on his helmet. Chow time!

Ellaz took a moment to respond. What?

Chow time, Cody replied. He frowned. What were you doing?

Updating the system, Ellaz replied. Is — oh, someone’s poking my arm. I guess I should go.

Go!

#

Okay, now you need to sleep, Cody thought to Ellaz, thirty minutes after he woke up from his four hour “nap.” I’ll call if I need help.

I’m not sleepy!

Get your helmet off, crawl back to bunk and lie down, Cody ordered. Close your eyes, get some sleep.

Can’t I sleep here? Ellaz half-begged.

No, Cody replied, you need to lie down, get some shut eye.

Okay, Ellaz replied glumly.

Cody waited a moment then reached over to tap her hand. I said go.

He felt Ellaz rise and the cabin shake as she moved back to the main cabin. She patted his arm as she left.

And Cody was alone with the command of a starship moving at Warp Nine. He checked on their monitor program and came to the conclusion that it was bored.

#

Are we there yet? Cody thought to Ellaz when he plugged back into the mind-link two days later. I never thought that space could be this boring.

Don’t jinx it, Ellaz warned. You good? I want to take a break.

Chapter Five

Cody slept in late and was woken by a splash of water on his face. Ellaz called grumpily to him, “Come on! Get up!”

Cody scowled at her and went to the restroom to clean himself up. He ate quickly, sitting in his cot beside Ellaz and then they rushed off to the Simulations Lab.

“Today, we’re going to start with Warp Nine,” Edie said.

“Okay, and then?” Ellaz asked.

Edie grinned. “And then things will go wrong.”

“We don’t even know if the ships will work and you want to practice disasters?” Ellaz growled.

Edie smiled at her and nodded. “Helmets!”

Warp Nine was a strain, even with the monitor program to help. When they were done — and they’d only been “gone” for two hours — both Cody and Ellaz were exhausted.

“Five minutes,” Edie told them, as she passed a drink to Ellaz. Jasmine had one for Cody. “Now, while you’re getting ready, what’s the first thing to do in an emergency?”

“Fly the ship,” Cody said.

“Wrong, check life support,” Ellaz replied. “If you can’t breathe, you die.”

“That’s part of fly the ship,” Cody said.

“It’s the first part,” Ellaz said.

“Hull integrity, power, nav, propulsion, comms,” Cody said, reciting the standard list for a shuttle.

“Warp ring?” Ellaz said. “Where does that fit in?”

“Propulsion,” Cody said.

“Time,” Edie said sternly.

“We’ve got fifty seconds —” Ellaz griped.

“Helmets on!” Edie said.

And they were in the simulation again.

Sorry, Cody thought as he felt a virtual hand touch his.

Fine, Ellaz thought back, giving his hand a squeeze.

“Prepare for Warp Nine,” Edie’s voice came to them. “And… enter!”

They entered. They flew. And then…

What’s that? Cody thought as their monitor beeped in warning. He and Ellaz examined the artificial world around them, spotted the problem — a chunk of something darker, thicker in front of them coming fast and —

“Good job!” Edie called as they dodged around the chunk of thick space-time. “Now, get back on course!”

That took more finesse than they’d used before but they got back on course. And then another chunk of thickness came at them.. They dodged it. And another. And another. Two more were just ahead and —
