“Well, sir, the way I see it there are three possibilities,” Jacob said, thrilled to be distracted and doing something useful.

“Yes?”

“First, we arrive in time to warn Deneb,” Jacob said. “Second, we are too late. Third, we arrive just as they’re being attacked.”

“If we’re too late?” Cody asked.

“The first thing we need to do, sir, is see if we can get refueled. Second thing, resupplied,” Jacob said. A glowing list appeared in the simulation in front of Cody’s eyes. “After that, I recommend Search And Rescue but —”

“But what?”

“Well, sir, should we do that or head on to Quark to warn them?” Jacob said. “I know Revenge is heading there but at Warp Five, only. At Warp Nine, we could get there in… just a bit under nine days.”

“And fuel?”

“Well, sir, we’d need to swap our AMC,” Jacob said.

“And if we have no swap?” Cody asked.

“Um… well, according to our calculations, we were about thirty per cent more efficient than planned,” Jacob said after a moment. “Which will mean that we have about thirty thousand kg of AM left.”

“And?” Cody prompted, glancing to the view of warp space in front of him, checking for any upcoming “clumps.”

“Well, we mass only two hundred and fifty three k-tons, sir,” Jacob said. “That might explain our performance.”

Cody grinned. “Probably. And…?”

“Well, our mass ratio with 30 k-tons AM would be 0.1185,” Jacob said. “Our initial mass ratio was 0.3952 although we’d calculated on 0.250 —”

“Jacob,” Cody interrupted. “What can we do with 30 k-tons of anti-matter?”

“Um…” Jacob brought up a routine, entered a few parameters and then said brightly, “About Warp 3.56, sir.”

“And? Time to Quark at that speed?” Cody asked.

“One hundred and forty-one point six days, sir,” Jacob reported glumly.

“And back to Meath?” Cody prompted.

“Eighty point nine days, sir,” Jacob replied. “But we’ve got consumables for the next thirty-five days.”

“So, neither approach is acceptable,” Cody agreed.

“Are we going to die?” Jacob asked miserably.

“Some day,” Cody said. “But… look what we did at Meath. We built a starship and in… Eighteen hours and forty-nine minutes and twenty-one seconds, we’ll get to Deneb.”

Ellaz made a face. “Now?”

“Yeah, now,” Cody told her, waving a hand toward her. “I wanted to show you something.”

“Okay,” Ellaz grumbled, following him with dragging steps.

The Lab was clear, Cody had checked.

“So what do we do?” Ellaz demanded as Cody sat in one of the seats in the center table.

Cody smiled at her, winked, and pulled his helmet on. With a sigh, Ellaz did the same.

Okay, now what? Ellaz demanded.

Now no one can hear us, Cody replied. I was thinking —

!!

Don’t joke, Cody said. Here, in the mind-link, I can show you.

Show me what?

In answer, their world shimmered, shook and — resolved itself into a cargo bay. The cargo bay on the Hornet.

Now you can see what I saw, Cody thought to Ellaz. And you’ll know that I wasn’t crazy.

Okay, Ellaz said as Cody relived his memories.

#

There was a noise from outside in the cargo bay. Cody froze. He listened. A faint whine and a thud. Was that normal?

Cody put down his rag and slunk down under the shuttle, leaning to one side of the curving hull to look around.

Cody’s heart thudded in his throat. Ellaz, where did all that energy go?

It was absorbed after it was converted, Ellaz replied. Did she sniff?

Ellaz, what was it converted to? Cody asked. And… did you absorb it?

I was the nearest mass, Ellaz said. In fact, it surrounded me.

And the energy?

We wanted to track it, Ellaz thought defensively

What sort of energy? Cody thought. But he knew… the sickness, the fatigue, the strange surge of energy…

Gamma radiation, Ellaz admitted. A lethal dose.

What? Why didn’t you say something? We could have — we could —

We could have done nothing, Ellaz cut him off. I was already dying when I got aboard your shuttle. It was just a matter of time, nothing more.

How long? Cody thought to her.

How long have I got? Ellaz replied. Well, my hair is already coming out. We figure I’ve got maybe enough time to get us there.

No, Cody thought. “No!”

I’m sorry, Ellaz thought to him, reaching to grab his hand. He jerked it away from her then, sheepishly, put it back over hers. I wanted to tell you, wanted to —

We can beat this, Cody thought. I’ll get Nora and we’ll —

No time, Cody, Ellaz broke in. I’m dying. You need to accept that. I have.

But — you still owe me a rematch!

I’ll give you a rematch, Ellaz told him. That’s been my project.

A chess program? Cody thought, surprised.

A memory, Ellaz corrected. My memory. Memories of me.

Here? In the link?

Here. In the link, Ellaz agreed. That way, you should be able to get to Deneb even if — well, even if.

You die too soon, Cody finished for her.

The program is watching us, watching me, learning from us, Ellaz said. It can’t be me, not perfectly but… I think it will help. At least with the ring.

How much time? Cody thought.

Not enough, Ellaz replied. That’s why I was so long coming back.

That’s what Nora wouldn’t tell me, Cody thought.

She’s good, Ellaz replied. You get her an implant, I think she’ll work. And Gail.

Gail’s seven, Cody shot back.

And Jasmine is six, Ellaz reminded him.

My point exactly!

No, Ellaz replied. You’re not thinking.

Chapter One

Cody was lucky when the world exploded. He wasn’t there.

Lucky, only he didn’t know it. Not yet. He was busy cleaning the fuel intake valve on the cargo shuttle Wasp, inside the docking bay of the star freighter, Hornet.

He had a rag and worked to make sure that there was no dirt, lint, or “other hazard” that might stop the valve from accepting the fuel line. Such hazards led to a bad connection which could lead to all sorts of messes — most of which Cody was certain he’d have to clean up.

The Hornet lurched and Cody looked up. Freighters in dock occasionally had to fire thrusters to maintain station. Perhaps that was it. He went back to work. He was pretty sure that he was done, that the valve was clean enough but he didn’t want to ask the cargomaster to look too early.

There was a noise from outside in the cargo bay. Cody froze. He listened. A faint whine and a thud. Was that normal?

Cody put down his rag and slunk down under the shuttle, leaning to one side of the curving hull to look around.

A coverall-clad spacer raced into view — and disintegrated, leaving only black dust where he had been. Cody stifled a hiss and ducked back, hoping he hadn’t been spotted.

Who the hell had a blaster like that? And why kill on a freighter? Pirates? Was that what that lurch had been earlier? Had they been boarded?

Cody turned his head toward a sound that came behind him. He caught just a glimpse of something — green, furry, tall. It looked sort of like a caterpillar but standing on its butt, upright. The caterpillar bulged at its midsection and a blue flash shot out. There was a cry and Cody spotted a small figure slump down to the deck and lay still. A girl. Maybe seven, maybe eight.

There was a loud blast and the alien caterpillar recoiled, turned, and fired its blue blast again. It moved out of the cargo bay, pursuing the shooter.

Cody hoped that the shooter got the alien.

“And you’re alive,” Cody said. Again, the rolled eyes. “The alien shot you. It shot Martin and he turned to dust.”

Ellaz patted her shirt. “Energy converter.”

“What?”

“I’m wearing a portable energy converter,” Ellaz said. “It’s experimental, of course.” Of course. Because the Whirly family was famous for their experiments. Then she pointed to the displays, “There. That’s major structural failure. We need to go. Can’t be certain how long the core will hold.”

Cody agreed. He thumbed the freighter’s emergency airlock controls and the cargo hold door blew out. Then he tapped the cold jets once, enough to start the shuttle out of the disintegrating cargo bay. Once outside, he tapped a series of quick thrusts that set the shuttle tumbling like it was out of control. And then, to make that real, he shut down their active systems.

“Holy shit!” Ellaz cried, pointing behind them. “They got everything!”

Cody followed her finger with his head and his jaw dropped.

The freighter Hornet was docked at Parminter Station Number One, the largest of four orbiting cargo stations for the planet Meath. Meath was a planet of over a billion people, with orbital satellites providing homes for another half billion. Was.

Parminter Station One and the dozen freighters that had been docked were only shards of metal and smaller objects floating haphazardly in the light of the planet’s star.

“They got the orbitals, too,” Cody said, pointing to a smaller object in the distance. The orbitals were — had been — giant circular space stations — habitats for the half billion people who preferred to live in their own artificial atmosphere. He made a face. “I can’t tell about the planet —”

“Infrared,” Ellaz said.

“We can’t use power,” Cody said.

“Passives,” Ellaz replied, tapping a command into the shuttle’s computer only to have her hand smacked away by Cody.

“No power!” Cody hissed at her.

Ellaz put her fingers in her mouth and glared at him. “You don’t know —”

“I don’t!” Cody agreed. “And until we do, we’re going to be a piece of debris.”

“If they can track IR, they can see our heat,” Ellaz said.

“Which is why we’re staying close to the freighter,” Cody said. “We’ll be in the thermal shadow.”

“And you’re alive,” Cody said. Again, the rolled eyes. “The alien shot you. It shot Martin and he turned to dust.”

Ellaz patted her shirt. “Energy converter.”

“What?”

“I’m wearing a portable energy converter,” Ellaz said. “It’s experimental, of course.” Of course. Because the Whirly family was famous for their experiments. Then she pointed to the displays, “There. That’s major structural failure. We need to go. Can’t be certain how long the core will hold.”

Cody agreed. He thumbed the freighter’s emergency airlock controls and the cargo hold door blew out. Then he tapped the cold jets once, enough to start the shuttle out of the disintegrating cargo bay. Once outside, he tapped a series of quick thrusts that set the shuttle tumbling like it was out of control. And then, to make that real, he shut down their active systems.

“Holy shit!” Ellaz cried, pointing behind them. “They got everything!”

Cody followed her finger with his head and his jaw dropped.

The freighter Hornet was docked at Parminter Station Number One, the largest of four orbiting cargo stations for the planet Meath. Meath was a planet of over a billion people, with orbital satellites providing homes for another half billion. Was.

Parminter Station One and the dozen freighters that had been docked were only shards of metal and smaller objects floating haphazardly in the light of the planet’s star.

“They got the orbitals, too,” Cody said, pointing to a smaller object in the distance. The orbitals were — had been — giant circular space stations — habitats for the half billion people who preferred to live in their own artificial atmosphere. He made a face. “I can’t tell about the planet —”

“Infrared,” Ellaz said.

“We can’t use power,” Cody said.

“Passives,” Ellaz replied, tapping a command into the shuttle’s computer only to have her hand smacked away by Cody.

“No power!” Cody hissed at her.

Ellaz put her fingers in her mouth and glared at him. “You don’t know —”

“I don’t!” Cody agreed. “And until we do, we’re going to be a piece of debris.”

“If they can track IR, they can see our heat,” Ellaz said.

“Which is why we’re staying close to the freighter,” Cody said. “We’ll be in the thermal shadow.”

Passage:
Cody didn’t need to be told twice. He pointed to Ellaz’s helmet. “We need to go in,” he said, pulling his helmet over his head.

They entered a dark world.

Edie? Cody thought. He felt Ellaz’s “hand” touch his in the simulation and he gave hers a quick comforting squeeze in response.

In the distance, they heard giggles. Cody “tugged” Ellaz behind him as he raced toward the sound.

We can’t get caught! Ellaz warned him just as he was about to jump down a hole that appeared suddenly before them.

Edie! Cody called out. “Edie!” he said out loud. “Can you hear us?”

Play, play, play! Laugh, laugh, laugh! It sounded like two voices, singing in chorus. Cody turned toward Ellaz and imagined her in front of him.

What do we do? Ellaz said.

Rope, Cody said, pulling a rope out of the air. Tie it around me, I’ll go in.

Ellaz considered his suggestion and started tying one end of the rope around her waist. This is a really stupid idea, you know.

What’s yours? Cody asked.

Build a bot to find them, Ellaz replied, snugging her knot tight.

Okay, Cody thought back, raising his hands out in front of him and sketching out a shape. Ellaz nodded, moved to join him, adding arms and a head. In a few moments they created a standard hand bot. Okay, boy, go find Edie! Bring them back to us!

Only the bot came back moments later holding one of its arms with the other. When Ellaz and Cody noticed it, the bots head fell off its shoulders and it collapsed into nothingness.

They got swords? Ellaz asked.

I’m going, Cody declared, imagining a shield on his right arm.

I’m following, Ellaz said, pushing him forward.

They went down the hole. They fell for a long time, following the sing-song voices.

When they landed, they found themselves on a pile of old diapers.

Ew! They thought in unison. The voices weren’t too far away.

They found two little girls in a meadow throwing leaves at each other and singing, Ring Around the Rosie, Pocket Full of Posies! Ashes, Ashes, We All Fall Down!

What’s that song? Ellaz said. I feel like I know it.

Passage:
“Captain, if you want, we’ll get you a seat on Wasp,” Nora offered. “Or my ship, Phoenix.”

“Or we could put you in command of the array and the mines,” Cody said. “You wouldn’t need anything big or fast but —”

“Deal,” Admiral Cartwright said. “And that’ll be me.” He pointed a finger to Captain Forster. “Put her in command, please.”

“Adam,” President Hanlan said, glancing toward Cody, “they built their ships in eight days. How many ships could we build in thirteen?”

“The ring design is owned by Edie Crump,” Nora said. “We can license it to you.”

“When there’s a fire, young lady, you don’t argue over the hose until after it’s out,” President Hanlan told her. “But we’ll take as many shares as you’re willing to give and license the fees.”

“She should be here in another thirty-six odd days,” Nora said. The others glanced at her. “Backup. So they’re going Warp Five.”

“In the same design?” Captain Forster asked.

“No, we trimmed down from eighteen shuttles to three for this build,” Nora replied.

“Admiral,” Admiral Cartwright said to Cody, “I know you need to stay here until your environmental unit is replaced, is there any chance we can keep your partner here, too? It’d help a lot in planning.”

“Gail can handle it,” Nora murmured to Cody. Then she smiled, “And we’ve got some catching up.”

“Let us check with Commodore Eber and we’ll get back to you,” Cody said. “Particularly, Admiral, we should —”

“People,” President Hanlan said, rising from his chair, “I think we’ve got a plan. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I’ve got a lot of calls to make.” He turned to Admiral Cartwright. “Admiral, do you accept Admiral Ford as Screen Commander?”

“Yes, yes of course,” Admiral Cartwright said. Then, he said to Cody, “Sir, how soon can we get you with our engineers?”

“Let me check with my fleet, let them know what’s up and…” he glanced to Nora “... say about three hours from now?”

“Excellent,” Adam Cartwright agreed, nodding to Captain Forster.

“We’re going to want to get building as quickly as we can,” Emma Forster said.

Passage:
There was a loud blast and the alien caterpillar recoiled, turned, and fired its blue blast again. It moved out of the cargo bay, pursuing the shooter.

Cody hoped that the shooter got the alien.

A large, wrenching metallic sound followed immediately by a sigh energized Cody as nothing else could. The ship was tearing apart. He raced around to the side of the shuttle, pounded on the airlock and rushed inside.

“Wait!” A small voice cried out. He turned just in time to be slammed into by a small person. The girl. “Now, go, go, go!”

#

Is my butt really that small? Ellaz thought as Cody brought them back to the vanilla world of now.

Ellaz! The alien! You saw it, right? Cody said, surprised that that would be her first thought.

Yeah, Ellaz replied. But it doesn’t have to be an alien.

Really? And how many upright caterpillars do you know?

Cody… that looks an awful lot like a warp bubble, Ellaz said. The bristles? That’s where it hooks back into normal space.

A warp — how could anyone make a warp bubble that small? Cody demanded. Can you? Could your mom?

Ellaz shook her head.

And the spacer? He was turned to dust!

Actually, that could be — someone turned the warp into a weapon, Ellaz thought very quietly. That looks like what happens when a warp collapses. All the atoms are — well, it burnt out the lighter materials and left — just dust. Carbon dust.

And the blue flash? From the alien? Cody pressed. Then, Wait a minute! Your shield! When you were hit there was a blue flash.

The energy converter, Ellaz agreed. It’s still experimental. It shouldn’t flash at all, just convert energy, absorb it.

The alien, Cody said. Why was it on the ship? I mean, they blew the whole ship up, why did it have to be — Ellaz?

I… I think it came for us, Ellaz thought back in a very small voice. Mom and me.

Because of the energy converter, right? Cody guessed. But how would an alien know?

Passage:
“Hey!” Georgie Cumming shouted much to Cody’s surprise. “You try building a fricking fleet in eight days with only survivors!”

“Eight days?” Ed said, surprised. “Don, is that so?”

“Perhaps it’s best if we speak in private,” Don replied.

“Right,” Ed said. “I can’t get you all into Genny, how about I put eight of you there, and the others spread out among Harriett and Ivy?”

“Sure thing,” Don said. “Route me — I’m the starship Hermes and I’ve just idented my transponder — into Genny. Meet me there, will you?”

“Oh, definitely!”

A moment later, Wasp received routing instructions. He was glad to see that Nora’s Phoenix was routed in with them, as was Gail’s Persephone.

#

Three hours later, a docking tube was attached to the port side of Wasp and opened to let the ship’s air mingle with the space dock.

“Whew! What’s that smell?” The yard hand at the far end muttered. “ECLSS? Tell them we’ve got a smell down here at slip five.”

“Sorry about that,” Juan Suarez said, coming up the tube and nodding to the man. “Our ECLSS went south and we’ve been limping for the past several days.”

“I’ll say!” the yard hand replied. “Why didn’t you switch it out?”

“Only have the one,” Juan told him.

“One? Mister, I’m no expert but who the hell flies with only one ECLSS?”

“Those who built a starship in eight days,” Juan said, smiling and nodding to Chitty Brooks who’d followed him up and out of the ship. “Where can we get new filters?”

“Mister, with a dud like that, you ought just swap it out,” the yard hand told him. In a lower tone, he added, “And maybe think of getting another ship.”

“Can’t,” Juan said, shaking his head. “And, you know? She’s alright, our little Wasp. Stinky as she is.”

“How many souls?” the yard hand asked.

“Just six,” Juan said as Cody came up behind him. “This is our captain, Cody Ford.”

“Pleasure to meet you,” the yard hand said, extending his hand.

Cody shook it. “Can you help us see to resupply? And where do I find —” Cody looked down at his wristcomm “— Sector Main?”

Passage:
“Captain Ford, sir?” One of them said, clearly in awe. Cody nodded and the man smiled. “We’re really lucky to find you!”

“We need to get turned around,” Cody said, sounding much older than he was. “There are people out there —”

“Yes, sir,” the man said. “I’m Clive Bamber, in charge of SAR. We’ve got a preliminary list of targets. We’re passing the first set to you —” he glanced around the shuttle. “How many can you take at a time?”

“If you get me the fuel and air, we can handle thirty, easily,” Cody said. “Fifty in a pinch.”

“Right,” Clive said. “We’ve only got two cargo shuttles available —”

“Don’t you have a full fleet?” Cody interrupted.

“And we’d use it but…” Clive frowned. “I’m afraid we’re not going to need them right now.”

“That bad?” Cody said, his heart sinking.

“Worse,” Clive admitted. “So we’re going to turn you around now, in hopes that —”

“Right,” Cody agreed. “So why did you pull us down? Why not refuel on the pad above ground?”

Bamber made a face. “We can’t, sir. Our pads are built for shirtsleeve access. I’ve been trying to get an upgrade for — hell, for two decades now.”

“Okay,” Cody said. He waved a hand back into his shuttle. “Do you need anything else or should I look at your download?”

“Do you need anything else, sir?” Clive said.

“Can you get a crew to top off our stores and add as many medpacks as you think we’ll need?” Cody said after a moment.

“Sure!” Clive said, he raised his wristcomm and called out a few orders. “They’ll be here before we’re finished fueling.”

“How are you guys on that?” Cody asked, meaning their supplies of fuel.

“We have nominal stocks,” Clive told him with a frown. “But… for this!”

“Yeah,” Cody said. “So, we’ll track down the signals, do the SAR and then we’ll probably need to talk more.”

“Yes, sir,” Bamber agreed. He made a face. “But, sir, if you can get us a few good wins…”

“Yup, got it,” Cody said. He held out his hand. “Now, if you’ll excuse me, I want to check the trajectories.”

Controller Bamber waved him away.

“Yes, sir,” the man said. “I’m Clive Bamber, in charge of SAR. We’ve got a preliminary list of targets. We’re passing the first set to you —” he glanced around the shuttle. “How many can you take at a time?”

“If you get me the fuel and air, we can handle thirty, easily,” Cody said. “Fifty in a pinch.”

“Right,” Clive said. “We’ve only got two cargo shuttles available —”

“Don’t you have a full fleet?” Cody interrupted.

“And we’d use it but…” Clive frowned. “I’m afraid we’re not going to need them right now.”

“That bad?” Cody said, his heart sinking.

“Worse,” Clive admitted. “So we’re going to turn you around now, in hopes that —”

“Right,” Cody agreed. “So why did you pull us down? Why not refuel on the pad above ground?”

“Do you need anything else, sir?” Clive said.

“That should —” the yard hand muttered. He held up his own wristcomm. “Just tap yours to mine and we’ll get you tied in to our network, sir.”

Cody tapped his wristcomm as suggested and blinked when a route appeared. “I’ve got to be there in five minutes, it seems.” He turned to Chitty and Juan. “You two okay?”

“Yes sir,” Chitty said. “We’ll get right on the gig list, you don’t worry.”

Cody smiled and rushed off, following the directions on his wristcomm.

“Admiral Ford,” Don Hartman said when Cody entered the spacious room that was marked Sector Main, “this is Ed Hanlan. He’s the president.”

“Of Quark Approach?” Cody asked, wishing he’d checked his wristcomm before entering.

“No, sonny, of the whole damned system,” Ed Hanlan told him with a growl and a look toward Hartman. “Ain’t he supposed to be in diapers, still?”

“Not since Meath,” Don Hartman said. “I forwarded you the vids.”

“I don’t believe ‘em,” Ed Hanlan said. “And I don’t believe the ones from Deneb, either.” He sucked in a breath before shaking his head. “At least I didn’t, until I saw those damned ships you all brought in.” He glanced to Cody. “Do you know how many safety rules you violated?”

“We had to get here, sir,” Cody said. “To warn you.” And Ellaz, with much glee, had informed him that they were in violation of at least six hundred and seventy-three Quark starship regulations. Cody blew out a sigh. “We lost two ships,” he said, glancing to Hartman.

“Yeah, I saw,” Don said with a sigh of his own.

“You built thirty ships in eight days,” Ed Hanlan said. “You broke most of the rules — particularly the one on speed — to build them and get here, in fricking shuttles to warn us.” Cody and Don nodded. “Okay, you’re here, now what?”

“You’ve got nothing to stop them,” Don Hartman said. “They’re going to get the jump on you —”

“It will take them about five hours to destroy your system,” Cody said. “It took three to get Deneb —”

“Less my hab,” Don corrected. “There are, as of when we left, only five hundred million people left in the system.”

“Ten, here,” Ellaz said. “How many diapers are used each day?”

“For the babies? Each uses about two point five,” Jacob replied.

“Okay so fifteen days times two point five times —?”

“Twenty-four,” Jacob supplied, referring to the number of babies.

“Is nine hundred, right?” Ellaz said. Jacob ran the numbers through his wristcomm and nodded.

“And we’ve got three hundred and twenty-two,” Jacob told her.

“So, we’ve got to find more diapers,” Ellaz said. She sighed, “Jacob, where do we find diapers?”

“I don’t know,” Jacob admitted glumly. He was spacer born, like Ellaz.

“They have these places where they sell supplies, called stores,” Ellaz told him, trying not to sound too pedantic. And failing. “Check with the computers, find the stores, see which ones are intact and send a crew out to get them.”

“Okay,” Jacob said. “Should I ask Mr. Bamber or Miz Collins?”

“No,” Ellaz said. “Just tell them that Nora said we need them.” Ellaz frowned. “How about formula and baby food?”

Jacob blinked. “Uh, that’s next on the list.”

“The same answer,” Ellaz said. “Can you do it?”

Jacob swallowed. He was only seven but he was smart. And he didn’t want to disappoint Ellaz. He nodded jerkily.

“If you’ve got a problem, just talk with Nora,” Ellaz said. “She’ll straighten it out.”

Ellaz’s comm beeped. It was Cody. Training.

On the way, Ellaz texted back.

#

“We get to play watchers this time,” Cody said as Ellaz entered the Simulations Lab.

“And we get to fly starships!” little Jasmine chortled, fingering the helmet in her lap excitedly.

Edie smiled at Cody and Ellaz and tapped two chairs. “You guys just need to watch,” she told them. “But —”

“Bail you out if it goes wrong, right?” Cody guessed.

“We’re going to run through the same simulations you did yesterday,” Edie said. “It should be no problem.”

“Okay,” Ellaz said. She smiled at them. “Have fun! We’ll have drinks ready.”

It didn’t work out that way. They were good in the Warp Two simulation and slightly better in the Warp Four but when they got to Warp Six —

“What’s that mean?” Ellaz said, pointing to a flashing red light on one of the computers.

“Warning, warning!” A computer voice cried. “Interface inconsistency!”

“Warp Four, out and back,” Edie called out.

This time it was easier because they had experience.

“Warp Six, but watch the ring,” Edie told them when they’d come back.

It was a lot, watching the systems and the ring.

Can we create a monitor? Ellaz thought. Cody got an image of something constantly checking on pressure, temperature, deformations.

Sure, Cody thought. He tightened his grip on Ellaz’s “hand” and started thinking furiously. They fell into a small space of time between everything else they were doing to play a game of building the monitor.

“Cody! Ellaz!” Edie called to them urgently. “What? Where are you?”

Here, Cody thought back. We were just —

“Don’t take your mind off the ring!” Jasmine cried. “You’ll blow up!”

— building a monitor, Ellaz said, pulling their new software interface into their view. Hang on, it’s going to POST.

“POST?” Edie repeated.

Power-On Self-Test, Cody translated.

“What’s it for?” Edie asked. Then she must have pulled up the schematics. “You’re going to trust a computer with the — huh, this could work!”

POST complete, all systems nominal, the software replied.

Engage, Cody and Ellaz thought together. The new display in their virtual world blinked to life with data flickering on its console. Ellaz and Cody pushed the software monitor into their command code — and it took over monitoring the warp ring. They’d built it so that it would alert on caution and act on emergencies — pulling power, balancing thermal output, and regulating the anti-matter flows.

“You two are three sigma, you know,” Edie observed moments later.

Compatible? Cody thought.

“Yes, and that’s really good,” Edie said. “You’ll probably get better the more you work together.”

Ellaz’s ghost hand squeezed his. He squeezed back.

“Okay, ready for Warp Eight?” Edie asked.

Sure, they thought together.

#

Cody came out from the mind-link gasping and drenched in sweat. Ellaz, beside him, was the same.

“Here, drink this,” Jasmine said, passing a water to Cody. Edie was doing the same for Ellaz. “It’s electrolyte, you lost a lot of moisture.”

“Why?” Cody asked, after draining the drink in one long gulp.

“Well, you were in there for six hours,” Jasmine said. “And it’s work.”

Edie looked impressed.

“Shuttle pilots do stuff like that,” Cody said to Jasmine triumphantly.

“Quick thinking,” Edie agreed, nodding to Cody. “I’ll bet you were a great help on ship.”

Cody grinned, not wanting to admit that he’d barely been on the ship before there was no ship to be on.

“Okay,” Clive said. “I think what we need to do is start a more comprehensive inventory, looking for food and air.” The others nodded. “The spaceport here is a good place to start.”

“I’ve got a couple of possibilities,” Jasmine said. Cody and Ellaz shot her a look. “That’s why I was using the cameras,” she explained.

“Do we have a list?” Edie said, turning to Moira Collins. “Supplies, quantities?”

“For what?” Moira said. She waved a hand around. “Adding in these twenty-one, we’ve got five hundred and forty-six survivors.”

“And food for five hundred,” Clive added somberly.

“What will they do with the babies?” Nora asked, eyeing the others nervously. No one answered. “They can’t — they just can’t —”

“Cryofreeze?” Moira asked. Then she frowned. “But we don’t have the facilities and —”

“If we go back, Mr. Bamber, what’s going to happen to these kids?” Nora asked. “Should we go back?” Then her mouth tightened. “I’m not going back if I can’t save the kids.”

“Right,” Cody said. He looked around. “So what we need —”

“Is a ship!” Ellaz said, turning to him and beaming.

“We’ve got a ship,” Cody reminded her, pointing to the deck of the Wasp.

“No, a real ship!” Ellaz said. She turned to Edie. “Could we make one?”

Edie was silent for a long moment. Then, she said, “You’d need —”

“We’ve got a shipyard,” Cody said. “What else do we need?”

“About ten thousand trained engineers,” Clive Bamber said.

“How big a ship do we need?” Ellaz asked. “Enough for a hundred, maybe?”

The AMC — amsee — that Cody had on tow behind Wasp would be the first construction element. What was hardest — and coolest — was the maze of connecting passageways between the various shuttles. He’d been right, he could get five shuttles ready in a single day so now he had the Warehouse bots setting up another twenty.

Ten days. And then… well, they’d see. By the time Moira got back with the others, they’d be down to seven days.

#

The bots were good, but they needed someone to check up on them. Some of the bots had been damaged in the attack and it took Cody a while — and mistakes — to separate the good from the bad.

“You know,” Edie said the next day, “if we’re building one we could build two.”

“Don’t we need —?” Cody began. He was going to say “ring material” but he realized that they only needed half as much as a regular freighter because they were only using one warp ring.

“You need to help Nora,” Ellaz said when Cody came in from repairing another ailing bot. She grabbed his arm and tugged him along behind her.

Nora looked up from changing a squalling baby, her face distraught, her hair unkempt.

“I got another volunteer,” Ellaz said, smiling to her.

Cody waved to Nora even as Ellaz bolted off. “What do you need?”

“Everything!” Nora cried. She pointed to the half-diapered baby. Cody took one look and finished the job. While he did, he started thinking.

“You know,” Cody began, “some of the bots might be able to —”

“I’ll take anything!” Nora said, dropping into a chair and looking around wildly. “What could they do?”

“Well, the right ones could diaper and feed,” Cody guessed. He thought for a moment and nodded firmly. If the bots could run wiring at micrometer levels, they could be programmed to change diapers. And clean dirty bottoms, too. Cody looked around and shouted, “Ellaz! You’ve got a job!”

“Really, what?” Ellaz called back from halfway down the corridor.

“I need you to program baby bots,” Cody shouted back, smiling down at the little boy who’d winced at his bellow.

“Baby bots? Don’t we have enough — you mean to clean them?”

“Pirates!” Other Cody snorted, shaking his head at Ellaz. Cody was used to Other Cody — as he called the simulation — and somewhat hopeful that if anything happened to him, his alter-ego would be able to help Nora raise their kids. Of course, that wouldn’t be this Cody because if anything happened to Wasp it would undoubtedly destroy their computers, too.

“They couldn’t be very good, given that they’ve stolen nothing from us,” Georgie said. Ellaz and Other Cody exchanged looks. Georgie noticed. “What?”

“Nothing,” Cody said, “just an inside joke.”

“Okay,” Georgie said. “So, we’re ruling out pirates?” The others nodded in agreement. “Refugees? That’s still a possibility?” Cody nodded. “So what are they looking for? A new homeworld?”

“Why would they attack ours if that was the case?” Gail’s ghost asked. “If they’re running, why would they slow down to hit us?”

“They’re aliens, they don’t have to make sense,” Ellaz said.

“No,” Cody said. “I think they do.”

Georgie, who’d turned her attention back to her 3D chess game with Ellaz, tipped her king over and said, “Show me.”

Ellaz grinned at her, righted the king and showed the next three moves that ended with the king in checkmate.

Georgie sat back, stared at the board, stared at Ellaz’s ghost and nodded. “Good, good,” she said to herself. “Want another?”

“Sure,” Ellaz said and the board was reset with the pieces all back in their starting places.

“Where’d they come from?” Cody said. “They seem to be — were they on a straight line course when they attacked Meath?”

“We don’t know,” Ellaz said. She pursed her lips and shot a look to Georgie. “Something might have distracted them. Maybe they —”

“They’re denying us to their enemy!” Gail said with sudden certainty. “They don’t care about us, they just don’t want the others to get us.”

“Others?” Georgie said, moving her piece. “Now there are two alien species? In three hundred years of space travel, we haven’t found any.”

“What if one of the aliens was destroying the others?” Gail asked. “I mean, look at Meath — a hundred years from now, will anyone know that it was inhabited?”

She moved closer to him. “Thanks for that,” she said in a lower voice, “I don’t think we could have got out.”

“Yeah,” Cody said, knowing that she meant their mind-link. “But we got good plans and now we have a chance.”

“And we know what the attackers used,” Ellaz agreed.

“What the aliens used,” Cody corrected her.

Ellaz shook her head. “We don’t know that for certain.”

“Why would humans destroy the whole solar system? Kill nearly two billion people?”

“And if this grav lance fails?” Eric asked.

“That’s why we’re here,” Cody said. “Because if it fails, there are twenty-four of us and over five hundred million on the spacehab Elantra, which we think will be the last target.”

“Okay,” Scott Ellis said, “And?”

“You want to ram them, right?” Eric Doohan guessed. He shook his head.

“We’ve got the shuttles,” Gail pointed out. “We can abandon ship and pilot her remotely.”

Or let Ellaz pilot it, Cody thought grimly to himself. He didn’t have his helmet on so no one could hear him.

“And then we’ll be in shuttles, in the middle of a war,” Scott said. He frowned. Then nodded. “I’m okay with that.”

“I’d like for us to vote,” Cody said.

“All in favor?” Nora called out, raising her voice and then pouting apologetically at the baby in her arms.

“All right,” Cody said. “So, I’ll be taking Gail, Jacob, and Nora with me on Wasp.”

“No you won’t!” Nora said. “You’ll be taking Gail. I’m not leaving my Phoenix.”

Chapter Two

Chapter Two

Base Commander Trudy Wilson worked in an office marked Administrator Wilson. Apparently, the emergency had changed things.

“Yes, Captain, we’ve activated our site-wide emergency protocols,” Wilson said when Cody had glanced at the sign. “And, may I say, you are looking extremely good. Youthful. Did you say it was a shuttle accident?”

“Yes,” Cody lied smoothly. “Fortunately, the ejectors worked brilliantly.”

“And your son?” Wilson asked.

Cody made a sad face. “He didn’t make it.” He put a hand on Ellaz’s shoulder. “We’re the only survivors of our line.” Well, that wasn’t quite a lie — just the number of clone lines involved was greater than one.

“And you saved twenty-five souls,” Wilson said, sounding pleased but not looking it.

“Yes, ma’am,” Ellaz said. “And we’re happy to —”

“What?” Wilson demanded. She shot an accusing look to Clive Bamber, like the controller was responsible for all the trouble.

“Commander, what are the immediate plans?” Cody said.

“We’re still taking stock,” Wilson said. “And, if you’ll excuse me, I’ve got a lot of work to do —” she gestured toward her desk and the various flashing screens on her displays. “I’ll leave you with the controller, he’ll handle your needs.” She waved them away, adding, “Later, we might want to formally recognize your generous deeds.”

Or not, Cody thought to himself. Between him, Ellaz, and the survivors they’d rescued, they’d added twenty-five more mouths to be fed. On a base that was designed for scientists, researchers, and a small, itinerant population.

“We’re still trying to square away quarters for you,” Bamber apologized as they headed toward the main cafeteria.

“We could bunk on the Wasp,” Cody offered.

“Don’t you want a shower and a change of clothes?” Bamber asked solicitously.

“That’d be great,” Cody agreed. “But… don’t you have a gym? We could shower there.”

Bamber considered the request and nodded. “But… well, we’ve got your sizes on file, we can fit you out with a change and launder your current clothes.”

“Great!”

#

“Sleep on the shuttle?” Ellaz said sourly as they closed the hatch to the Wasp. “Why?”

“You figure it out,” Cody said, striding into the cockpit and firing up the controls.

“Can you keep a secret?” Cody said as they sat down next to her in the cafeteria. They were all eating rations, saving the better microwave food for the ships.

“What secret?” Nora asked.

“I’d like you to be the First Officer on Hope,” Cody said. She blinked in surprise. “You’re good with people. Everyone’s seen that.”

“So why does that have to be a secret?” Nora asked.

“Do you want the job?” Cody pressed.

“Not until I know the secret,” Nora said.

“Cody and Ellaz will run the ring,” Edie said. Nora nodded and gestured for her to continue. “They matched to three sigma.”

“That’s really good, isn’t it?” Nora said. She glanced at Cody. “You’ve got implants?”

“That’s not the secret,” Edie said. “But I suppose you shouldn’t tell the others, just yet.”

“What’s the secret?”

“Jazzy and I aren’t compatible,” Edie said. She held up a hand. “At least, not at Warp Nine!”

“So you’re going to go slower,” Nora guessed. Edie nodded. “In Revenge?” Edie nodded again. “Okay. And you don’t want people to know… why?”

“We don’t want to scare people,” Cody said. Nora’s eyebrow rose. “Not more than we all are already.”

“So you want me to lie to people?” Nora said. “Or just not mention that one ship has a better chance of blowing up than the other?”

“No, we’re about equal in the risks,” Edie said. “We’re not going Warp Nine in Revenge.”

“They can handle Warp Five,” Cody added. “Heck, they’re going to use the known routes and get to Quark in eighty-three days.”

“Quark?” Nora repeated.

“That’s part of the secret,” Edie said. “Redundancy.”

Nora considered that and nodded. “And the ship will be good for eighty-three days?”

“If not we’ll go to Deneb in thirty,” Edie said. “But if the ships are built to plan, they’ll stay together.”

Nora nodded. She’d seen the plans for the ships and approved. “Ninety days on ECLSS — that’s doable.”

“They’re rated for a full year,” Cody pointed out.

“You know, there’s a reason ships carry four separate units,” Nora objected. Then she sighed. “But we can’t build bigger. Not in time.” Then she shot Cody a look. “I’m taking the babies.”

“Deep Space One, this is Wasp, twenty-three souls on board,” Cody radioed. “Returning to base.”

The reply took over two minutes to get back. “Roger, Wasp. Understand twenty-five?”

“Yes, we got lucky and found five trapped in an airlock,” Cody said.

“Come on back,” Bamber replied. “Can you send us the particulars?”

“Wilco,” Cody said. It would take them six hours to get back the farside of the moon Nettles; he figured that he’d wake Ellaz in three.

Edie nodded in understanding. Ellaz shot a look to Cody, “The last I heard, only one per cent test into implants.”

“Actually, half a percent,” Edie corrected her, smiling at Cody.

“And Jasmine?” Cody asked.

Edie’s smile twisted. “I may have rushed it,” she admitted. The other two blinked in surprise. “Oh, there’s nothing showing up on tests but… sometimes… well, it’s a mother’s right to worry!”

“Abnormal implant rejection symptoms include violence, extreme paranoia, and catatonia,” Ellaz recited.

“Also AI imitation,” Cody added.

“‘Lost in the clouds,’ we call it,” Edie said in agreement. “But Jazzy’s passed all her tests and —”

“She helped you with this new ring design,” Ellaz guessed. “It’s wider than the regular rings, right?”

“Wider and formed,” Edie said. “Instead of a simple ring, it’s got a parabolic curve forward, less so to the rear.”

“To project the fields,” Cody guessed. Edie smiled and nodded at him. He frowned. “If you extended the field far enough forward, could you make a lance?”

“A lance?” Ellaz said. “You mean an energy lance?”

Cody nodded.

“Possibly,” Edie said. “But why would you — oh!” She gulped down her food and glanced to the other two. “Are you coming?”

They raced back to the command center, put on their helmets and linked in to the main computer systems.

Five minutes later, they each pulled off their helmets, their expressions ashen.

“Warp lance,” Cody said.

“They used a warp lance,” Ellaz agreed. “They tore everything apart.”

“What about the planet?” Edie asked.

“The lances warped the atmosphere,” Cody said. “No one below had a chance.”

“If the gravity didn’t twist them to pieces, the radiation was instantly fatal,” Edie said. “But — did you see the size of them?”

“I only caught glimpses, just the edge of the lances,” Ellaz confessed.

“Interpolating from the lances to the warp, the ships had to be massive,” Edie said.

“I counted twenty-six,” Cody added.

“That’s the double of a prime number,” Ellaz said. Cody shook his head at her. “Well, it is!”

“Doesn’t mean anything,” Cody told her. “But I got a timing… I think. From first shot to last was less than two hours.”

“That’s not counting what they did out at Xerxes,” Edie added.

Cody waved a simulated hand around. “Go find out,” he said, waving to the computer interface. Cody turned his attention back to the view in front of them. Then, he said, “How do we see this?”

It’s an interpolation based on energy density, Ellaz replied. But — you think we could refine it? Turn it into some kind of radar?

Well, isn’t it? Cody said. And what if the computers get it wrong? For that matter, how are they seeing in warp?

Warp gravitics, Ellaz replied immediately, with a condescending tone. Honestly! Didn’t they teach you anything?

About shuttles and normal space, Cody reminded her.

When you’re in warp, you’re not completely cut off from the rest of the universe, Ellaz lectured. So we can look through to normal space and interpolate what’s in front of us, like big rocks and other hazardous clumps.

And the faster we go, the harder it is to see, Cody agreed. Which is why we award probabilities, make the images bigger and fuzzy.

Yes, Ellaz agreed. But that doesn’t help you detect warp bodies.

Wait a minute! Cody thought. Parts of a warp bubble hook back to normal space. He thought of the fuzzy alien he’d seen on Hornet. So there are traces back in normal spaces. Like little spikes or slivers.

But they’d be so small, Cody, you couldn’t separate them from space dust, Ellaz said.

Space dust traveling at warp speed? Cody countered.

Then you’d need a really large array and super high speed computers with imaging resolution that… Ellaz stopped. It could be done.

And we’re sort of doing it already, Cody thought back.

“Cody?” Nora’s voice came to him. “I’m ready to take over.”

“Hang on,” Cody told her, waving his hand. “Ellaz and I are onto something.”

Nora was silent for a long while. Then, “Okay, so let me take over and you two go pow-wow on your own.”

“Right,” Cody said. “Number One, I request relief.”

“Captain, you are relieved,” Nora said, her voice bright with emotion. He felt her tap him on the shoulder and she whispered, “Thanks.”

Cody nodded absently but his concentration was on Ellaz and the problem in front of them.

Cody found a layout of the shipyard and examined it. There were twenty slips — building sites — of which only ten had been occupied. “We found food, and… well, you might want to come see what we’ve got,” Bamber said. Cody frowned, remembering Ellaz’s worries.

“I’m in the middle of something,” Cody said. “Can you just tell me? Or send an image?”

Bamber sighed. “We found the shuttle bay,” he said. “Rather we found the shuttle warehouse. There are about —”

Cody perked up, tapped a command into the computer systems. There were ten ships on the building slips which meant, with a crew of roughly one hundred, there had to be four shuttles for each ship. Maybe they weren’t all here but…

“Forty shuttles?” Cody guessed.

“Only about twenty in this warehouse, at a guess,” Bamber replied. “And they’re in mothballs.”

“Mothballs?” Ellaz piped up.

“I mean they’re not prepped, they’re wrapped up for storage,” Bamber replied.

“Then why didn’t you say so?” Ellaz murmured acerbically.

“Spacers know mothballs,” Cody said.

“Not this spacer,” Ellaz corrected him.

“So…” Cody typed in a series of queries, tied it in with Bamber’s location and said, “If you go from there across the field, you’ll find Warehouse Two. There should be another twenty shuttles there.” Of course they’d need fuel, charging, oxygen and… well, it was something.

“I’ll check it out, right after I pull up the systems in this other warehouse,” Bamber replied. “And Captain?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t fall asleep!”

Cody shook his head and looked back at the screens in front of him.

Plans. Tried-and-true. Because building a starship wasn’t just science, it was art, too.

They needed a power plant, no matter what. Preferably a “tried-and-true” plant and, more importantly, they needed one that was here, at the shipyards, ready to be installed. Only… there were only so many power plants lying around.

The power plant sized the ship. A big ship, a big power plant.

And all that depended on the size of the ship. There was no way they’d be able to build a two megatonne starship in less than four months. And they didn’t have four months. So, what was the biggest ship they could build in three weeks?
The computers didn’t have an answer to that. What was the fastest ship they could build?

Passage:
Hope shimmered in the space around it and then the ship slipped away from normal space and time.

#

“All systems nominal, thirty minutes into flight,” Nora reported. Then, “Whee!”

Cody grinned and smiled at Ellaz who nodded back, muttering, Amateurs.

Cody ignored her as they pulled more and more warp around them until they were finally registering Warp Nine.

“Five days,” Cody reported.

“Roger, five days,” Nora said. Then, “I don’t know about you, but I need to pee.”

Me too, Ellaz thought. Can you manage for a few minutes without me?

I’ve got the monitor running, Cody said in agreement. He felt Ellaz pull out of the comp-link and concentrated more on the “space” ahead of them, looking for any of the darker clumps that indicated a dangerous mass. The way was clear.

They were taking the standard Warp Five route out of Meath, only they were going much faster, of course. Warp Five was a mere 214 times the speed of light, they were traveling more than seven times faster than that. Fifteen hundred and sixteen times the speed of light.

Cody looked at the ring readings on his displays. All were green. Fuel consumption was… huh! A bit lower than imagined. He verified that they really were at Warp Nine but… yes, they were. So maybe the ring was more efficient than they’d guessed.

He pulled up a schematic of the warp bubble around them and grunted in approval when he saw that the end of the forward spindle was a good fifteen hundred kilometers in front of them. The rear was only a thousand kilometers behind them. And little Hope, not more than two hundred meters in length, was cocooned inside.

He felt Ellaz appear beside him. She grabbed his hand quickly and he squeezed back. It had become their secret handshake, here in the mind-link.

A-OK, Cody reported.

Good, Ellaz replied. I figured you could manage without me for a minute or two.

We’re going to have to sleep sometime, Cody reminded her.

You wish! They watched the ring temp, watched the energy flow, examined the warp bubble and were silently amazed. Warp Nine.

Yeah, Cody thought back.

Two hours later, Cody thought, Are you okay? I have to pee.

The trouble with mind-link was compatibility. Incompatible minds were so different that they couldn’t mind link at all. Minds with slight compatibility came across as harsh and high-pitched, draining. Ellaz’s mind was just right. She was still Ellaz, warts and all, but they weren’t painful warts.

Good connection, Cody told her. Her “hand” — it was imaginary — squeezed back in agreement.

“Okay, so acceleration? Direction? Navigation? Control?” Cody asked. Each question was answered by an overlay of displays. “Power?” Another display. “Astrogation links?”

Why is that different from Navigation? Ellaz asked.

“Because navigation shows where you are, Astrogation shows where you want to go,” Jasmine’s voice came back in answer.

“Almost, sweetie,” Edie said. “Astrogation includes warp buoys and other pointers. Particularly, you know that it’s problematic to warp through large masses, right?”

The greater the speed, the smaller the mass, Cody replied through the mind-link. We don’t want to bump into something that might smash us out of warp.

What if we do? Ellaz asked.

Three possibilities, Cody replied. We drop out of warp, we drag the object behind us and slow down, or — we go boom!

Okay, so let’s not do that, Ellaz said.

“Now, we’re going to do a quick run,” Edie said. “Set course for Deneb, power up to Warp Two then reverse course to Meath.”

Why Warp Two? Ellaz asked.

Baby steps, Cody told her. Ready?

Ellaz’s ghost hand squeezed his. Control and Power.

Cody didn’t need to hear more to know that she was going to handle the power and the controls. He checked their astrogation screen, verified with the navigation display and set their speed to Warp Two.

It took them a while to get the hang of Warp Two. At that speed, a lot of the stars were still visible. And, when in warp, they streaked by in an amazing display of reds and blues — reds where the stars were approaching them, blue where they were receding behind them.

“Very good,” Edie said. “And how’s the ring?”

Nominal, Ellaz replied. Cody agreed with her. The ring, taking anti-matter and twisting it into something that warped space, was not overheated, nor was there any sign of buckling or twisting which could render it inoperable.

“Ellaz?” Cody said, sipping his coffee. “If you’ve got a communicator, do you have a radar, too?”

“What?”

“A way to detect and range tachyons,” Cody explained. “Because every warp bubble gives them off, right?”

“Oh, Cody!” Ellaz exclaimed in awe. “That’s brilliant! And that’s why I woke you up!”

“You’ve got it?” Cody asked, sitting himself down in a chair with the hot breakfast tray and opening it up.

“No, but I will!” Ellaz cried gleefully. “Get ready and come forward!”

Cody ate slowly, freshened up, changed, and came forward to the cockpit, pulling on his helmet as he sat.

Look what we’ve got! Nora’s ghost cried gleefully. And Cody’s eyes went wide at the vista that exploded in front of him.

Is that real?

No, Nora said sadly, it’s a simulation. We need a couple of things —

Like a receiving ring, Ellaz added.

— before we could do this, Other Cody thought. But when we do —

What’s the range?

It varies, Ellaz said, the higher the warp, the further out we can detect it because higher warps produce more powerful tachyons.

See there? Nora said, pointing to a bright white blob in the distance. That’s fifty megatonnes at Warp Nine. And over there? That dark blue light? That’s a ship less than a hundred kilotonnes at Warp One.

Huh! Impressive, Cody thought. And how soon until we can build one of these?

Not just this, but the tachyon communicator, Ellaz added. When we get a shipyard with a good physics lab? About two months, we think.

There’s the question of ring size and power, Other Cody added. We’ve got a preliminary design but —

Accidents and such, Cody thought. Yeah.

But, Cody, this is… it’s dangerous, Nora’s ghost thought to him.

In the wrong hands, Gail agreed. We don’t want to give this away.

Not immediately, Other Cody thought. Because…

Well, if we’re right — wait a minute! Ellaz could we use this to spot those missing ships?

Only if they’re in warp, Ellaz replied. And they’re probably not.

But — what’s the probability that the aliens have this?

“I might sir,” Chitty told him with a wink. “I might.”

“Thanks but it’s months away,” Cody said.

“With babies, you can never be too early,” Juan told him.

“Well, sir, we’ll let you get back to work,” Chitty said in what was clearly a dismissal. “And we’ll be sure to bring Susan and Henry up to speed.”

Susan and Henry Lucks were a brother and sister pairing. Cody couldn’t believe that they were fifty-five and fifty-seven years old. Not that that was very old — even for a spacer — but it would be another forty years before he’d be close to their age. The two had volunteered, had come out of retirement, in part because they were good at their jobs and, sadly, because the rest of their family had been lost on the surface of Deneb.

“Sure, thanks,” Cody said.

“And if you ever want a game of chess…” Chitty offered.

Cody smiled and waved as he turned back to negotiate the tubing from ECLSS back up to his shuttle, Wasp.

#

Days and nights blurred together as Cody and his “crew of imaginary friends” — as ghost Nora liked to say — worked and reworked their plans for the upcoming fight.

“Cody, Cody, Cody!” Ellaz yelled the morning of their eighth day.

“Ellaz, Ellaz, Ellaz!” Cody repeated back, pushing off his covers and looking around — only to realize that she’d been talking over the speakers. “Is there an emergency?” He was pretty sure that she would have reacted differently if there had been — like fixing the problem and then letting him know later in her cocky, self-assured manner.

“No, of course not!” Ellaz replied. “But I’ve got it!”

“Got what?” Cody said, moving to the back of the main cabin and heated up some coffee and a breakfast tray. “And can it wait?”

“Well,” Ellaz sighed, “yes. It’s going to have to wait.”

“So why couldn’t I sleep longer?”

“Because I had to tell you,” Ellaz said. “I’ve got the tachyon communicator.”

Cody’s eyes went wide. “You do? Now?”

“No!” Ellaz said, irritated. “I’ve got the design. Do you want to see?”

“Can I eat and get dressed first?”

“I suppose,” Ellaz grumbled.

“No, of course not!” Ellaz replied. “But I’ve got it!”

“Got what?” Cody said, moving to the back of the main cabin and heated up some coffee and a breakfast tray. “And can it wait?”

“Well,” Ellaz sighed, “yes. It’s going to have to wait.”

“So why couldn’t I sleep longer?”

“Because I had to tell you,” Ellaz said. “I’ve got the tachyon communicator.”

Cody’s eyes went wide. “You do? Now?”

“No!” Ellaz said, irritated. “I’ve got the design. Do you want to see?”

“Can I eat and get dressed first?”

“I suppose,” Ellaz grumbled.

“I’ve got a better idea,” Ellaz said, around her gum. She fired up a comm link and set the shuttle’s main antenna searching. “We tap into the comms and see what we can see.”

“What? Why?” Cody said, blowing another bubble. He pulled it of his mouth, frowned at it critically, then threw it behind him, high in the air.

“Ew! What did you do that for?” Ellaz demanded.

“Going to microgravity. Don’t barf,” Cody said, adjusting the controls.

Ellaz closed her mouth tightly, glaring at him and chewing furiously.

“Is that gum ready?”

“How should I know?” Ellaz complained.

“Can you blow a bubble?” Cody said, repeating himself.

Ellaz tried. It burst. Cody shook his head and reached a hand out to her. “Give it to me.”

“What? You’re a barbarian!” Ellaz said. Cody ignored her, reaching into her mouth and pulling out the gum. With a frown, he popped the half-chewed piece into his mouth, passing her another stick.

“Get that one going,” Cody said, chewing and blowing out another bubble. He examined it, pulled it out of his mouth and threw it behind him.

“Patches,” Ellaz said with sudden enlightenment. “Why didn’t you say so?” She started chewing furiously on her new piece even as Cody started on a fresh stick.

“No time,” he told her.

“Does that really work?” Ellaz said. “I thought it was just a spacer story.”

Cody, turned the pack of gum to her. It was labeled, “Ford’s Fancy.” The fine print added, “Refreshing Life-saver. Guaranteed.”

“Any of the bubbles find an air leak and they’ll stretch out, dry up and change color,” Cody said with a hint of pride.

“Did you do that?” Ellaz asked, impressed.

Cody shook his head. “My grandsire.” He adjusted the cabin circulation to blow more air. “But it works.”

Ellaz offered him her next chewed piece. Cody took it, blew out his bubble and took her chewed gum to create a fourth floating balloon.

“They just killed everyone,” Ellaz said.

“I was there,” Cody said.

“No, I mean they went after any atmosphere, destroying it,” Ellaz said. “They didn’t care about any survivors, just the main infrastructure.”

“They got our ship,” Cody countered.

#

When they were done, they all — everyone except for the babies and the nurses, of course — suited up and wandered out to their ship. Hope looked like a really weird maze with tubes wandering all around the outside of the ECLSS, power, AMC, and propulsion units. There were also two big radio dishes — outsized because they were stolen from the hulks of freighters — attached fore and aft of the AMC.

“It looks like a bowl of spaghetti,” Nora announced as they stopped just short of the construction zone. “When are we placing the shuttles?”

“And the ring?” Ellaz added.

“We’re going to jack her up later tonight,” Cody said, checking the construction schedule. “Then we attach struts and slip the ring on them.”

“And the shuttles?”

“Day fourteen,” Cody said. “Then day fifteen —”

“We fly!” Nora said.

“Um, after we get all the supplies on board,” Cody said.

“I thought we’d agreed to put them in the shuttles,” Nora said.

“Food, consumables, yes,” Cody agreed. “But soil, plants, that sort of stuff —”

“If we’re just going for five days, do we really need that?” Jacob asked.

Cody shrugged. “Who says we’re only going to be gone five days?”

Jacob raised his spacesuit helmet up to peer at Cody.

“Yeah, Jake,” Ellaz added, “who says?”

“It’s best to be prepared,” Nora said in agreement. She glanced at her comm. “Okay, we’ve been out long enough, everyone back inside.”

“Oh, do we have to?” Gail complained. She waved a hand toward the ship. “I mean, she’s so pretty!”

“Radiation, squirt,” Nora said to her. “You don’t want to get too much.”

“Or you’d get sick,” Cody said. He turned back to the airlock.

Ellaz stumbled behind him, was steadied by Jacob and then grumbled, “I’m okay! I’m okay!”

They may have scouted the whole Fifth Quadrant, Nora thought.

Well, they only have twenty-five ships, Cody reminded them. And we’re going to do something about that.

“Not for a month,” Ellaz said. Cody shot her a look. “Well, smartass, as you could hack into the network, I could download the manifests of all the space stations. The next ship is the Twilight Star, scheduled to arrive from Earth in twenty-nine days.”

“Shit.”

“What? I mean that’s good, isn’t it?”

“How long does the food last?” Cody replied. “And… what if the aliens found us by tracking our ships?”

“Well, if you’re going to imagine the worst —”

“Ellaz, the worst has already happened,” Cody said. He gritted his teeth. “Man is spread out to ninety-three stars.”

“Ninety-two,” Ellaz corrected. “I doubt we’ll survive here long.”

“How long did it take the aliens to destroy everything?” Cody said. “Less than a day, certainly. So… if they’ve got fitl that we don’t understand, they could destroy us all in another ninety-two days.”

“That’s assuming they don’t have more ships and haven’t already attacked elsewhere,” Ellaz reminded him.

“Okay,” Cody said. “So we need to get out of here.”

“We need to build a starship,” Ellaz said.

“Yup,” Cody agreed. He frowned. “What if we could take the tanks from one of the farms? That’d give us fuel.”

“We still need a ship,” Ellaz said.

“We have a ship,” Cody said, waving a hand around them.

“A starship,” Ellaz reminded him. “I mean, can you make a shuttle into a starship?”

Cody frowned. Then he turned to her, “Whirly, can you?”

Ellaz was silent, tapping on her keyboard. She glanced over to him. “The fastest a starship has ever been built was twenty-two days. And that was at the Lunar yards in orbit around Old Earth. And…” she tapped some more “... they had a total construction crew of thirty-three thousand seasoned builders.”

Cody considered that. Then he said, “We need to get out of here.”

“Yes,” Ellaz agreed.

“We need to go to Carlow, to the bases,” Cody said.

“But they’re gone, we saw that!”

“You said the aliens attacked the habitats,” Cody replied.

“I said the attackers destroyed the habitats,” Ellaz corrected. “You said they were aliens.”

Cody ignored her, typing frantically on his keyboard. A moment later he sat back and smiled at her. “You ready for a trip?”

Cody nodded.

Tom Walker strode in, looked for Brenda Hogg and marched over to her, standing above her with his tray in his hand while he rattled off a quick bunch of comments.

Cody frowned. Brenda seemed to sag under Walker’s tirade. She spotted Cody, grit her teeth and shook her head — begging him not to get involved.

Nora and the four engineers handled them with growing confidence even as the three nursery attendants managed the twelve babies with aplomb. Of course, the nursery was on-going, the only difference was that they added the chatter from the emergencies to the mix, to see how the kids would handle it.

“We are going to mute that klaxon!” Mandy Barquess said when they came up to their first debrief. “It set all the babies off.”

“But what if it was a real emergency?’ Scott Ellis replied. “What then?”

“Um,” Nora began slowly, “in the case of a catastrophic emergency in warp…”

“We die,” Ellaz said. She shrugged. “I mean, we’ve got all the shuttles as lifeboats but… well, we’d best not have that sort of emergency.”

“Because we’d be drifting somewhere in interstellar space,” Nora agreed with a slow sigh. Then she brightened, “Which is why we practice.”

“We should move it,” Cody said with a lump in his throat. “She’s slightly radioactive and… well, there’s nothing more we can do for her.”

“Put her in Shuttle Ninety,” Scott Ellis suggested. “Let her go down with the ship, if we have to.”

“I think we should move her regardless,” Nora said, giving Cody an apologetic look.

“And what about her ghost?” Thomas Wong asked.

Cody shot him a look.

Thomas smiled. “Do you think we didn’t know?”

The others smiled and exchanged glances.

“She’s kind of a busy-body, you know,” Eric Doohan said. “She sent me messages, after she’d died.” He shrugged. “I didn’t have much to do, so I traced them. To the ship’s core memory.”

“I’ll explain later,” Cody promised. “But, please! Don’t call her a ghost. The longer she can feel real, the longer she’ll last.”

The others considered that and nodded. “Right,” Eric Doohan said to himself, “I won’t think about that too much, if you don’t mind.”

“In the meantime,” Cody said, “I’d like to have everyone think about abandoning ship.” He raised a hand. “It’s a last resort but we should be prepared.”

“Okay,” Franny said. “So we keep the babies here. The bots stay with them. But I don’t know how to navigate or fly this shuttle.”

“We’ll get you help if it comes to that,” Cody said. He turned to Jacob. “Jacob?” Jacob nodded.

“And if we get the alien ship with the lance? And the others flee? What then?” Eric Doohan asked.

Cody shook his head.

“Then we’ve won,” Nora said, smiling at them all. “We’ll deal with it after.”

“We win, we’ll be heroes,” Eric noted.

“We win, we’ve got to send someone back to Meath,” Thomas said.

“And we’ve got to send someone on to Quark, just in case,” Gail added.

“And we’ve got to fight back,” Cody said. “We win and I’m going to get them. All of them.”

Passage:
But the greater the rewards, the greater the risks. Particularly for ships carrying information. Pirates could catch them, steal their information, and use it for their gain. Which is why most couriers carried a squad of armed men and some even carried small space lasers. Of course, pirates didn’t need live crews if they could get a ship’s computers intact.

Deneb and Meath had made an agreement that they would provide some warships to patrol the normal warp routes. What that usually meant was that a warship would take on the identity of a regular courier — and woe to any pirate that tried to stop them!

Sixty-seven ships reported missing or lost. And that was up from forty-eight the year before and thirty-seven the year before that. The only reason they had the data was because it was a standard part of all ships’ downloads — a list of missing ships so that possibly they might be found.

Okay, this is getting nowhere, Cody thought to himself. Do we have any increases in specific routes or —

Cody broke off as a display appeared to his left and he saw plots of the reported missing ships as lines in three-dimensional space. All that was known was point of departure and point of non-arrival. Nothing popped out at him.

But, Ellaz, who had popped up the display, added, here are the same losses ordered by time.

The view changed. What was particularly alarming was that the older reports were further away from Meath. The newer reports were beyond Deneb in the other direction.

Scouts, Cody thought. They sent scouts.

To steal ships, Other Cody agreed. Cody looked up at him and saw Nora standing beside him, smiling.

We want to look at the oldest reports, Cody thought. Those nearest the warp line from Meath to Deneb but backwards, away from —

Ellaz changed the display. There were three dots. They’re all recon ships.

Title: Cody's War - Flight of the Hope 13pt 5.5x8.5 Glossary Cast
Chapter: OEBPS/Cody's_War_-_Flight_of_the_Hope_13pt_5.5x8.5_Glossary_Cast-9.xhtml

Passage:
It’s a nursery rhyme, Cody replied. Then, It’s from the time of the Bubonic Plague.

Ellaz looked at Cody and a tear dripped down her eye. They’re sad!

Right, Cody replied. They got pulled down by their worries.

No time, Ellaz thought, rushing over to the taller of the two girls and wrapping her arms around her. Come on, it’s time to go home!

Home! Home? No home! All gone! Edie’s childlike voice came back to them. She started howling in despair. Beside her, Jasmine added her wails.

Edie, Jasmine, come on, it’s time to get out of here, Cody thought. We’ll get you drinks and some rest —

He and Ellaz shared an instant gestalt thought, running through data that the simulator provided like a flood, and realizing that Edie hadn’t had nearly enough rest in the past several days. Also, she was an adult, she felt the loss of so many billions of people more thoroughly than either of them.

They pulled the two out of the doldrums and back to reality.

Red flashing computer lights stopped flashing and the room got quiet. Cody pulled off his helmet, raced to the small fridge and pulled out two drinks just as Ellaz was pulling the helmet off of Jasmine.

“Here,” Cody said, passing one drink to Edie and the other to Ellaz who fed it to Jasmine.

“We’re doomed,” Edie said as she tugged a desultory sip from her drink. “Doomed.”

“No, we’re not!” Ellaz said. “You two got sucked into a hole, that’s all.”

“We’re not compatible,” Edie said, tears flowing down her cheeks as she looked to her daughter. “I’m sorry! I never thought that —”

“It’s okay, Mommy,” Jasmine said with forced humor. “It was our first time, we’ll work it out.”

“No,” Edie said, “at least not right now.” She turned to Cody. “You two are the only ones watch rated.”

“So we split up, Cody on one ship and —”

“No,” Edie said. “That won’t work. You’re going to need two of you, one has to sleep sometime, you know.”

“We could take stimulants —” Ellaz said.

“No,” Cody said. “There are too many side effects.”

Ellaz pursed her lips but said nothing.

“We don’t need two ships,” Cody said. “One was a spare.”

Passage:
She’s right on the probabilities, Ellaz admitted. There’s a far greater chance that this is one simple traitor and not a whole world or combine. She waved a hand toward the main cabin. Go on, get your coffee! You’re no use without it.

Cody nodded, turned around and walked through the virtual world back to the main cabin with his helmet on. He found the coffee, grabbed it and — his hands slipped through it.

Cody, you’ve got to bring a copy into the virtual world with you, Other Cody told him.

Cody reached again, imagining the real cup and its simulation together. This time he felt the warmth of the cup and picked it up. He raised it to his lips and sipped. Ah!

Thanks, OC, Cody thought to his ghost.

My pleasure, OC thought back.

Back in his seat, Cody pulled up the first of the virtual files. He skimmed all sixty-seven missing ship reports, some dating back to fourteen months prior.

Traders and scouts were a rare breed. Cody’s freighter, Hornet, was part of a corporation with set routes, times, and cargoes. The traders were much smaller ships — usually not more than two hundred k-tons. They carried rare cargo and traded information. They flew at higher warps than freighters because time was money, particularly when it came to selling information to the highest bidder. Most traders rarely went faster than Warp Six which still gave them a nearly two week advantage in time over regular freighters. So they could carry news quicker. Those ships willing to risk — and pay for — Warp Seven could have a nineteen-day advantage over regular freighters.

Some small ships were used as couriers, particularly by the larger interstellar corporations that spanned multiple worlds and they’d even go as high as Warp Eight which would get them the twenty light-years from Deneb to Meath in just seven point one days — not quite the five days that Hope had done at Warp Nine but still very respectable, especially when compared to the twenty-nine point two days required at Warp Five.

“Well, sir, the way I see it there are three possibilities,” Jacob said, thrilled to be distracted and doing something useful.

“Yes?”

“First, we arrive in time to warn Deneb,” Jacob said. “Second, we are too late. Third, we arrive just as they’re being attacked.”

“If we’re too late?” Cody asked.

“The first thing we need to do, sir, is see if we can get refueled. Second thing, resupplied,” Jacob said. A glowing list appeared in the simulation in front of Cody’s eyes. “After that, I recommend Search And Rescue but —”

“But what?”

“Well, sir, should we do that or head on to Quark to warn them?” Jacob said. “I know Revenge is heading there but at Warp Five, only. At Warp Nine, we could get there in… just a bit under nine days.”

“And fuel?”

“Well, sir, we’d need to swap our AMC,” Jacob said.

“And if we have no swap?” Cody asked.

“Um… well, according to our calculations, we were about thirty per cent more efficient than planned,” Jacob said after a moment. “Which will mean that we have about thirty thousand kg of AM left.”

“And?” Cody prompted, glancing to the view of warp space in front of him, checking for any upcoming “clumps.”

“Well, we mass only two hundred and fifty three k-tons, sir,” Jacob said. “That might explain our performance.”

Cody grinned. “Probably. And…?”

“Well, our mass ratio with 30 k-tons AM would be 0.1185,” Jacob said. “Our initial mass ratio was 0.3952 although we’d calculated on 0.250 —”

“Jacob,” Cody interrupted. “What can we do with 30 k-tons of anti-matter?”

“Um…” Jacob brought up a routine, entered a few parameters and then said brightly, “About Warp 3.56, sir.”

“And? Time to Quark at that speed?” Cody asked.

“One hundred and forty-one point six days, sir,” Jacob reported glumly.

“And back to Meath?” Cody prompted.

“Eighty point nine days, sir,” Jacob replied. “But we’ve got consumables for the next thirty-five days.”

“So, neither approach is acceptable,” Cody agreed.

“Are we going to die?” Jacob asked miserably.

“Some day,” Cody said. “But… look what we did at Meath. We built a starship and in… Eighteen hours and forty-nine minutes and twenty-one seconds, we’ll get to Deneb.”

“Gum?” Edie Crump said, turning to Cody. She swiveled her head around the cabin and spotted the two hull patches. “You used gum to patch your ship?”

“We used gum to find the holes,” Cody said. “We put proper patches on when we’d found them.”

Edie looked impressed.

“Shuttle pilots do stuff like that,” Cody said to Jasmine triumphantly.

“Quick thinking,” Edie agreed, nodding to Cody. “I’ll bet you were a great help on ship.”

Cody grinned, not wanting to admit that he’d barely been on the ship before there was no ship to be on.

“Okay,” Clive said. “I think what we need to do is start a more comprehensive inventory, looking for food and air.” The others nodded. “The spaceport here is a good place to start.”

“Because it’s not nearly as trashed as the rest of the base,” Ellaz agreed.

“I’ve got a couple of possibilities,” Jasmine said. Cody and Ellaz shot her a look. “That’s why I was using the cameras,” she explained.

“Do we have a list?” Edie said, turning to Moira Collins. “Supplies, quantities?”

“For what?” Moira said. She waved a hand around. “Adding in these twenty-one, we’ve got five hundred and forty-six survivors.”

“And food for five hundred,” Clive added somberly.

“What will they do with the babies?” Nora asked, eyeing the others nervously. No one answered. “They can’t — they just can’t —”

“Cryofreeze?” Moira asked. Then she frowned. “But we don’t have the facilities and —”

“If we go back, Mr. Bamber, what’s going to happen to these kids?” Nora asked. “Should we go back?” Then her mouth tightened. “I’m not going back if I can’t save the kids.”

“Right,” Cody said. He looked around. “So what we need —”

“Is a ship!” Ellaz said, turning to him and beaming.

“We’ve got a ship,” Cody reminded her, pointing to the deck of the Wasp.

“No, a real ship!” Ellaz said. She turned to Edie. “Could we make one?”

Edie was silent for a long moment. Then, she said, “You’d need —”

“We’ve got a shipyard,” Cody said. “What else do we need?”

“About ten thousand trained engineers,” Clive Bamber said.

“How big a ship do we need?” Ellaz asked. “Enough for a hundred, maybe?”

“And we don’t have three days,” Cody said. “Or… maybe we do.”

“What?” Georgie said.

“Well, when we get in system, let’s see what’s what, particularly with the rest of the fleet. Maybe we can get the nice people of Quark to let us use some of their slips,” Cody said. “After all, we’re going to save their planet.”

“And in three days… what?” Georgia asked.

“Well, not all ships have to leave at the same time,” Cody said. “We could send one group out ahead while the others —”

“You’re thinking we can build the tachcomms?” Georgie said. “How?”

“Well,” Cody sighed. “It’s a long shot but if we could get our virtual crew to work with a fab lab —”

“And what about the power?” Georgie protested. “How does that work?”

“Look, all I want is a simple Morse system,” Cody said. “Nothing too powerful but something we could put on each ship —”

“No time, that’d take weeks,” Georgie objected.

“The command ships?” Cody suggested. He shook his head. “No, that won’t work.”

“But your flare, that might work,” Georgie said.

“Huh?”

“A set of big flashes,” Georgie said. “We could probably tow another AMC and set it up to —”

“Blow with a tachyon trigger!” Cody said. “If we put our ships out of range and set the array to look for the aliens, we’d get a flash that would warn us and they’d head for the wrong target.”

Cody found a dinner he could tolerate, heated his, grabbed some cutlery and found a table with chairs still around it. Ellaz joined him a moment later. Edie came over, glanced around and sat with them.

“So… implants?” Edie said in a quiet voice while stirring up her meal. She nodded to Cody. “Starship?”

“We were hoping,” Cody admitted.

“And energy?” Edie said, glancing to Ellaz. Ellaz hissed in surprise, forced her mouth to work in an attempt at a reply but was cut off by Edie’s raised hand. “I’m a ring master, I keep my eyes open.”

“No, why don’t you tell me?” Edie broke in.

“Yes,” Cody said.

“Who was your mother?” Edie asked in a softer voice. “I’ve worked with some Whirly’s in my time.”

“Elle Dann Triple Vonn,” Ellaz said.

Edie’s eyes went wide. “EDTV?” Ellaz nodded. “And you are…?”

“Ellaz Conn Venier Four,” Ellaz replied. Cody blinked at her. “The other names are mutation listings.”

“Aren’t the CV4’s supposed to be really good at math?” Edie said. Ellaz nodded. “And you?”

“I’m still learning,” Ellaz admitted.

“You’ve got implants,” Edie told her.
